1778014: I was Instructor Pilot, low time student pilot was in the left seat. We were practicing ground reference maneuvers, specifically S-turns across a road. Except we used the river as a 'road.' My thinking was that no traffic should be near us if we are 1,000 feet AGL (1;200MSL) at that location. Boy, was I wrong.My student had completed a few S-turns across the river and was just turning westbound to cross the river again when I noticed a target on our ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast) in display less than a mile to our right (north) -- actually, much less than a mile -- showing 100 feet below us, coming straight toward our right rear quarter. It looked like a 90-degree track compared to ours, meaning the offending aircraft was heading roughly 190 while we were heading approximately 270 (all magnetic). I took control immediately, raised the right wing, and looked intently to our right rear and all other parts of our right side in an effort to make visual contact. Alas, no joy.Since the ADS-B track showed he was likely to pass behind us, I went full throttle in order to give the other aircraft the best chance of doing so. That appeared to work, but we only knew that when the target (after what seemed like an eternity) moved to our left rear on its same heading. Finally, we were diverging. We both looked in the direction of the target, still no joy. Never saw the guy. Thank goodness for ADS-B in this case.Let me add that I was scanning for traffic the whole time my student was S-turning. Whenever he banked left, I took the opportunity to look under the raised (right) wing. When he turned right, the other raised wing. Nonetheless, no joy whatsoever.We were not monitoring any radio frequency at the time since we were not close to an airport traffic pattern nor in a designated practice area (the 'west practice area' near there is several miles west of our position). Now this: Thanks again to ADS-B, I was able to find both our flight tracks on FlightRadar24 (FR24). I identified the other aircraft's N-number, looked it up in the FAA database, found the owner's information, and called him. Nice, retired fellow on this third Cirrus, based at the airport 3 NM to our north-northeast, ZZZ. He had just departed ZZZ Runway XX and was climbing, per the FlightRadar24 track, via track 235 degrees at a ground speed of 132 knots. Our track at the time, per FlightRadar24, was 283 degrees with a ground speed of 71 knots. So roughly 50 degrees different in ground tracks, not 90 as estimated above.I asked the owner, who was the pilot in the Cirrus, if he saw us either visually or on ADS-B. He said he did not recall seeing us on either and that he did not get a traffic alert on his ADS-B device. I think we received an alert, but not positive in retrospect. I am just glad I glanced at the display when I did.The Cirrus pilot said that he always announces his takeoffs from ZZZ on the CTAF, which is Multicom 122.9. I admitted that I should have been monitoring that frequency for traffic awareness.I mentioned as gently as possible to him that the FAA recommends (via AC 90-66B, Non-Towered Airport Flight Operations) that airplanes departing a non-towered airport should fly straight out until reaching pattern altitude, then continue straight out or turn 45 degrees in the direction of the traffic pattern for that runway. This gentleman did neither. His FR24 shows that he went straight out off Runway XX for less than a mile, then turned 65 degrees!! To his right!! Even though Runway XX is a left-traffic runway. He did not seem impressed when I mentioned that to him, he was more eager to repeat that I should have been monitoring CTAF so we would have known he was departing.The upshot of our conversation for me was to guard the nearby CTAF whether or not I am in a location where I 'shouldn't' need to do so, and to realize that pilots operating at quiet, non-towered airports will do whatever they darned well please regardless ofany FAA guidance.Lastly, I offered to do his next flight review or IPC for free since I have never been in a Cirrus and would be eager to be his 'passenger.' Scolding him will not do any good, but perhaps by instructing him, should he decide to take me up on my offer, I may be able to remind him of proper non-towered airport procedures.
1778026: I departed ZZZ on an IFR flight plan to ZZZ1. The aircraft had sat for roughly 3 days over the weekend before this flight and was difficult to start that morning (battery seemed weak). 40 minutes into the flight, the first symptoms of an electrical malfunction began to show up. I was roughly 15 nm from the IAF for the RNAV XX approach into ZZZ1 at 8,000 feet MSL, in actual IMC with light to moderate rime icing. I had just switched from ZZZ2 Center to the CTAF for the ZZZ1 airport when the auto-pilot for the aircraft unexpectedly disconnected. All of the lights on the autopilot control panel went dark, and the autopilot would not turn back on. Initially, I decided to continue the approach by hand and have maintenance check the autopilot malfunction on the ground. After briefly troubleshooting the autopilot, I returned to my instrument scan. At first glance, my HSI indicated that I was on Heading/Course. Needles were centered and heading bug was situated at the top of the instrument. But when I looked over at the Garmin 430 GPS, it indicated that I was off heading by 20-30 degrees. By the time I looked back towards my HSI, there was a 'HDG' flag starting to flicker in the top right hand corner. I looked across the panel at the co-pilot's instrument cluster and noted that the co-pilot's artificial horizon was flopped over, indicating a 45* right bank and 20* nose up attitude. The co-pilot's side DG was also off by 90* from my magnetic compass. As I looked back towards the pilot's side instrument cluster, my HSI began spinning around and around like a top.At this point, I had obviously determined that several of my gyroscopic instruments had failed, and I had difficulty determining which instruments were trustworthy and which were not. From this point on, I did my best to maintain straight and level flight with my remaining instruments and the Garmin 430 GPS ground track. I looked out the window at my wings (I was still in IMC and light to moderate icing [at] this point) and saw that during my troubleshooting I had enough ice accumulation that small 'horns' of rime ice were begging to grow on the leading edges and my de-ice boots were mostly white with a layer of ice. When I pressed the switch on the overhead panel to activate my de-ice boots, nothing happened. I immediately switched back to ZZZ2 Center and [received priority], advising them that I had gyroscopic instrument failures and inoperative anti-icing equipment. I requested an immediate climb in an attempt to escape the icing conditions and find visual flight conditions before my remaining instrumentation failed, along with vectors back to ZZZ (which I knew had good VFR weather conditions...ZZZ1 conditions appeared to be worsening when I had last listened to the automated weather). ATC was extremely helpful and professional. Immediately offering any assistance they could, giving me no-gyro vectors towards ZZZ and approving a climb to 12,000 feet MSL. I had difficulty maintaining a heading and climb pitch-attitude initially, but got vaguely stabilized within a few minutes. Once stabilized, I noticed that the left alternator light was on, I attempted to re-cycle the alternator master switch twice without success. I then began to load-shed all electrical equipment which was not absolutely necessary for the continuation of the flight, and I advised ATC that I had experienced an alternator failure. I initially broke out of the top of the cloud layer and entered VMC around 10,000 feet roughly 15 minutes after the first indication of electrical failure. I had to request a higher altitude shortly thereafter as the tops of the clouds sloped higher towards ZZZ. ATC cleared me for a block altitude 8,000 feet to 12,000 feet, then eventually up to 14,000 feet, and authorized any course deviations necessary for me to remain in VFR conditions.Upon leveling off, I was initially concerned about what appeared to be a fairly significant performance loss. My first assumption was that it was due to ice build up on the wings/tail. In a level flight attitude, at 38 of manifold pressure and 2400 rpm (typical climb power) I was only getting 120 knots indicated airspeed. 160 knots to 170 knots indicated is more typical during cruise flight at a much lower power setting (30'/2300rpm). I alerted ATC that I was seeing abnormally low air speeds. But after a quick glance at my GPS (which was showing a 230 knots ground speed) I realized that the airspeed discrepancy was most likely due to pitot icing. ATC confirmed that they were showing me with a ground speed in the high 220's. By this point, the aircraft was out of icing conditions and flying just fine in VMC. So most of the potential danger had past. The last thing I had to do was search around for a hole in the clouds so that I could get back into ZZZ (there was an overcast layer between my aircraft and the ground). With the help of ZZZ3 Approach, ZZZ Tower, and several other aircraft in the area giving pilot reports, I found an opening near ZZZ4 and circled down for a visual approach into Runway XXL at ZZZ. The vast majority of the ice which had accumulated on the aircraft came off in the decent due to higher airspeeds and increasing temperatures. I landed without further incident, parked the aircraft, and immediately took down notes regarding the order of events while they were still fresh in my mind. I then called the Chief Pilot to relay what happened."
1778041: While conducting RNAV Runway 15 approach into ESN, received a low altitude alert from Easton Tower while at our MDA of 440 ft. MSL. We immediately climbed to 550 ft. MSL and conducted a missed approach once at the MAP. My assumption is that the aircraft descended too rapidly, causing us to be below glide slope as indicated by the PAPI's.
1778042: While entering the downwind via the 45 for Runway XX, right traffic at ZZZ, we were following a Cessna. I was sitting in the passenger seat as the NFP (Non-Flying Pilot)/Safety Pilot observing my friends landing. We completed our landing checks and continued following the Cessna. As the Cessna reached our four o'clock position I told the PF (Pilot Flying) that he was clear to turn base leg behind the Cessna. We made our radio call, and turned to base leg. After we made another radio call to final, a young woman flying some sort of low wing canopy glass cockpit airplane turned directly in front of us and cut us off in the pattern. She did make a radio call announcing her turn to base. Approaching her turn to final she then queried 'how many airplanes are in the pattern and where are you'. I am sure she was completely unaware of our position. Out of the turn we were approximately less than a quarter of a mile at her seven o'clock position. Clearly she had no idea that she had just cut us off and was now on a simultaneous approach with another aircraft. The PF did not have the conflicting aircraft in sight until late after turning final. In the interest of safety, I took control of the airplane and elected to fly a parallel to her track. I passed by her left wing approximately 400 feet lateral distance and nearly level with her aircraft. Once I knew we were safely passed her aircraft I executed missed approach. We then came around for another successful landing to a full stop. As background, ZZZ was heavily congested with training and weekend aviators. The approach to the downwind leg was reported via UNICOM as 4NM southeast to enter a 45 - downwind entry. We coordinated spacing with another crosswind aircraft to follow us for spacing in the pattern. Our aircraft was operating with LED strobe lights and all landing lights for visibility to other aircraft.Reported downwind, uneventfully. And recognized the aircraft we were to follow and mimicked their pattern to minimize spacing conflicts. Reported our base turn to UNICOM, uneventfully. Our track on base leg was approximately 2 NM from the end of the runway. At no time was our location questioned by the conflicting near miss aircraft.Reported a base-to-final turn, uneventfully and unquestioned. Upon the completion of the turn to final, I focused on vertical alignment to the runway and did not see the conflicting near miss aircraft. The PNF (Pilot Not Flying), in a radio call questioned the conflicting near miss aircraft to determine her position upon hearing the UNICOM base report. After it was determined the conflicting aircraft turned inside of our location, resulting in cutting us off placing our aircraft in a hazardous flight profile, PNF took control of the aircraft in a professionally coordinated manner. At this time, the conflicting near miss aircraft was well within 1/4 NM and somewhat above our altitude, which was approximately 300 ft. AGL. Because of her proximity to us, and her apparently being unaware of our location, the resolution was complex. Keep in mind in her base to final turn (Right Hand pattern) with a low wing aircraft she would have then been unable to locate us visually. In a UNICOM radio call, the conflicting near miss aircraft questioned 'how many aircraft are in the pattern and where are you', indicating her further lack of awareness to traffic as she was a close in final, an inappropriate time to establish traffic.Suspecting her unpredictable actions, we were prevented from a turn to side step since it would have blocked our ability to monitor her activities. Our inter-cockpit discussion created the point, given our closure rate, that our only recourse, in the interest of safety, was to parallel her path, fly past her which would have given her awareness of our location, then when ahead of the conflicting aircraft, we could safely initiate a missed approach, which we did.We remained in the pattern for another approach and full stop landing, uneventfully.
1778045: After two right 360s we were told to extend downwind for runway X, and look for helicopter traffic (Aircraft Y) three miles west of the field at 700 feet. We called out traffic in sight, and continued. After Aircraft Y didn't respond to two radio calls, we were told to do another 360. Rolling out of the 360 we were told to look for Aircraft Y one mile ahead at 900 feet orbiting. We called traffic in sight, and began a climb to 1,300 feet. It appeared as though Aircraft Y was still climbing as they passed in front from our left to right. After a controller change, Tower called our position to Aircraft Y, they did not respond. Shortly after that call, Aircraft Y made a sharp climbing right turn directly into our flight path. To avoid a collision, I took the controls and made a climbing left turn as sharp as I could. Shortly after I started that turn, Aircraft Y banked sharply to their right to avoid us. I can't put an exact number on the distance between us, but it was close enough that I felt the need to bank sharply towards traffic on final, and Aircraft Y banked hard enough for us to see the bottom of their helicopter. Once a safe distance away, we turned to rejoin downwind, and began a descent back to pattern altitude. After that, Aircraft Y asked tower to keep aircraft away from that area while they followed a pursuit. Hearing other aircraft have difficulty with separation, we departed the pattern to ZZZ1 to avoid a similar situation.It is normal for us to fly over helicopter operations at 500-600 feet while in the pattern at 1,100 feet. It is not normal to fly the pattern with unpredictable traffic at the same altitude.
1778067: R-side working Columbus/Pike/Parkersburg airspace, Charleston Approach and Columbus Approach airspace at the same time. Having little effective contigency plan for approach controls shutting down. Working multiple aircraft into unfamiliar airspace with unfamiliar approaches to three airports all within 15-20 miles of each other, while managing holding aircraft, other enroute aircraft and aircraft wanting approaches to airports where we provide approach services. A laser event also occured around the ZZV VOR while this was occuring, with a green laser hitting an aircraft. Luckily no injuries were reported. Have a baseline contingency plan that includes aides for the controller, including LOAs between facilities, suggestions like establishing holding stacks, downstream speed reductions, local best practices used by respective approach controllers, etc. Also, try not to shut down an entire approach control facility during peak traffic times, especially on one of the busiest travel holiday weekends of the year.
1778068: Aircraft X departure ZZZ IFR enroute to ZZZ1. I released the aircraft with a heading of 130 degrees & 2,000 ft. off Runway ZZ. This is a fairly standard procedure for releasing IFR aircraft off ZZZ when the metroplex is in a north flow. This keeps the aircraft away from the ZZZ2 finals which are just a few miles to the west of ZZZ. At the time, ZZZ2 was in the middle of an arrival push. Once the aircraft became airborne & I established communication with him I called ZZZ Tower & requested control so I could turn the aircraft back to the west across the ZZZ airspace. I turned Aircraft X westbound toward ZZZ1 & pointed him out to the appropriate ZZZ2 arrival sectors & handed him off to ZZZ TRACON. My plan was to keep Aircraft X low (2,000 ft. MSL) below the ZZZ2 finals where all the arrivals would be at 3,000 ft. MSL. A couple minutes later I noticed an aircraft in very close proximity to Aircraft X on a similar course. I called traffic but Aircraft X couldn't locate the aircraft. Due to the ZZZ2 traffic I couldn't climb Aircraft X for the traffic nor could I descend him due to the MVA of 2,000 ft. I again called traffic to see if Aircraft X could acquire the target visually. He still couldn't & the courses were converging while Aircraft X was overtaking the target. I called ZZZ Tower to see if they were talking to him or see if they knew what he was doing. They told me they thought he was heading to ZZZ3 which is very close to ZZZ1. The target had just departed ZZZ. I vectored Aircraft X to the north to in an attempt to increase the distance between him & the unidentified target. I then turned Aircraft X back to the southwest to go behind & to the left of the target to try & increase the separation even more. Once I was satisfied the two targets were safely separated I transferred communications of Aircraft X to ZZZ TRACON. I believe Aircraft X was on a heading of either 250 or 260 degrees at the time. It was brought to my attention later that while Aircraft X was on the heading I gave him when I transferred communications that he clipped a 2,100 ft. MVA while still at 2,000 ft. MSL. This occurred before the ZZZ TRACON controller was able to turn the aircraft. I didn't realize the heading would allow Aircraft X to clip the MVA. The MVA is a very small area, approx. 1-2nm wide 'shelf' of a larger MVA. I would not have given the aircraft a shortcut by taking him under the ZZZ2 finals. I was attempting to be as efficient as possible. However, with the amount of traffic in the area at the time I should have just taken him to the south off ZZZ & then westbound from there. This would've added approximately 30-40nm to his route but would've prevented this from happening. In the future I would also ask ZZZ Tower if they have anyone departing to the west who would be in conflict with this aircraft when I asked for control for a westbound turn. This also would've impacted my decision making.

1778141: Prior to top of descent we briefed the NNCEE 1 RNAV Arrival into IAH. The arrival says to plan on flying the RWY 8R transition. So we briefed the ILS RWY 8R approach. Houston Approach Control then told us to fly the RNAV (RNP) Y RWY 9 approach. The CA was the PM and told the FO he would change the approach in the FMC. After selecting the new approach the CA told the FO that there was a discontinuity at HOWLN. By selecting the HOWLN transition two separate HOWLN fixes were created separated by a discontinuity. The discontinuity appeared at the top of page two in the legs page of the FMC. So the CA brought up the second HOWLN fix and entered it into the discontinuity boxes and assumed that this action closed the discontinuity. But he never went back to page one to verify that the discontinuity was closed and he did not ask the FO to verify it as the FO was busy managing the descent. The MCP displayed LNAV and VNAV were engaged and so did the FMAs. Approach Control then said at HOWLN you are cleared the RNAV (RNP) Y RWY 9 approach. So the CA set FAF altitude of 2,000 in the MCP. Tower immediately cancelled our approach clearance and vectored us for the ILS RWY 9 approach. The contributing factors were both pilots did not verify the legs page after the Captain cleaned up the discontinuity and the high workload environment in IMC. Additionally it was the FO's first trip in over a month. I briefed the ILS 8R per listed as the runway for flying the NNCEE1 Arrival. During our descent when checking in with Houston approach we were given a new runaway RNAV Y runway 9. The captain put the new runway into the FMS and Verbalized he was cleaning it for the RF. I was reviewing the approach plate and didn't verify his FMS inputs. The CA noticed right away that the plane should be starting to turn for the RF, which ATC cancelled our approach and told to fly a heading.
1778144: On the arrival into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ1X arrival, we were told to maintain 250 knots to ZZZZZ, cleared the approach, ILS DME X rwy XXR. 1778159: I am concerned about having to wear a mask at cruise altitude while a Flight Attendant is on the Flight Deck. I feel we are putting Flight Attendant mask concerns over safety of flight concerns. If we experience a Rapid Decompression at FL 390, time of useful consciousness is measured in single digit seconds. A Rapid Decompression would be stressful, disconcerting and confusing. 1778219: Seconds after takeoff from ZZZ we smelled a burning-rubber like odor. It was strong and acrid within seconds. Passing through 2,400 ft. we made the decision to level off at 3,000 ft. and put our O2 mask on. I instructed the jumpseater to don his mask as well. I advised ATC as the First Officer was pilot flying. I coordinated an air return to the same runway we took off from and asked the tower to call our dispatch to notify of the diversion. Approach and landing was normal. I had Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting approach and inspect the plane before taxiing back to the ramp. Our mask were on until that point, but the fumes had subsided. The First Officer, did an amazing job, and I am grateful to have had such a professional with me at the time. We were only airborne for a total of 8 minutes. For hours after the event, I was short of breath and felt chest discomfort, a slight headache and inability to process thought. I elected to get checked out at the company provided medical center close by, escorted by Assistant Chief Pilot and was released. I am still not feeling 'normal' but hope to be by tomorrow. I feel as though I definitely took in some of the fumes, although it also seems that it was not for very long as I got my O2 mask on so quickly. After takeoff we had a strong burning smell. We advised ATC, leveled off at 3,000 ft. Donned O2 masks. Remained VMC. Vectors for Runway XX. Same as departing runway. Landing uneventful.
1778242: Leaving ZZZ, we turned left on Taxiway XX out of FBO to taxi to [Runway] XXR. When we turned left, ground told us to expect 15 minute delay due to departures on the center runway. We therefore proceeded to wait to do the taxi checklist until we were holding short. Approaching [Runway] XXR, I switched to Tower, and within a matter of seconds we hear Company Traffic is on a 4 mile final, and from there I do not recall what I heard. I do not recall because we were then doing the taxi and before takeoff checklist. I remember going up and hitting all of the lights on, which in my mind I must have thought that we were cleared for takeoff, and not line up and wait. We both verified the runway, did all the checklists, took the runway and took off. We never got corrected by ATC to abort takeoff because we weren't cleared. Everything seemed normal, we then got handed off to Departure, and a few minutes later we got asked to copy down a phone number for a possible pilot deviation. At this point both my partner and I looked at each other confused, not knowing what we did. We arrive in ZZZ1, we call the number, they said if they needed us they would call us, they then called us on the Monday after the incident and told us that we took off without clearance. Apparently, I did read line up and wait correctly, though I do not remember what I said due to the last minute high work load. We were called the morning of Monday [Date] from the supervisor telling us what we did. I then told him our side of it. He told me he had to do a report, I told him we would do the same on our end.This occurred because of task saturation. We went from a very calm and slow environment, to a very fast, high workload and task saturated environment. Part of doing the checklists requires a lot of talking between the flight crew. Having to do two checklists, the end of a briefing, as well as listen to ATC all last minute, we clearly didn't hear/comprehend the full ATC instruction. Which, led to us taking off without a clearance. The fact that neither of us caught it, and still didn't know what happened until we got a call, just shows to me how fast we were working. That is a pure reminder to remember to take things slower to make sure this does not happen again.Both my partner and I immediately started doing a report from the incident, when we found out what we did. We made sure that we timely called the ATC facility on the day of the incident as instructed.This occurred because of task saturation. We were thrown off guard getting a clearance 10 minutes before we were expecting to, and were rushing to complete everything. Rushing is never a good thing. We should have stated that we need a minute to finish some checklists and not agreed to the clearance, and if there was ever a doubt in our mind that we didn't understand a clearance we should have double checked with the Tower. We were given taxi instructions from FBO via [Taxiway] XX to Runway XXR and told to expect a 15 minute wait at the end of the runway. Once all checklists were done I preceded to takeoff. I do not recall hearing the lineup and wait instructions as my mind was rushed to complete both checklists. Looking back I clearly should have denied instructions to take the runway and take my time to complete checklists.We were notified after takeoff of a possible deviation and even at that time we did not know what we did. 1778254: We were given descent from 12,000 feet to 4,000 feet. As we approached 9,700 feet, ATC amended the altitude to 7,000 feet for traffic. 1778255: This was a rapid pressurization. After single engine start, I asked the FO (First Officer) to accomplish the single engine after start checklist. We received taxi clearance to Runway XXL. I began taxiing about 50 feet and the aircraft began pressurizing immediately. Everyone on the aircraft began feeling their heads squeezed together. Immediately the EICAS gave a 'PRESN AUTO FAIL' caution. What would you do? Are you going to let the airplane keep pressurizing until it reaches 14,500 ft while simultaneously running the QRH and then aircraft drops masks mid checklist? I used my instincts and immediately stopped the aircraft, set the parking brake and pressed the 'dump' button near the pressurization panel to dump the pressurized air. I only knew to immediately do this because I've personally thought of this scenario plenty of times in situations where the boarding door was closed and external air condition was hooked up. I always thought to myself if the door couldn't open quick enough then I'd need to dump the air, so my instincts reacted as such when this actually occurred. This is not something I was taught, this is not something the company teaches, however it should certainly be a point of emphasis. Moving along, after I dumped the air, the aircraft began depressurizing as expected just enough for about 3 seconds and then immediately began pressurizing again. I unpressed the 'dump' button and pressed it again. Nothing happened. I did this instantly. Afterwards I pressed the manual pressurization button, and rotated it to 11 o'clock position and waited 2 seconds, nothing happened, I then rotated full clockwise but the aircraft kept pressurizing and I wasn't going to wait to run the checklist as the aircraft altitude kept climbing. I have read this checklist before and ran through this procedure on my own time once or twice due to curiosity, so I knew what to do personally. I then pressed the EMER CALL button to the flight attendant, and told him to immediately open the galley door. Keep in mind all of this happened within 15 seconds. I also told him the galley door because I didn't want passengers to panic and run out the boarding door thinking their heads were going to explode. This is how it felt. When the flight attendant opened the door, it slammed open, as expected, despite the pressurization knob fully rotated to the right. Then I ran the QRH. Keep in mind we were not losing pressurization, we were rapidly pressurizing, oxygen masks were not my immediate thought on the ground. The checklist says to don oxygen masks during rapid decompression. I made the PIC authority to open the galley door once the pressure would not dump properly because I knew it would completely depressurize the aircraft. After I ran the QRH, I called Maintenance and they wanted to MEL the Auto Pressurization, and have me continue with the aircraft to ZZZ, an airport with a field elevation of 3200 plus/minus 100 feet. One, I've never controlled pressurization manually in flight, and secondly I've never been to ZZZ, a high elevation airport. So I refused. Nonetheless, we went through the QRH, I ran through the proper steps from instruction from the book, and Maintenance. I did what the QRH said, which I actually did myself already, then I personally went to go close the galley door myself, in case it didn't properly pressurize. I at least considered running through the proper MEL procedure, however I was still not sold on taking the airplane. Once I closed the door, the same thing happened, aircraft began over pressurizing. I immediately opened the door again. I went back on the phone with Maintenance, after a quick discussion with my First Officer & flight attendant, I told Maintenance Control 'I will not take this aircraft.' He said ok, we ended the conversation, then I began coordinating with OPS for a gate return. I did not want to taxi with the galley door open, nor did I feel it was safe to close the door as well, so I simply turned off the #2 engine, the only one running, and asked to be towed back to the gate. I sent an ACARS message to Dispatch 'returning to gate, need new aircraft.' They responded 'copy.' After a few minutes a tug came, we were towed, I blocked in and I then I called Dispatch and explained to him the situation. He said he'd call me back. In a few minutes he did, he said he spoke to Maintenance and they wanted to MEL the issue and keep the same aircraft, I refused again. The aircraft was not safe to fly. No one knew what the actual issue was, and unless you felt your head being squeezed in an airplane uncontrollably on the ground, you wouldn't know how that felt. I can't imagine what it would have felt like if we were flying at 3,000 feet and the aircraft wanted to over pressurize to a higher altitude and the dump feature didn't work properly, because opening the door inflight, is obviously not an option. A few minutes later Dispatch called and said they'd reach out to the Duty Manager and call me back. The Duty Manager then called me, he said the same thing the Dispatcher said, to MEL the aircraft, and continue on the same plane. I respectfully refused again. The aircraft was not safe to fly. The Duty Manager then coordinated a new aircraft and I swapped to one about 30 minutes later. I must repeat, if you were not on the aircraft, you do not know how it felt. The crew was light headed, myself included, and the passengers had to have been as well. As a crew I felt we made the right decision, despite pressure to take out the same aircraft. About an hour later, when my new aircraft was being boarded, the previous aircraft was adjacent to us being worked on by Maintenance. In other words, it was not a simple MEL procedure. The aircraft was not safe to fly. Our new plane was just fine, we boarded, and proceeded to ZZZ safely and landed about 2 hours late. The QRH procedure is for inflight, and mainly focused on cabin depressurization, we were being over pressurized. There wasn't enough time to run a QRH all while solving the issue as the aircraft continued pressurizing on the ground. I wasn't sure how much time I would have. There were children on board, I immediately thought about everybody, and since I knew opening the door would solve the issue, I made the decision to open. I didn't know of any other checklist action item would actually stop exactly what was happening. There isn't even a tab here for cabin over pressuring. You had to be there.
1778256: We were cleared to descend from FL180 to FL050. We ran the descent checklist and approach checklist as necessary. During descent ATC advised of a VFR target approaching our descent path at our roughly ten to eleven o' clock position. We scanned visually for traffic as well as verified the target on TCAS. ATC then advised us to descend to a higher altitude of FL070 to avoid the traffic. We amended altitude, visually scanned as the target got closer in vertical and horizontal path. As we began to approach the TCAS advised with a 'traffic, traffic' alert. Our altitude to the best of my memory was roughly between 10,000 feet and 9,000 feet. We scanned for traffic appearing to be around the 12 o' clock position of the aircraft. ATC issued a vector turning northeast bound which we complied with, however the TCAS RA went off immediately with a 'climb, climb' resolution. I disconnected the autopilot, put the thrust levers into the maximum position and adjusted the aircraft pitch to the vertical speed resolution. I believe we were about 9,000-8,700 feet before completing the RA TCAS. The separation showed about 300 feet. We climbed until clear of conflict to 9,500 feet and continued the ATC vector. After the 'clear of conflict' we leveled the aircraft, advised ATC of the TCAS RA and returned back to new given ATC clearance. We continued the flight to land safely at ZZZ. This was a huge learning experience to maintain separation and situational awareness of other aircraft and ATC instructions.
1778259: We were descending via the DRLLR5 arrival for Runway 26R transition and we had everything briefed and ready to go. At the end of the arrival there's a fix named ZOEEE, right upon crossing that fixed, my First Officer selected HDG sync, immediately follow by HDG mode. And just like that, we were auto sequenced for the approach. ATC then came to us with right turn for a right base followed by another right turn turn intercept the localizer for Runway 26L. At that point the FO (First Officer) armed APP and we confirmed APP1 was armed. So we continue with the approach but the airplane didn't intercept the LOC but instead it continued. Before we reached the final approach course I told my First Officer 'Be careful I don't think it's going to intercept' (he didn't acknowledge) right when we reached the course I told my First Officer 'turn now...turn now!' But he didn't, so at that point I said 'I have the flight controls' and I hand flown the airplane back the final approach course. At that point ATC came to us to let us know we were showing left of course to what my First Officer responded 'We are correcting. This happened like at about 3000 ft. AGL. After I restablished the airplane on it's final approach course I asked my First Officer if he wanted the controls back and he said YES. So I transferred the controls back to him. Then I quickly checked the information and I verified that the FMS was loaded with the ILS26L, we had a good preview with right identifier IJYV and we were showing an inbound course of 267 and APP 1 was armed. So I had to reach the FMS and I activated vectors then I forced V/L on the Pilot Flying side after asking the flying pilot if he agreed with every single step. Then the airplane's automation 'woke up' and the First Officer followed the FD all the way. We were stable at 1000 ft. and we continued to landing. I think the new FMS program has a glitch or something. Apparently it doesn't auto sequence the approach the same way. This happened in another aircraft which has the latest FMS update. From now on I'm not going to trust the auto sequence on the new loads and I am going to manually sequence it from a fix on the final approach fix. This should prevent the same issue from happening again."

1778381: During preflight planning, the airport was reporting [Field Condition (FICON)] NOTAM of 'Runway 03 FICON 5/5/5 40 PCT 1/8IN DRY SN OBS AT 2010XXXA09' and APRON ALL FICON ICE OBS 2010XXXA12.' 1778439: We landed on Runway 4 and due to the snow removal operations that were occurring at the time as the front had just cleared the city, with numerous taxiways closed or impassable, we were instructed to exit onto Runway 13/31 and taxi to hold short of Lima. We were then cleared onto Lima, Alpha to the gate, but it turned out that there was on outbound Company coming out of the alley. We then were told to hold short of Bravo on Lima. We did and then I heard Ground give the outbound Company aircraft instructions to taxi Lima, Bravo. I said to my FO (First Officer) that I didn't think we had room for him to clear us. As he came past Spot X I was concerned. As he started onto Lima I said 'I think this is too tight.' As he started his turn onto Lima I knew it was unsafe and I instructed him three times on Ground frequency to stop. He did. We were staring at his right winglet very close to us. I then coordinated with Company and Ground to get a tug out to us. Because we were inbound, I had the Ground Crew push us back towards Runway 13/31 on Lima to allow [the Company aircraft] to continue his taxi. We then continued to the gate. I have since talked to and debriefed the other Captain to get his view of what occurred and to talk about the safety concerns that I had. No metal was bent, but it would have if we hadn't both realized his close proximity to our aircraft. There were parallax concerns from Ground's view and the other crew's view. Speaking up is critical when things don't look right. The substantial numbers of snow removal trucks and plows along with closed taxiways that were constantly changing made it even more challenging.
1778454: I don't know what to make of the most recent bulletin about pilot mask usage and COVID-19. To date there is no concrete directive about mask usage in the cockpit. My own policy as Captain is to direct mask usage at all times possible while in the cockpit other than while eating or drinking or obviously in an emergency while using oxygen. I believe this to be congruent with CDC guidance for when someone needs to be in close contact with someone else who does not live with that person. This procedure is not perfect but the best I can come up with outside of pre-departure rapid COVID testing. As pilots we usually fly with new coworkers on every new trip and to date there is no way to determine that the person you are flying with is not an asymptomatic carrier of the virus.This whole situation is a failure of:The pilot group as a whole: We should do better than thisUnion: Our pilots are more at risk from death or injury from COVID than any other operational threatAirline: The safety protocol enforced outside the cockpit should extend inside as well, no exceptionsFAA: If none of the above will take action the FAA needs to step inMy First Officer on the flight associated with this report agreed in the briefing phase to comply with my directives for mask usage. During the flight I detected a problem though. I generally try to be friendly and conversational not only to pass the time in pleasant way but also to provide a comfortable environment to empower my First Officer to be a helpful partner in the flight.This wasn't to be on that flight and it culminated in my FO intentionally removing his mask on descent into ZZZ. Stating when asked about it that 'It is interfering with my duties.' The interference he was referring to was that I didn't hear the altitude ATC assigned and I asked him to ask ATC to confirm. I don't know how his mask interfered with ATC transmissions.I honestly think he was looking for an opportunity to remove his mask in defiance.I asked him to replace his mask and offered to work the radios if it's a problem.Later at the hotel I restated my objection to flying with someone who refuses to wear a mask and asked if that would be a problem in tomorrow's flight. He stated it would not. There were no mask issues on that flight, however it was not the most pleasant environment, quite sterile.Mask-less cockpits are dangerous.Unfortunately this is not my first time experiencing the mask resistance in the cockpit.The current guidance on this is weak and shows a lack of leadership on all involved.My experience is that a surgical type mask does not interfere with my duties, is easily and quickly removed if necessary, and by medical consensus prevents contagious droplets from dispersing to a great extent.Please enforce mask usage and prevent the sickness or death of our brothers or sisters in the cockpit.
1778455: Before push checklist and Ramp tower clearance to push were completed / obtained per procedures. Following standard pushback verbiage from the ground crew, I released the brakes. Pushback and No 2 engine start proceeded without incident. Ground crew instructed to 'Set Brakes' - at this time I read back 'Parking brake set, pressure normal' while the FO (First Officer) and I visually checked the red parking brake indicator for illumination and Brake Press gauge for 2800 PSI. Ground crew then announced 'Aircraft disconnected by-pass pin removed' to which I replied 'Disconnect headset.'Shortly after this statement the aircraft appeared to move forward unexpectedly. The ramp agent came back on headset with 'Set brakes set brakes' to which I applied brakes.Apparently the parking brake was not set, as we had intended and thought, and an uncommanded aircraft movement had occurred. The ramp agent came on the interphone and indicated that all was fine on the ground, and standard signals were given for ramp departure. Upon crew debrief, one of the threats that we identified was the sun shining into the cockpit, making the red parking brake light less apparent to the crew. Another threat was the general distraction of normalcy and not blocking out the sunlight's glare to verify aircraft condition.We are glad no one on the ground was injured and will learn from this experience. Before push checklist was completed. Received our push back clearance and the Captain communicated with the ground crew standard tow bar less pushback clearance and released the brakes appropriately. Pushback was completed uneventfully and during so we were cleared for engine start after which the Captain had me start the No. 2 engine. The ground crew instructed to 'Set Brakes.' I saw good brake pressure - 2800 psi, and what I believed to be the red Parking Brake light illuminated so I continued my duties of setting the packs appropriately.The ground crew announced 'aircraft disconnected - bypass pin removed' and I heard the Captain respond with 'Disconnect Headset.' Shortly after this the aircraft began an uncommanded movement forward, ground crew came on headset Immediately saying 'Set Brakes Set Brakes' to which brakes were applied and the aircraft stopped the slow roll and the Parking Brake was appropriately verified engaged at this time. The ramp crew came back on the inter phone and indicated all was fine on the ground, and standard signals were given for departure. Apparently our parking brake was not set after all when we initially thought, and upon debrief we both agreed the threats encountered were the glare of the sun on the parking brake light illuminating it more red than usual, as well as the general distraction associated with starting engines and push back tasks in general. We did not properly block the sun's glare and we should have been more vigilant to ensure it was set properly. We are both thankful nobody on the ground was injured and we will learn from this experience in order to prevent it from happening again.
1778464: Aircraft was out of balance at start of my shift. It required the last row to be blocked. I sent a message to ZZZZ to do so and they did. At about 10 minutes before departure aircraft went out of balance again and I determined that the last 3 rows now needed to be blocked. ZZZZ called to find out why weights weren't generating and I advised that last 3 rows now needed to be blocked. He advised that aircraft was already out so I said I would handle it with Captain. I sent Captain that info via ACARS to block last 3 rows, but when I went back to double check the Load Program (LP) to verify that in fact the additional 2 rows needed to be moved and blocked, this time LP indicated that no rows needed to be blocked. I checked it 1 or 2 more times because it didn't seem right to me. LP again indicated no rows now needed to be blocked. So now I quickly sent Captain an ACARS to disregard moving the additional 2 rows of people as that would now be an unnecessary waste of time since no longer needed. I sent the disregard message and then released weights. Departure [load] control now did not indicate to block any rows-although row XX had been blocked from the beginning. As I thought about why LP would show 3 rows needed to be blocked, and then it indicated that we now didn't need to LP any rows, I checked the seat map (aircraft was airborne by then) and sure enough, Operations had gone in and shown last 3 rows blocked but never spoke with the crew. They should not have touched the seat map since they did not physically move anyone. And since they are not supposed to do that, it didn't occur to me that they had. But that is why LP did not show I needed to block rows, it was reading that the rows were already empty. I called Dispatch and asked them to find out from crew exactly which rows were blocked on take-off. The answer was just row 34-the last row. I verified with ZZZ, and they advised that they had not told crew to move anyone, they just showed passengers moved out of last 3 rows. I advised ZZZ never to indicate passengers moved seats unless they have physically accomplished the move. They understand now.
1778465: I was working Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZZ1 at gate and had planned the flight according to the [Manifest]. One of my agents connected a cart of freight going to ZZZ2 to a string of carts that was going to ZZZZ1 unbeknownst to me. Since all of the carts were together, I scanned all of the carts for the flight going to ZZZZ1. The last cart of freight was a pallet going to ZZZ2. At first I had no idea that it was going to ZZZ2 so I scanned it just like I scanned the other cart before it since it was DG for ZZZZ1. When I scanned the cart for ZZZ2 the barcode wouldn't scan so I had to enter it manually. I did and confirmed the weight. I did not get an error message stating this was freight for ZZZ2 the scanner allowed me to add it to my flight for ZZZZ1 and I continued on my work. I was moving from AFT to FWD of the aircraft to ensure the operation runs smoothly on my gate. I am the Lead. I instructed my agent in the back to load up a cart of bags and a cart of DG (freight) and to surround the DG with 15 bags. I went to the front of the plane to check on the crew working there. 1778482: I was Pilot Monitoring on flight [on] DRLLR 5 RNAV STAR to IAH. Aircraft X had one MEL for right FMS inoperative. Single FMS operation. We entered the STAR during preflight and 26R runway per the DRLLR 5 STAR. ATC instructed us to change to 26L just prior to MPORT. This changes the final point on the STAR from SKLER to ZOEEE. I entered the new runway and verified that no duplicate waypoints existed. I also verified and noted that the waypoint sequence on the MFD looked correct, noting the large gap between ZOEEE and BOZZZ on the 26L approach. I also noted the line on the MFD depicted from DOMNO to ZOEEE. For unknown reasons the airplane approached DOMNO, overflew DOMNO, and the autopilot went immediately into ROL mode and continued flying straight. It did not sequence to ZOEEE as expected. We noticed the change immediately, selected heading mode to start the turn to ZOEEE, and then re-engaged LNAV after verifying the FMS was sequencing properly to ZOEEE. As we started to sort out the flight path error, I was distracted when ATC issued heading calls and pilot deviation calls, which removed my attention from assisting the pilot flying. No other deviation occurred that we were aware of. Both pilots were fully engaged in managing the flight. We acted as fast as we could to regain flight path control. [I] suggest verifying the integrity of the FMS arrivals into IAH. Delay pilot deviation calls until on the ground and the airplane has been secured. We were on the DRLLR 5 arrival and planning for Runway 26R. We had checked the route for no double waypoints and all altitudes were correct. We were assigned Runway 26L and made the appropriate checks of waypoints and altitudes. At DOMNO the plane went into Roll mode and continued south. We saw it right away and began left turn as ATC told us to turn left and gave us a heading (070 I think). A few minutes later the controller gave us a phone number to call about a possible deviation. This plane had the #2 FMS MEL'd which may have contributed since we don't often operate with 1 FMS. Better planning for operations with one FMS. Closer attention while passing DOMNO, which has known issues. However we had no duplicate waypoints so this may be a new issue.
1778504: Great weather, normal fuel burn. Entering terminal area we were vectored around then low and slow which created more fuel burn in terminal area. Did go-around for XXL due to an animal on runway. Aircraft in front of us did same. Declared minimum fuel on go-around in order to expedite landing since fuel now was an issue with extra fuel burn and not much to play. Controller was going to extend us downwind behind an arriving aircraft which would have added more time and fuel so I elected to [request] an immediate turn to the FAF for XXC. I didn't want XXL because of animal issue and another possible go-around. Controller vectored preceding aircraft off their approach and cleared us for visual XXC. Landed uneventfully with 3.9 fuel.....2.10 left tank and 1.8 right tank. Reserve Fuel on Flight Plan was 3.78.Cause: Dispatched with normal arrival fuel with very good weather. Controller vectored us low and slow which increased fuel burn. Suggestions: Next time I will not accept so many vectors and low and slow increasing fuel burn when I do not have extra fuel to play.
1778510: Descending on the DSNEE 4 arrival from EMLLD, we became aware of congested airport environment with two different TCAS traffic alerts very close by. Approach had us at 190 knots departing DSNEE, and we were expecting the visual to runway 20R. We had gone to flaps 2 configuration. We were handed off late to the final controller, and when we switched over we heard a company call sign with nearly identical numeric as ours, cleared for the RNAV (RNP) Z runway 20R. We heard the other aircraft read back the clearance, we knew a VERY similar call sign was on frequency. We thought we might be cleared for the same approach. We checked in and asked if we were going to get the RNAV approach, and the controller said no, we were going to get a visual unless we asked for the approach. Shortly after, the controller cleared an aircraft to descend to 3000', but neither of us were sure that it was our call sign. The First Officer (FO) attempted to clarify, but the controller was very busy and talking nonstop. We flew a few more miles, and before we could clarify he repeated the clearance to descend to 3000' and asked if we had the airport in sight. We called the airport, and said we were high. He cleared us to fly through final approach course and intercept from the right. FO read back the clearance, and we both agreed it was going to be tight. I immediately called for gear down and got the flaps to full, I also used the speed brakes as long as safely practical. We switched over to tower control, and I made the glideslope at approx. 1400' AGL, but we were still 40kts fast. I told the FO we were going to do a 'Soft Go'. At 1000' AGL I called for 'Go Around, Takeoff/around (TOGA)' and advanced the thrust levers to TOGA. I then called 'climb' as I brought the thrust levers back to what I thought was the climb position, but was actually the Maximum Continuous Thrust (MCT) detent. The tower initially held us to 2000', so I reduced our climb rate - we were accelerating rapidly. As we cleaned up and were cleared to 3000', the FO recognized that we were in MCT detent and brought it to my attention. By then we were clean and rapidly approaching 250 KIAS. I brought the thrust levers back to idle as we passed 260, and we saw a maximum speed of about 280 before we began to slow down again. I selected speed mode and set 220 KIAS, positioned the thrust levers in the climb detent and re-engaged auto thrust. We slowed and turned back into a right downwind for an uneventful visual approach and landing at SNA.Causes(1) Late clearance to descend. SNA is challenging even when on a normal profile, and a few miles made all the difference.(2) Task saturation. The L.A basin is one of the busiest airspaces in the world. Two Traffic Alerts and nonstop chatter from the approach controller indicated that he was task saturated, as well.(3) Call sign confusion. The scheduling shop should never have had two call signs separated by one digit arriving at the same airport at the same time.(4) Approach expectations. We were going to do a visual, and changed our setup and expectations when we heard preceding traffic approach clearance.(5) Fatigue. Our FAR 117 duty day limit was 10 hours. We had been awake since 3.5 hours earlier to make sign-in, and were at 9:00 of our 10:00 limit when we arrived at SNA. When we knew we were too high to likely make a successful approach, we could have asked for a vector and more time/distance to descend. Flight scheduling needs to de-conflict call signs so very similar ones are not scheduled to arrive at the same airport at the same time. The ATC controllers seemed very busy, perhaps a few more controllers on-shift would help divide the workload better. Crew scheduling could alleviate fatigue factors by avoiding sequence builds that have crews flying into airports at the back end of their duty periods that are known to present unusual challenges (even if they aren't officially 'special qualification' airports).
1778523: Arrived at destination and load crew advised us that DG can door was not secured to ULD (Unit Load Devise), can was resting on main cargo deck door. Load crew noted that all DG was still secure to floor of ULD (Unit Load Device) and intact. The cause was DG agent in ZZZ failed to secure door to DG ULD (Unit Load Device) after presentation of DG to flight crew. The reporter recommends load crew not leave cargo area until DG door is visually confirmed closed. DG Inspection checklist listed in FOM does not require flight crew to verify DG door reattached after presentation although common sense should be applied. Positioning of this particular DG container would not have allowed 'double checking' of secured door through smoke barrier windows. Reliance on other parties to perform job correctly is inherent in our operation. This was just a mistake by the ZZZ DG agent.
1778551: During the baggage loading phase I loaded a small box containing approximately 6 small bottles of recreational Oxygen. We departed ZZZ with a final destination of ZZZ1 and the flight proceeded uneventfully. Upon arrival all baggage was unloaded and the First Officer questioned me after the passengers left regarding the contents of the box. At no time up to this point did I consider the possibility of this being HAZMAT or anything not authorized to be carried by us. Upon further research I felt compelled to reach out to the Chief Pilot for guidance. I suggest a more thorough training of company policies, procedures, and specifically HAZMAT information. Access to more detailed information regarding Hazmat material. The owner and family arrived to the airplane ramp side. I went to open the exterior baggage compartment, to load the luggage. While loading bags the line personal were bringing me, I saw the Captain was also loading bags/backpacks etc. inside the cabin of the airplane. After the the baggage was loaded in the exterior baggage compartment of the airplane, I walked into the airplane greeted the owner and family and sat down in my flight deck seat to preform the rest of the pre-takeoff duties for the flight to intermediate stop to pick up two passengers and then finally on to final ZZZ1, our final destination. All flights were uneventful. When we landed at ZZZ1 while unloading the baggage, I noticed the box contained portable Oxygen containers which the Captain had loaded at our initial departure airport. After the passengers were on their way, I mentioned to the Captain about the box and it's contents. I said I don't think that was something we could carry, as it may be considered Hazmat. We further discussed this and performed research of company FOM and HAZMAT. The Chief Pilot was contacted to get clarification and guidance on this issue. I suggest more specific HAZMAT guidance and possibly more comprehensive HAZMAT training. Also a more detailed description of carry and non carry items would be helpful.

1778605: During cruise, observed oil entering cockpit through the firewall. Decided to make a precautionary landing. Uneventful approach and landing.Post flight inspection revealed a catastrophic failure of the fiber gasket in the Stratus Tools (Tempest) Model CO-300 spin off oil filter adapter. This is a known issue which has led to 3 fatalities and has recently been identified by the NTSB in a report 'Stratus Oil Filter Adapter Assembly Leaks' dated 30 NOV 2020. Note this was released just 17 days before my event. Please be advised. The NTSB refers to the manufacturer of the part by the parent company, Stratus, not the Tempest branded part most commonly known to pilots and mechanics. Previously this same part was manufactured by F&M.Key Takeaway- The NTSB needs to advise operators by using the Tempest brand to create maximum awareness. Better, the FAA needs to make this an Airworthiness Directive (AD) per the NTSB recommendation.Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association (AOPA) ran a story- 'NTSB Flags Oil Filter Adapter In Continental Engine Failures' (8 DEC 2020) and brought this to the attention of many pilots, myself included. Unfortunately, I did not know that Stratus (also F&M) is Tempest. Had that distinction been made clear, I never would have flown without checking the part as per the NTSB recommendation. I have since reached out to AOPA and asked them to re-run the story. Thus far they have only made the correction.I could never be so lucky again. I caught this failure in flight just in time in order to make a precautionary landing instead of a forced landing. Perhaps your good office could get this word out. If it can happen to me it can happen to anyone. Thanks for your efforts to be a PROACTIVE safety tool.
1778607: After landing, ground loop off the active runway. No injuries.
1778630: On an empty repositioning flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 to then continuing on to ZZZZ. Preflight was normal, checking the site gauges on each engine indicated full oil quantities. After my walk around I briefed my First Officer that the preflight was normal and the oil quantities were full. Departure was uneventful and normal. I was flying the aircraft on autopilot navigating direct to ZZZ2 and we were in a normal cruise climb passing FL380 climbing to our assigned altitude of FL390 approximately 35 mins after departure from ZZZ when we noticed the oil pressure reducing rapidly to zero followed by the red CAS message 'right oil pressure low' The zeros turned to dashes and the CAS message and Master Warning extinguished. This happened a couple of times. Center cleared us to FL410 and we advised them that we would like to discontinue our climb and that we were working an issue. All engine parameters were normal except for the right engine oil pressure which was dashed and oil temp was slowly and steadily rising. I called for the oil pressure low checklist from the QRH. I continue to fly the aircraft on autopilot while my First Officer initiated the checklist in the QRH. We requested a diversion to ZZZ2 which was the closest suitable airport. We completed the Oil Pressure Low checklist verbatim and secured the right engine. Center gave us vectors for our descent for ZZZ2 due to being very close to the airport. We were cleared for the visual approach to Runway XXL backed up with the ILS an uneventful approach and landing was made without incident.
1778670: On Day 5, the crew desk called me to assign me to a trip on Day 6 with a XA:40 report time. I called in fatigued on Day 6 at approximately [3 hours prior]. I had just finished a 4 day trip from Day 2 to Day 5, with each day requiring subsequently later report times and the last 2 days requiring late or all night flying. Additionally, even though this trip spanned 4 calendar days, it only included 2 sleep cycles.The previous 4 day trip created a significant cumulative sleep debt, as tracked my my Apple Watch. Day 1-Day 2, 6:38 of sleep at home prior to reporting for my 4 day trip. Day 2-Day 3, 8:44 of sleep in the ZZZ hotel. Day 3-Day 4, 5:26 of sleep after landing in ZZZ1, but I woke up at XA:00 am local time and had a XR:59 departure that night. I attempted to take a nap prior to reporting for duty but I couldn't fall asleep and was awake for about 18 hours prior to flying a redeye. Day 3-Day 4, No sleep due to redeye. I flew a redeye. Extremely tired during the flight and took a 25 minute nap during cruise. When I returned home, I slept from approximately XA:45 until the crew desk woke me from deep sleep shortly after XG:00. After the crew desk woke me, I packed my bags and prepared for the new trip. I attempted to go back to bed at XK:00 but could not fall asleep. I realized that it was not safe for me to attempt to fly my 3rd transcontinental trip in 2 days so I called in fatigued. Day 5-Day 6, No sleep due to crew desk interrupting my recovery sleep from the previous redeye.Of note, my previous trip involved a significant cumulative clockwise circadian rhythm disruption in which every day required a later report time and each day flew later into the night. Clockwise disruptions such as this are generally easier to tolerate compared to counter-clockwise disruptions. However, this 4 day trip also was engineered to accumulate sleep debt. Day 1 was 11 hours of duty and 20.5 hours of rest, which equates to a 31.5 hour long duty/sleep cycle. Day 2 of my 4 day was 7:15 of duty and nearly 25 hours of rest, which was a 32 hour duty/sleep cycle. Combined with each day's later duty periods, it was generally easy to fall asleep at the beginning of the rest periods. However, it was not realistic nor possible to achieve 2 circadian rests or resets during the layovers, which meant that each day I would be awake for a longer period of time prior to reporting for late night flights. This culminated when I reported for my redeye after being awake for 18 hours. Upon landing I was absolutely exhausted and needed to catch up on the previous 4 days of missed sleep. Unfortunately the crew desk interrupted this much-needed sleep and assigned me the new trip on Day 6. In other words, the crew desk expected me to shift from my previous XM:00 pm and XS:00 pm local report times to a XA:40 am report time after disrupting my rest and being awake for over 12 hours. Furthermore, the crew desk did not consider the larger picture of the 4 day trip and subsequent 2 day trip as a single 6 day long physiological marathon. Considering the operational design of my previous 4 day trip, combined with a back-to-back 2 day trip, I do not think it's physiological possible or safe for anyone to endure such a disruptive 6 day period especially after the crew desk wakes you up in the middle of a much needed restorative sleep period.
1778675: Arriving DEN on the CLASH2 arrival from the southeast, I planned and briefed an easterly flow arrival to land 17R. ATIS advertised 17R, 16L, 16R ILS, visual and RNAV Z approaches. I briefed for the RNAV RNP Z 17R. The final point for the arrival was QWIKE intersection and I left a discontinuity between that QWIKE and the QWIKE point starting the RNAV RNP Z 17R. Denver Center gave us a clearance to descend via the CLASH2 arrival landing south.The PM (Pilot Monitoring) and I confirmed that that was what we briefed and the FMC was properly programmed. The PM checked on with DEN Approach and we were told to expect RNAV Z to 16R. The PM installed that approach and I briefed the new arrival points and crossing restrictions on the CLASH2 that coincided with that runway, which were now a west downwind, the final fix being CLFFF. I briefed the approach as well. We did the same thing, leaving a discontinuity between CLFFF on the arrival and CLFFF as the IAF on the approach. The PM pulled the landing data for 16R and we briefed the changes on the engine-out missed approach which was slightly different then 17R. Approximately EVRLY intersection as we were descending through FL180, DEN Approach then said runway change, expect visual or ILS (I can't remember) to 16L. I remember it was at FL180 because it coincided with the altimeter change and the need to verify that VNAV is still able to maintain. The PM installed runway 16L and I did a briefing for the ILS 16L. This changed the FMC to an east downwind, the same fixes as for runway 17R but I did not note the changes in arrival fixes. As we were approaching JURKY intersection, I noticed on the FMC that the next waypoint was not what I was expecting. I had in my mind that we would be on a west downwind for the 16 runways. I said to the PM, it's not the correct fix next for runway 16R. The PM then asked DEN Approach to verify the runway assignment.Approach responded with a frequency change but did not respond to the request for runway clarification. This was at the point where we needed to go left or right depending on the runway. I thought it was 16R, so I went to the next fix for that runway, ROOTZ. As soon as the PM checked on with the next frequency, the Controller asked our runway assignment. The PM said we were trying to clarify. Approach then gave us 16R as a runway assignment. In fact, the previous clearance was for runway 16L. And that runway is an east downwind, not a west downwind even though the runway is on the west side of the airfield. This was absolutely my responsibility to ensure the correct runway and corresponding waypoints for the arrival. Going forward my personal correction will be to write down the runway assignment given by ATC each time it changes, whether on the yoke clip notepaper or on the iPad graphic. I also got complacent after doing 2 full briefings into DEN on a clear day. With the 3rd briefing, I did an abbreviated briefing. A full briefing, stepping through every arrival point would have caught it earlier. Additionally, as suggested by the Jump Seater, instead of clarifying the runway and having to verify the points quickly, I will ask ATC for the next waypoint they are expecting in order to give myself some time to figure out any ambiguities between the FMC and the chart. If we are adding to the data for DEN arrival deviations though...I didn't think this could happen to me. We briefed the threat of runway changes going into DEN. But DEN giving runway changes that impact arrival points without sufficient time for us to properly program and confirm was a contributing factor. Its 11.4 miles from EVRLY where we got the change to JURKY where the arrival splits. To reprogram, confirm, brief, get landing data and brief the engine-out profile changes while monitoring the descent is challenging. CLASH2 RNAV into DEN we initially planned for a Visual Approach to 17R backed up by the ILS. Initial Controller told us to expect 16R so we loaded RNAV/RNP 16R with the CLFFF transition to the approach, per ATIS. Cleared to descend via the CLASH2 arrival so we set 11,000 feet in the MCP (Mode Control Panel). ATC then advised us to expect Visual Approach to 16L. I then loaded the 16L ILS in the box and the Captain continued the descent on the arrival around the JURKEY fix. We changed our altitude in the MCP to correspond to the 13,000 feet minimum at ROOTZ while we checked in with the final Controller. Upon checking in the Controller asked us which runway we were planning on. I asked again which runway as we were not certain at that point. He then stated Visual Approach 16R. 1778699: Departing Runway XXR ZZZ we were filed ZZZ1 Departure ZZZ transition then ZZZZZ [fix]. Upon receipt of CPDLC clearance there was a route modification that was obtained that had us routed via the ZZZZA3 ZZZZZ. I loaded the flight plan per the CDU prompt and accepted the clearance and printed it out. There was plenty of time as loading was delayed. When I reviewed the loaded clearance it came up ZZZZA3 ZZZZA ZZZZZ. I then went back to the DEP/ARR page and checked the runway and SID which I had previously selected to ensure it was still in the FMC. I did notice that the routing had us now going south to ZZZZZ and thought the ZZZZA ZZZZZ was a short cut ATC wanted due to light traffic and time of day. I also looked at the printout and didn't see the period between ZZZZA3 and ZZZZZ as in ZZZZA3 DZZZZZ verses ZZZZA3.ZZZZZ meaning that ZZZZZ was the transition. Once we were airborne ATC cleared us directly to 12,000 which we were initially given 7,000 in the clearance. ATC then came back and said maintain 12,000 unrestricted which in my mind validated the shortcut because usually you get the phraseology 'Climb via the SID except maintain XXX'. ATC then informed us our deviate and asked us if we were on the SID. I said affirmative except from ZZZZA we were direct to ZZZZZ which was incorrect according to the clearance. After getting to cruise the Captain and I discussed the situation looking at both the clearance, the FOM and the loaded routing from the CPDLC. We realized that two errors were made. When I loaded the SID I did not reselect the runway and SID with the ZZZZZ transition because when I checked it was in the box and because we both missed the period in the printout and ZZZZZ was on the regular routing I thought ATC wanted us to cut that part of the SID off because of low traffic volume. It was pilot error and it's a difficult lesson. I am fully aware that a period means a transition but I missed it on the printout and assumed ATC wanted a shorter routing which has become the norm is so many ATC environments with COVID. I also realize that I will always double check every period on the CDU against the printout copy as it's easier to see. In addition I will ensure that every modification in the future requires an input of both the runway and SID even when uploading clearances from CPDLC which I'm aware to do but I didn't see the period on the printout. I take full responsibility for this mistake and I feel really bad I missed such a small but signification part of the clearance. I know better so there's no excuses for this missed detail. First leg (and only leg) with FO, blocked XX mins late for loading, so not rushed. Filed FP was ZZZ1 ZZZ transition, ZZZ [VOR], ZZZZZ, RXXX ....CPDLC had 'route change' (I was doing exterior prefect when it came): cleared ZZZZA3 ZZZZZ, RXXX ... climb via SID except maintain 7,000 feet. The actual printout was 'ZZZZA3. ZZZZZ', which means the ZZZZZ transition with the 'dot' in between. We missed that dot. We both assumed the clearance was direct from ZZZZA to ZZZZZ. The ZZZ1 does not have ZZZZZ as a transition, yet it was on our filed flight plan. To add some justification for our assumption, the ZZZ1 goes way north and west before heading west. The ZZZZA SID went south of ZZZ [airport] and more direct west on course. Add that is was [early] in the morning (very light traffic plus Covid19 low traffic) we assumed we were cleared a more direct routing south of ZZZ [airport]. And the Controller gave us climb unrestricted to 12,000 which also made sense for the Direct ZZZZZ we had in the FMC. And then climb to FL340 but then stopped us at 15,000. But we were wrong. He questioned us and we discovered the actual clearance was the entire transition out to ZZZZZ. At that point he cleared us to ZZZZZ and to climb to FL340 again. No TCAS or other traffic was in the area. This was a crew error. We both were very disappointed with the mistake. We reviewed the FOM and saw our mistake. We have both done this correctly many times but the 'ZZZZZ' on the filed route threw us off. No other excuse. And as the Captain I take responsibility.
1778736: A vibration / rumble was noticed during the No.2 engine start. During taxi the Captain performed his flight controls check so fast that I was unable to keep up with the call outs. It had been this way the whole trip, in fact I had insisted that it be repeated on the 1st leg so I could correctly check the control position. Whilst holding short of Runway XXL the Captain indicated he would turn the anti-ice off on taking the runway. I pointed out that the published ATIS reported runway conditions of 3;3;3 with 50% compacted snow, 50% compacted snow, 75% compacted snow. He was still inclined to turn off the anti-ice so I tried again suggesting should anything happen any investigation would focus on this. Reluctantly the anti-ice remained on and having lined up it was obvious that the runway was still significantly impacted by snow. On departure I chose to call for autopilot 2 at approx 100 ft in case the controller was busy. This allowed me to notice during the initial turn towards / at ZZZZZ that on the E / WD the title Engine" was flashing as well as "N1 VIB" was flashing green 9.9. An increase in noise and vibration was perceived from the right engine. Anti-ice was reapplied and after a short while the indication reduced to 8.2. The indication returned to 9.9 after the anti-ice was turned off during climb and it remained this way until the engines were at idle during the descent. During cruise I suggested the possibility of a bad sensor, the Captain's opinion was that we had a vibration. Later during the leg I commented on the vibration and now the Captain's opinion was that we may have a bad sensor. We were initially cleared to FL360. As we approached level off the Captain requested a climb to FL380 earlier than the flight plan fix of ZZZZZ1. On reaching cruise I reduced then increased managed Mach by 0.01 to investigate the potential of a harmonic vibration. Once established at the new speeds there was no difference in the indicated vibration so I returned to the managed speed with the intent to divert should the situation deteriorate. The Captain took out his QRH and referenced the High Engine Vibration procedure. It was given to read and after a discussion the Captain elected not to follow it as it would require descending from cruise altitude. For the remainder of cruise the Captain returned to reading his magazine. I monitored the indications, changed assigned radio frequencies and from time to time closed my eyes to concentrate on feeling whether the vibration had changed or the ambient sound had changed. We began flying the arrival. During the descent, Approach instructed us to increase speed to 310 kts or better. I felt that this was a bad idea and expressed this by saying ' I don't want to do that ' and 'I am uncomfortable with that'. 'So what it's only 20 kts' was the reply and seeing no intent to inform Approach of our situation, I felt that I had pushed as far as I could and increased speed. The Captain gleefully declared that the vibration had dropped to 2.2. I countered stating that the engines were now at idle as the aircraft attempted to stay on the profile at a higher speed. It was at this point that I decided to reach out and have myself removed from the trip. ZZZ1 was landing north with reported winds of 160/6 so a landing approach calculation was performed for the tail wind landing. On short final the Captain elected to increase Vapp unilaterally leading to a long float during landing. A new landing approach calculation for the new numbers was not performed. On landing I briefly deployed reverse thrust and quickly closed down the right engine before it could spool up and exacerbate the vibration problem. I moderated the thrust from the left engine and relied mainly on wheel braking to slow the aircraft. Control was passed back to the Captain at approx 60 kts for the taxi to the gate."
