1778776: During normal climb out of ZZZ, passing roughly FL240, we got a single CAWS Overspeed warning, FMA indicated FMS speed, however aircraft had accelerated into the MMO range I Reduced the speed from Mach .81 to .79 and pressed FMS speed to edit a new lower FMS speed. Reaching cruise at FL350 returned to normal FMS ECON Cruise .83 Mach Two hours into the flight, in cruise with no changes to pitch or power with autopilot on, aircraft started to overspeed by roughly 15 kts beyond the MMO in a couple seconds Both Primary Flight Display's indicated the same speed fluctuation We were alerted by the CAWS and the aircraft started to climb The First Officer took the controls as he was first to identify the problem, turned off the ATS reduced the power I pulled the speed brakes and called for the controls, reduced the speed from .83 Mach to .80 Mach Airspeed spread was about 60 kts and we were at optimum altitude Once the aircraft speed and altitude were under control, I reengaged the FMS speed and ATS These previous events, helped influence my decision making for the primary event.......All three crew members had been in the cockpit, with the door closed, together since departure I got up to use the lavatory about an hour west of ZZZ1, 3 hours into flight As I opened the cockpit door I detected a very strong smell of oily fumes I turned on the lights on the courier deck and the main cargo deck Air was hazy I went to the cockpit and got my flashlight turned off the lights on the main deck opened the smoke curtain and confirmed the presence of blueish smoke on the main deck in my bright flashlight beam I asked the Load Master to please come back to the courier station and check She confirmed the presence of smoke and fumes I returned to the cockpit and I ran the Emergency Non-Alert SMOKE/FIRE/FUMES checklist As per the checklist, I determined the source to be the Bleed 3 as the smoke smelled oily, not acrid, and I've heard of this problem in the past on this aircraft, also the Dangerous Goods Form did not list any hazmat on board and all systems were still functioning normally I turned off Bleed 3 per the checklist and started looking at nearby airports in my iPad The smoke began dissipating slowly I asked the First Officer to please go back and make sure the smoke is not coming from a ULD He returned after a few minutes and confirmed the smoke was dissipating and it was not coming from any of the cargo He said it seemed to concentrated above the wing box but dissipating I was reviewing the previous logbooks and current logbook pages for any smoke occurrences during the previous flights to help come to a decision to divert per the Quick Reference Handbook or to continue per the Quick reference Handbook Before I could finish reviewing the logbook Autopilot 1 disconnected, the aircraft started deviating from altitude and we got a LEVEL 2 alert for FCC 1B FAULT, a master caution and my flight director disappeared I immediately switched to Capt on First Officer Flight Director and stabilized the aircraft, checked all the parameters and engaged Autopilot 2 I called for the LEVEL 2 FCC 1B FAULT checklist After the checklist was complete, I consulted with the crew and made the decision to divert to ZZZ1 as it was a Company flight, it was en-route, weather was good, we were very familiar with the airport and we have maintenance there I gave the controls and communication to the FO and began running Checklist I told the FO to advise ATC that we would like to divert to ZZZ1 for technical reasons We were 39 minutes from ZZZ1 and cleared direct to a point on the STAR We advised NCC via ACARS of our diversion On the STAR when we were passing 11,000 ft at 245 kts, we were cleared to 6,000 ft, I reduced the altitude to 6,000 ft on the FCP and selected IDLE and confirmed on the FMA The aircraft began to climb instead of descend, speeds were normal and aircraft was in clean configuration w/ local altimeter set I disconnected the autopilot and hand flew thelast 50 miles We were cleared for ILS On final as we set Flaps 15 we got a LEVEL 2 FLAP DISAG, this was expected as the right outboard flap had been 'X' out since the FCC Fault We set flaps 35 Flaps showing 21/22/20/X on both PFD's I elected not to extend the flaps further or retract and retry to extend them as the airplane was light and controllable, runway was long and insight, weather was clear and winds were light I elected to maintain MIN auto brakes however I informed the crew I was going to use all 3 reverse and to advise tower that we would be rolling to the end Before landing checklist was completed I announced 'no green box' due to flaps not beyond 25 degrees We landed with no further incident and taxied to the ramp. Excellent job from my First Officer and Load Master They were invaluable to me during the flight. I identified the haze/fumes when I left the cockpit to use the lavatory I found the upper deck full of fumes. [Probable cause of the] smoke was Engine oil leaking into Pneumatic system [Probable cause of the] FCC issue is unknown. Followed SOP, make decisions while weighing input of crew. [As my response] recommended Preventative Maintenance.

1778813: Today I taxied to the ZZZ strip with ATIS weather to ZZZ Runway XX. I noticed 4 or 3 maybe snow removal vehicles working around but not yet on the runway. I have caught miscommunication from the Tower in the past coming in on floats but was able to talk it out.
1778822: The incident occurred while on the initial climb from runway 25 at Orlando Executive Airport (ORL). The probable cause appears to be communication and pilot error. Our aircraft was a Aircraft X. The student and I were remaining in the pattern practicing touch and go landings. An Aircraft Y [faster aircraft] was following us throughout the pattern. Our call sign was occasionally [mis-stated] which contributed to the confusion. During our pattern practice we were told to extend our downwind and that Tower would call our base. While we were in the right downwind and extended right downwind for Runway 25, Aircraft Y was noticeably gaining on us as shown on our MFD's traffic feature. Our base was approved and we were number 1 cleared for a touch and go Runway 25. [Aircraft Y] was cleared for a touched and go number 2 behind us. While on short final, it was noticeable once again on the MFD that Aircraft Y was gaining on us significantly. Our approach speed in the Aircraft X is 65 kts. With the headwind component that day our ground speed was undoubtedly slower than 65kts. Aircraft Y was told by Tower to do an s-turn on final for spacing as it was apparent they were getting close. The problem arose on the initial climb out following the touch and go, Aircraft Y overtook our aircraft while on the departure leg at approximately 800 feet, resulting in a near miss.The traffic we were following was told to extend upwind and we were expecting to receive a similar instruction for ourselves. The confusion seems to have begun when Executive Tower radioed for Aircraft Y to continue in the upwind and that they would call their crosswind. We did not respond to this call, as we assumed it was intended for Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y responded confirming to extend their upwind until their crosswind was called. This transmission must have stepped on the Tower's transmission because as soon as Aircraft Y was finished broadcasting, the end of tower's transmission came through with the only audible portion being '...end upwind.' (Most likely 'extend upwind.') This stepped-on call was most likely a follow up to [us], but Aircraft Y then responded to continue their upwind for a 2nd time. Tower then called for Aircraft Y to extend their upwind. At this point the instructor in Aircraft Y, clearly confused, read back the extend upwind instruction for the 3rd time. We realized that the extend upwind call to [callsign] was most likely for us and we continued the upwind as instructed with the traffic ahead of and behind us being on extended upwinds.During this time, we again noticed Aircraft Y gaining on us on the MFD traffic. We continued in our upwind climb as Tower called for Aircraft Y to follow traffic ahead to the right (us). They responded that they had us in sight as they continued climbing and closing in on our left hand side. This is the approximate time that [we] was overtaken by Aircraft Y at approximately 800 feet MSL. Aircraft Y passed by us at roughly 200 feet off of our left wing, while both of us were still climbing to pattern altitude in the upwind leg.
1778828: I was approaching F70 from the southeast after a personal flight while making radio calls every few miles as I noticed on my ADS-B in several targets circling around the airport due to intense student activity.Someone made a radio call a few minutes before I was in the vicinity of another aircraft cutting them off on downwind too and I prepared myself for heavy traffic in the pattern and trying to find an opening so I could join the downwind.Upon entering the 45 for downwind I noticed visually an aircraft on the upwind taking off and repeatedly asked his intentions and if he could see me.There was no answer and seeing him proceed on runway heading I continued on the 45 for downwind being confident he wouldn't start a turn to crosswind until he reached close to pattern altitude as is recommended for the noise abatement procedure out of F70 for departures from Runway 18.Then I saw him maneuver for the crosswind maybe 500 feet below my altitude which was at pattern and make a radio call in that regards. At this point I had contacted him several times regarding his intentions and whether he could see me but without any answer.Seeing him turn and put me on the direct collision course with me although 300 ft. below me I decided to execute a 360 degree turn saw him coming extremely near me. Finally he acknowledged my presence in a subsequent radio call.I continued the full turn and reentered downwind.F70 was extremely busy that day with several schools on the field and at one point I saw no less than 5 aircraft in the traffic pattern. Needless to say a Tower is badly needed in that field for the safety of flight as the indiscriminate addition of several aircraft from several schools without any sort of coordination between those schools makes this urgently needed.A bit of courtesy goes a long way too and someone was nice enough to extend their downwind for me earlier in the day so I could depart as I had to hold short of the active runway at least 10 minutes as one aircraft after another was landing with no end in sight.On my side I should have waited outside the pattern on a hold in a safe area until there was no aircraft on upwind and the downwind leg would be fully opened, with adequate radio communications ensuring everyone in the pattern has knowledge of any other traffic with acknowledgement for all.This was my first experience with this field with that many aircraft in the pattern and the lesson learned here is to stay outside an uncontrolled field until there is fewer than a set limit of aircraft that one can set as personal limit.Such a personal limit is not taught at all as part of any training curriculum nor in the AIM in my knowledge.Most uncontrolled field are uncontrolled because of very low traffic but some reach levels just below the threshold needed for a tower and F70 seems to be in that category.Also the schools on the field could coordinate some kind of schedule among themselves so not everyone is up in the air at the same time. Poisson's law dictates things happen in bursts unless there is coordination to avert it.
1778829: We were flying east at 3,500 VFR and Aircraft X was 3,500 Westbound. We noticed the Aircraft X at very close range and made a turn to the right to avoid the aircraft. 1778831: Post flight the aircraft was parked at the unmanned self-service fuel station to be refueled before returning it to the hanger. 1778856: Aircraft X was on the RNAV Z approach for Runway 22L. The aircraft had been cleared to land. The approach naturally brings aircraft in on a slight angle to the runway. 1778860: Initially coming in on the IAH LINKK1 Arrival expecting 27 but then just before descent, we were switched to NNCEE arrival expecting 8R (parking north side). Started setting it up, reprogrammed the box and reconfigured the aircraft. We then received 'maintain 200 until advised, level 6;000MSL at HOWLN'. Came out of box to open MCP speed window for 200 (FMC VNAV speed would be 210 per the arrival). Looked back down and saw us going through TEXXN where the ARC was supposed to commence.I immediately clicked off autopilot and started 30 degree turn to get back on ARC. Halfway through the turn (past HHOOG) received call from ATC stating he saw that we went past TEXXN and to turn left to 300 but we were already 45 off from runway (base). ATC asked if we had runway in sight, we confirmed and were then cleared visual Runway 9. Visual approach was executed and landing was normal. We programmed FMS to perform RNAV 9 from HOWLN but don't think it closed the loop automatically like it does on LINKK1 to 27 approach and that's why the aircraft continued past ARC point.
1778862: Initial setup and brief was LINKK arrival, with visual ILS 27. Weather was clear, with excellent visibility. At TOD IAH changed to East flow, and we were given the NNCEE arrival. Approach control said expect RNP Y 9. We requested 8R since our parking gate was on the north side. Were told 'standby, we'll see'. Frequency change, and no reference to 8R request. Then cleared RNAVP Y 9 via HOWLN, maintain 200 knots. I observed Pilot Flying choose RNAV Y 9, with HOWLN transition. Other radio calls and congestion and nonstandard speed change prevented from looking into the LEGS page to see it tie into the HOWLN we were proceeding toward. Immediately after TEXXN we realized it did not turn and turned the aircraft with heading select.Approach queried about being outside the turn as our actual heading turned through approximately 330. Approach control said maintain current heading'. I immediately asked what heading do you want, we are currently in the turn. First response was 260 heading. We initiated a turn reversal, then approach said, I see you are in the turn, turn right 060, descend 3000, cleared the visual runway 9. I acknowledged. Soon thereafter were given 'maintain 6000, turn heading 100.' Responded with climbing back to 6000. Controller asked if we were still visual with 9. (It was perfectly clear, with unusual 30+ mile visibility). Responded yes, still visual. Re-cleared the visual runway 9. Flew the visual to an uneventful landing."
1778902: Landed Runway 35R and was instructed by DFW tower to taxi Q - Z hold short of Runway 35C. Approaching Runway 35C DFW Tower instructed us to cross 35C at Z landing traffic will land and hold short. As we began to proceed across Runway 35C, after crossing the hold short line, the Runway Entry Lights (REL's) illuminated red. Landing traffic was still airborne on approach to Runway 35C. Since we were already moving, I determined it would be safer to continue across the runway and exit rather than stop in the runway environment. Notified Tower Controller once clear of the Runway that the REL's illuminated as we crossed Runway 35C. The Controller apologized and stated that was not supposed to happen since they were in Land and Hold short (LAHSO) operations.Possible ground equipment failure or programming error.Not certain. Perhaps a question for DFW Tower. Landed Runway 35R and was instructed by DFW Tower to 'taxi Q-Z, hold short of 35C.' Approaching 35C tower instructed us to cross 35C at Z, landing traffic will land and hold short. As we began to cross 35C, the runway entry lights illuminated red. Landing traffic was still airborne on approach and we were already across the hold short line, so we decided it was safest to continue and exit the runway. The Captain notified the Controller that the REL's had illuminated, and the controller apologized and said that shouldn't have happened.Possible equipment malfunction. I don't have any suggestions other than checking the operation of the equipment.
1778926: We were dispatched [to] ZZZ without alternate fuel. Forecast for ZZZ was few clouds at 25,000 and more than 6 sm visibility. This forecast did not require an alternate.While on downwind leg, a fog bank rolled in over the airport and the weather dropped below CAT II mins. ZZZ1, normally a good diversion airport was also reporting fog. We estimated such a diversion would have put us with only 1,500 lbs of fuel remaining. Enroute we were given several delay vectors. Running low on fuel and out of options, we decided our safest options was to execute the CAT II even though visibility was below our required minimums of 1,200 RVR.Approach and subsequent landing were uneventful. We landed with approximately 2,900 lbs of fuel remaining.Unforecast weather, ZZZ is notorious for unforecasted fog in the late fall and winter. Anytime with clear skies and close temp dew point like today, I will ask for an alternate even if official forecast does not require.
1778932: We were conducting Aircraft X at night into ABE, vectored from the north, and then given a clearance for a Visual Approach. As always, we had an approach set up, ILS 24, and while descending from the north side of the airport from 3,000 feet, the vectored altitude, to 2,400 feet, at an altitude of about 2,650 feet we received a one time (only 1) 'Terrain' warning from the TAWS (Terrain Alert Warning System), while descending very gently at about 300 feet per minute. We leveled off for a moment, there was no other terrain warning and never a 'Terrain, Pull Up' command, then as we intercepted the final, we continued to the 2,400 feet glideslope intercept altitude. There was a ridgeline north of the ILS course, which we had briefed on, but it did not show an altitude greater than 1,000 feet, so we did not think it would be a problem to start a shallow descent from 3,000 to 2,400 feet, especially at a shallow rate. This is a potential problem at night, as there are no obstacle lights on the ridge line, so I believe Approach should simply provide vectors to the ILS approach instead of just giving a 'visual.' A little more work for ATC but a safer way of operating. Caused by ATC clearing crew to do a night visual instead of providing vectors, knowing that there are unmarked, unlit, terrain ridge lines to the north of the airport. Also caused by crew not requesting full vectors to the ILS at night. Most ATC facilities in small airports don't want to work that hard. Suggest that crews start asking ATC at small airports to provide vectors to the Approach being used to back up the Visual when in night VMC conditions, as a means to improve the level of safety, even if it means that ATC might have to work a bit more.
1778938: We were descending on the JANNY5 Arrival. At the KOPLE waypoint, we were given 'Direct JANNY at 8,000' by ATC. We began our descent with Joshua Approach. Around the JANNY waypoint, we were transferred to SoCal Approach for terminal instructions to Burbank airport. The controller initially gave us a 'descend 7,000' instruction which was followed shortly thereafter with a 'descend 5,000' this descent was well prior to the usual instructions given to Aircraft X from this location. The crew complied with all instructions from ATC. We were receiving vectors to intercept the ILS-Z Runway 8 Approach into Burbank. We became aware that the controller was vectoring us to intercept the localizer between the SILEX and BUDDE intersection. While approaching from the north at 5,000 ft MSL, we were heading over one of the small mountains northwest of Burbank Airport. We were vectored near the highest point on that hill which is charted at 3,734 ft. While going over the hill the aircraft gave us a 'TERRAIN, TERRAIN, PULL UP.' I looked at the RA as the first 'TERRAIN' was enunciated, and saw the RA indicator show around 1,500 feet, then jumped immediately to 2,500 feet. The warning was only given once by the aircraft. The PF (Pilot Flying), Captain, reported not seeing any altitude indication on the RA. We continued the approach and the remainder of the flight was uneventful. We aren't sure whether it was an erroneous aircraft indication or if ATC may have descended us a little too low for that sector. Clarify with ATC on altitude assigned and whether assigned altitude is appropriate for sector.
1778972: The flight departed the from Gate X in ZZZ1 at XA:10z and proceed to flight level 200 to ZZZZZ intersection to join the arrival into ZZZ without incidence. At approximately XB:10Z while descending through 8,000 MSL for 7,000 MSL in IMC conditions with heavy rain and continuous light and occasionally moderate turbulence we received a single chime and an ELT ON Master Caution message was displayed on the EICAS primary page. Approximately one to two seconds later a very loud ELT signal began sounding through the flight deck intercom system. I notified ATC that we had an indication that our ELT had activated and that it was in error and could be disregarded. I further advised them that the ELT tone was sounding on the flight deck and it was making radio communication and flight deck communication very difficult. I turned the number two comm radio off of the guard frequency and reduced the volume, but it did not have any effect on the volume of the ELT. The First Officer (FO) began to attempt to find a resolution [in] the QRH and we attempted QRH procedure several times to try to silence the tone without success. The noise was deafening and flight deck communication and air to ground communication was very difficult. At 4,000 MSL we were given a heading of 360 degrees then descended to 3,000 MSL and turned to a heading of 085 degrees and instructed to join the localizer for Runway X. At this time both aircraft localizers failed, and a red LOC indication was displayed on both PFD's. We advised ATC and asked if there was a problem with the localizer. ATC queried several other aircraft and all advised they were receiving the localizer. We broke off of the approach per ATC instruction and attempted to set up for the ILS to Runway YL but could not receive any ILS signal. I advised ATC that we would need a GPS approach and we were instructed to prepare for the GPS YL. After having set up the GPS YL ATC advised that the wind had shifted and were now from 275 degrees gusting to 25 kts. We were further advised that the airport was now in a west flow. We requested RNAV YY and began preparing that approach. We received radar vectors to RNAV GPS YY and completed the approach without incidence.Due to extreme flight deck noise from the ELT throughout the event communication on the flight deck and with ATC was very difficult. The noise and inability to communicate throughout added a high level of stress and complexity. Continuous turbulence and instrument meteorological conditions were present throughout, with ceilings and visibility at or near minimums on arrival at the runway. The double failure event coupled with the inability to sync the two MFD's due to a previously existing MEL added complexity and were additional threats. To mitigate these factors myself and my FO followed SOP to the extent that we were able. We resisted the urge to rush and after preparing the RNAV approach we briefed the approach, and the runway change items in an attempt to slow down the process and bring the flight back into the normal envelope as much as possible. In hindsight I wish that I would have tried the EMER function on the RCP (Remote Compensation Panel). I don't know if it would have helped but the noise made concentration and communication very difficult and it was very fatiguing. Overall I was satisfied with my actions and those of my FO given the circumstances and without the benefit of hindsight I thought that we met or exceeded expectations.
1778973: On the Visual [Runway] XXR approach into ZZZ. Cleared for the approach about 5 miles out, and given a heading 090 to join the localizer. We joined the localizer and got a TA and noticed another RJ (Regional Jet) headed around 150 degrees to join the localizer for [Runway] XXL, which wasn't going to be a factor. At this point we received a RA that the [Runway] XXL RJ had blown through the localizer and was right over the top of us, about 300 feet of vertical separation. I told ZZZ Tower we had a RA and he was swamped today so he initially wanted us to go around, to which I said we had flown the breakout and were established on the approach - going around and flying his instructions would've led to a second RA since we were instructed to climb right into that jet that just flew over the top of us. Tower changed his mind and gave us [Runway] XXR landing clearance. ZZZ ATC workload was extremely high and the [Runway] XXL RJ didn't intercept the localizer at all, nor were they aware of the traffic around them (us).High ATC workload and neighboring jet on the other approach had low SA (Situational Awareness).ZZZ workload review and talk to the crew who blew through the [Runway] XXL localizer and crossed into us.
1778988: I operated Aircraft X. When I had shown up to the aircraft the FO (First Officer) was already at the aircraft. The FO had the aircraft powered up and had started the preflight duties. During the before start checklist it was acknowledged that the preflight was completed. The FO did not indicate that anything appeared abnormal during the preflight. Before the pushback the ground personnel said all secure below, FOD walk complete, steering disengaged, standing by for parking brake. The ground personnel did not report any panels that were open. Some point above sterile we heard a thump noise. We then called the flight attendant to ask if everyone was okay. The flight attendant indicated everything was fine. We checked the EICAS and all the engine instruments were in the green. We then checked the MFD pages and everything was normal. We preceded onto the destination as there was nothing to indicate any abnormality. We have no way of knowing if this was related to the latches underneath the engine coming open. When we had arrived to the gate the ground personnel had told us that there was two latches underneath the engine hanging down. The two doors open underneath Engine Number 1 was the engine oil service door and the air turbine starter access panel. Me and the FO proceeded outside during the walk around to look at the access panels underneath the engine and relayed the information to Maintenance. The access panels had also caused holes in the engine cowling.The cause was the access panels underneath Engine Number 1 came open during the flight. During the preflight during before departure nothing was noticed abnormal.A thorough preflight was done before the flight. Nothing out of the abnormal was indicated by the FO or the ground crew. A thorough preflight was accomplished and should before every flight. No other suggestions at this time.
1779045: Enroute ZZZ-ZZZ1 on the red-eye at FL 33,000 ft. into the flight we had an ANTI ICE STBY PITOT ECAM. QRH was used. later we were at FL 35,000 ft. and Autopilot 1 disconnected, I attempted to reengage #1 or #2 autopilots and neither would engage. The FMAs went blank on both the F/O and my PFDs. Autothrust disengaged and went into Thrust LK. Thrust levers were matched with power setting and IDP switches used. We had our route displayed in the ND on both sides and MCDUs were operating normally. ECAM displayed:AUTO FLT AP OFF (RED)AUTO FLT A/THR OFF (AMBER)L/G SHOCK ABSORBER FAULT (AMBER)Indications looked similar to an FMGC Dual Failure except we had both NDs displaying our route, our MCDUs did not go into a subsystem page and no FMGC (Timeout) was observed. The Shock Absorber Fault ECAM had me thinking this may be a different malfunction that I have never witnessed or a coincidence. We contacted Dispatch/Maintenance via phone patch using the 'CALL ME' function on ACARS. Maintenance was perplexed of what was causing our malfunction. They had us reset the Auto Flight C/B's B1 (MCDU 1) B2 (FMG 1) and hold. C/B's were reset with no change. We attempted the Long Reset in the QRH Dual FMGC Failure with no success. Mintenance had no other options available.ATC was advised of our equipment malfunction and our inability to remain in ZZZ airspace. We were cleared down to FL 27,000 ft.. Review of our fuel, weather and capabilities with my F/O. Dispatcher we agreed to continue to ZZZ1 with the caution that if we had additional malfunctions, we would consider ZZZ2 as a divert airport. ATC was given our new suffix with the inability to operate in RVSM airspace.Purser was informed of our status.Prior to touchdown at FL 27,000 ft. both FMAs began to populate. Autopilots and Autothrust became available. All malfunctions except for the STBY Pitot cleared. We reengaged the Auto flight functions and remained at FL 27,000 ft. We landed on Runway XX at ZZZ1. Malfunctions were recorded on in the ELB, including a information writeup of what happened. Technician met the plane and we explained what happened.
1779047: I was Pilot Flying (PF). Autopilot (AP) on. Approaching top of descent for DRLLR arrival near TORNN level FL330, Fort Worth Center gave us descent to FL310, then changed it to FL320. 1779057: Assigned DRLLR 5 arrival into IAH. We were planning 26R RNAV Y. We were cleared to descend via the DRLLR 5. 6000 was set in altitude window and aircraft was in LNAV/VNAV. 1779072: 45 minutes into the flight we received a Dispatch message that Passenger X in seat X5 has tested positive for COVID. Passenger X was traveling with 3 others which all were in row X. I contacted medlink and was disconnected. I asked my entire crew if they had any experience with this which none of them had and I hadn't either. I asked Dispatch for the name of the passenger and protocol to follow. I retried medlink and followed their instructions to minimize contact with Passenger X and get row X off before all others. We asked for priority handling. Dispatch informed us the station will meet us at the gate. Before getting to the gate we asked all passengers to stay seated with seat belts on at gate arrival for a medical situation. I opened the cockpit door to make sure everyone was complying and only Passenger Y wasn't. I said 'Please everyone stay seated' and he sat back down. Later he made a rude comment deplaning and complained to Customer Service. We deplaned row X only and met them and Customer Service in the jet way to assess Passenger X. Passenger X was a young woman that had COVID a few months ago and was 100% healthy. Customer Service followed them to baggage claim for another test. Customer Service cleared us to deplane so I made a PA explaining the situation. Customer Service informed me many people that have had COVID in the past test a false positive. Received Dispatch message indicating passenger in [seat] X5 received an airport COVID test that came back positive. We were located about 1 hour from ZZZ. Continued towards ZZZ, declared a medical issue on board indicating positive COVID passenger. ATC turned us into a priority handling. Coordination through medlink provided some guidance and we were met at the gate by appropriate personnel to evaluate the passenger. Passengers were informed of the medical issue and told of the possible positive test at the gate. ZZZ supervisors cleared us to continue our trip.
1779080: We started out vectored off our arrival by ZZZ Center to the southwest with several step down altitudes. 30 miles from the airport we found ourselves at 20,000 MSL which is about 10,000 feet higher than usual for a normal descent. ATC, specifically ZZZ Center, was overloaded with aircraft going into south State X. The Controller brought us around and eventually around 10,000 MSL he told us to go direct to the ZZZ airport. At that time, we were about 15-18 miles away at just under 10,000 MSL. A few minutes later the Controller asked if we had the field in sight to which we replied that we did, but we needed a vector because we were too high to safely attempt the visual approach. We were given a left 360 degree turn and cleared down to 3,000 MSL also while given direct to the ZZZ airport. Upon leveling off at 3,000 MSL we were in a cloud layer and couldn't see the field. We requested lower and were given 1,500 MSL. Once we reach that altitude, we could see the field and was cleared the visual approach to Runway X and to switch to Tower.On final, after fully configuring the aircraft, Tower told us to turn right to a heading of 180. Very confused, we asked him to repeat the instructions at which point we executed a missed approach for a disabled aircraft on the runway. Tower never actually told us to go-around. We were given heading 180 and a climb to 4,000 MSL. Following the level off we were instructed to hold present position however the aircraft will not hold present position on HDG mode. It can only PPOS HOLD while on and active FMS leg with less than .25 NM cross track. Knowing this, we told the Controller we needed a fix to hold and we were given the ZZZ2 NDB which doesn't exist in the database. We instead requested the missed approach fix for the RNAV X approach.We weren't sure or told how long the runway was going to be shut down so the crew started to discuss diverting options which ZZZ1 was the only real viable option. The FMS indicated it would take about 3,500 lbs of fuel and we had about 2;300lbs of reserve fuel on board. From my quick calculation, I had to make a decision fairly soon considering the following: we had about 5;700lbs on fuel on board, unknown runway closure, time, FMS calculation of 3,500 lbs of fuel required to ZZZ1, high volume of ZZZ Center traffic and high controller work load. I sent a message to Dispatch informing them we would attempt one more approach and if unable to make it in we would divert to ZZZ1.We notified ZZZ Center Controller we needed to attempt another approach or we would soon have need to divert. We were given vectors around and cleared for the visual to Runway X once again. As the pilot flying, I opted to proceed direct to the FAF of the RNAV X and continue the visual approach. At about the base leg portion I turned off the autopilot and turned towards the runway. I believe that a slight turn inside of the FAF did not sequence the approach nor the glide path information which led to a position above the glide path. I flew down to correct the glide path all while in and out of 1,000 FPM VVI. I acknowledged the momentary deviations of descent and quickly corrected as I was now on the visual indications from the PAPI's. On short final, a thermal briefly interrupted our descent and with a quick correction back to glide path I corrected the path for a safe landing.I believe the accumulation of all factors above could have led to a critically low fuel situation much quicker than expected. I believe the saturation of airspace on a very busy travel day could have been underestimated in the current climate of understaffed controllers. ZZZ Center controllers were so saturated with aircraft that any chance to hand an aircraft off to a visual approach whether it was really safe to do so or not was attempted. Unsure about divert fuel and runway state created a high-importance, high stress moment of deciding when a divert should occur without having proper data supporting it. Lastly, in a heightened sense of urgency with a tight turn inbound to the runway and sub-sequence 'Cutting the corner' led to the aircraft being in a position higher than the glide path.I would suggest the following for operations into ZZZ Captain only approach and landing. I believe most captains take it upon themselves to make the approach and landing due to the short runway as it is. There should be more 'hip pocket' information whether in the form of a bulletin or some other format that provides rough numbers of divert options, fuel required, routing, etc when a formal alternate is not filed. I also suggest fuel planning take into account busy travel days and add as much fuel as practical for contingencies even on days with VMC conditions that does not preclude landing due to being over max landing weight. I also believe during all forms of training (initial, recurrent, etc) special authorization airports and airports such as ZZZ are discussed. It is my suggestion that ZZZ be a mandatory training event. I can tell you everything you need to know about flying to ZZZ2 yet we don't actually go there in the aircraft. However, airports such as ZZZ are rarely mentioned when we fly there every week. I suggest more 'hangar flying' where scenarios are discussed (such as this one) in a classroom/training environment to get captains to start thinking about scenarios such as these. I'd also like to recommend that one or two approaches from ZZZ3 be included in our Jeppesen charts or company pages. Should ZZZ be shut down for any reason and there is not enough divert fuel to safely make it back to the mainland there will be a 10,000 foot runway available, especially in IMC conditions. Lastly, I suggest that pilots refrain from attempting to cut corners while approaching the runway from greater than 90 degrees. Instead, they should fly the published approach in its entirety including glide slopes or glide paths so that they maintain a safe, stable approach to the runway.
1779082: We were flying a parcel of contaminated blood. The box had the UN1845 on it as well as the Dangerous Goods Form. I thought about it and felt it was correct. Later that evening after signing off duty and the next day I was thinking that the parcel should have also had a UN3373 as well as a category B bio substance label. I only saw the Dangerous Goods Form and parcel that was labeled UN1845.I saw the parcel and inspected it and it's associated paperwork during preflight.Possible incomplete labeling of HAZMAT.At the time I looked the information up in the Dangerous Goods manual as well as online and determined in the short time we had that it only needed the UN1845 and nothing else. The more I thought about it however, I feel that it may should have had the UN3373 and cat B bio labels as well.[More correct procedure];verify with the manuals and if still not sure, discuss it with Dispatch or the Chief Pilot.
1779094: Reflecting back on this flight today, I fear we may not have obtained verbal landing clearance from Tower before touchdown on Runway X at ZZZ. This was my first flight in over two months, and was assigned with another Captain as my First Officer, with no one else present on the flight deck. I had also been on leave earlier in the year. Before we flew, I briefed that two captains flying together as a two-pilot crew complement is a threat, as it does not happen often, and there is an operational bias for the acting First Officer (co-Captain). During the descent, Air Traffic Control vectored us to a close-in base leg to Runway X. Approach Control asked us if we had the field in sight, and I elected to continue with a visual approach, which I believe now was not the best choice for myself. My acting First Officer momentarily lost sight of the field during my turn from base to final, however I had it acquired visually the entire time. I pointed out the field to assist, and the pilot monitoring re-acquired it. This should have resulted in a go-around to rejoin the approach, as this is a team environment, and a two-pilot airplane. I know I did switch the nose-wheel landing light to 'on' during the final approach leg, as that is SOP after being cleared to land, according to FOM. I was focused on flying the plane, slowing down early, and ensuring a stabilized approach. I was not completely in tune with what my co-captain was or was not doing. Stabilized approaches are a topic often discussed in training, so it weighed heavily in my priorities on this day. My co-Captain (pilot monitoring) may not have switched to Tower as it was somewhat a high workload environment and unusual operation, at least to me.I should have recognized the threat of two captains flying together, along with my low state of landing currency, would lead to a chain reaction easily. I should have requested the full ILS to Runway X, or at least a longer final approach leg. I would recommend after a Captain returns to the line after a lengthy vacation, and in my case leave earlier in the year as well, to not pair up with another Captain, but only a highly current First Officer. Although everything was completely my responsibility, this would have eliminated the threat. I recognize that sound aeronautical decision making as it relates to all phases of duty, is the number one factor influencing safety, and it must be practiced even in high-workload environments.
1779133: This [anomaly] was isolated to the APU bleed and even when MX (Maintenance) was still smelling the odor they still signed the aircraft off, given that it went away with engine start. An APU MEL should have been the first thing they did here instead of trying to get the aircraft back out into service. I as Captain was doing the preflight for our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. During the preflight we had a fume event once I selected the APU bleed on. The estimated duration of the event was about one minute. The foul smell came on very strong and immediate. Even with our face coverings (per COVID policy) on in the cockpit it still overwhelmed us, it was that strong. I immediately turned the APU bleed off and opened the cockpit windows. Maintenance then came to the aircraft and did their procedure agreeing the smell was throughout the entire aircraft and coming through on both packs. MX did their procedure and once it was returned to service I had them explain what they did. [MX response] an engine run at the gate and a pack burn. Once we stepped back on the aircraft we still could smell the lingering odor and when I asked about it he said, oh it goes away once you get the engine started'. I believe they knew it was still an issue and still signed it off. With the windows open we turned on the APU bleed again and once again the smell came back. This time sending my First Officer and two flight attendants to the hospital. This also resulted in the cancellation of the flight. When I asked about why they didn't just defer the APU in the first place I heard from someone that the high pressure air cart was broken."
1779136: Pitch trim inop above 250 kts. Returned to departure airport. Pitch trim inop above 250 kts. Returned to departure airport
1779138: While preparing the aircraft for departure from ZZZZ to ZZZ I made contact with our Dispatcher to address a minor deferred maintenance item. While I was on the phone I learned we were getting new paperwork due to the ZZZ1 ATC Center shutting down for sterilization. The Dispatcher was still working on the details due to severe weather to the east of ZZZ1 and indicated that it would be sent to me and the normal station location when it was finished.The Load Master came in wanting me to complete the weight and balance so he could leave. I notified him that we needed new flight release paperwork and told him it should be sitting on his printer and to look for revision 1 at the top of the front page.The Load Master came in again later and indicated that he wanted to do the weight and balance paperwork. I told him I wanted to wait till I had the new paperwork in hand and reviewed. Eventually the paperwork showed up and once we reviewed and did a few more items to finalize the preparation I turned around to notify the Load Master that I was ready for the cross check. If it turns out to be accurate we should possibly notify any crews that will be going into ZZZZ.This flight was already scheduled later than normal due to crew rest requirements and due to the delay in receiving the hard copy of the amended flight release it was running approximately 10 minutes later than the newly scheduled time. 1779152: As I am greeting passengers and handing out wipes, Passenger X seated in X, boards the aircraft with mask barely covering his nose or mouth, him and his family. I gently as them to please cover nose and mouth to board, they comply. Keep in mind even kids barely have mask. They all boarded with mask on chin. When they get to their seats they still have it on. 1779182: My flight began at ZZZ1 with the intent to fly direct to ZZZ for touch and goes and return to ZZZ1. I have flown this particular airplane multiple times with no issues. The return flight was uneventful.
1779188: Flying ZZZ-ZZZ1 the flight experienced a severe updraft in clear air at FL270, which caused the airplane to climb 1,600 ft. despite any attempt to arrest the ascent for roughly 20 seconds. 1779262: Pre-flight planning with ForeFlight didn't show icing conditions where I encountered them in flight. The ZZZ1 live weather cams looked promising too. I should've used multiple resources instead of just ForeFlight. Years of multiple flights on this route gave me a false sense security. I was aware of a small storm moving in. I pushed my limits, trying to arrive before the storm while taking advantage of tail winds.These are all examples of what lead up to my problem. I encountered MVFR conditions over the mountains approximately 40 miles southwest of ZZZ2 at approximately 14,500 ft. I noticed light rime icing, air temp -20c. I climbed and notified ATC I would return to ZZZ due to weather. This was a safe decision. While Heading back at 17,500 ft., it appeared I could make it safely over the top of the weather. I planned to overfly ZZZ2 and look for a safe opening in the weather. I had done this many times before and was still feeling complacent and confident. I informed ATC of my plans to turn around. This was NOT a safe or intelligent decision and caused my problem. I should have acknowledged my original weather concerns and continued back home. While close to ZZZ2 clouds built up vertically rapidly. I started icing up and informed ATC of my situation and needed to climb to FL 18,500 ft. I was at my service ceiling, with few options. Despite pitot heat and MVFR, my pitot tube froze up. I lost all primary instruments, switched to secondary steam gauges, also my O2 tank malfunctioned. This all happened in a matter of minutes. Lack of practice on partial instrument panel failures did not help my situation. I informed ATC I was unable to copy IFR clearances at this time.Maneuvering around building IMC icing conditions, on steam gauges, at my service ceiling, without O2, and now fighting headwinds was very challenging. Flying the plane had to be my sole focus and ATC understood. ATC made me a priority aircraft for me due to my unwillingness to copy my IFR clearance. As I headed southwest my instruments came back online and the weather improved. I subsequently picked up an IFR clearance. I requested lower, plus cancellation of IFR from ZZZ Center. ZZZ Center asked if I was still in distress. I assured ATC everything was fine now. I was no longer considered an aircraft in a priority handling situation. As a preventative safety measure, planes without deicing equipment should not fly near icing conditions even in VMC. Traditional VFR cloud separation rules, while legal are not always safe, especially when potentially hazardous conditions exist. A good preventative measure would have been not to fly at all that day.

1779386: Descending on LINKK 1 arrival ATC cleared us at some point (think above 10.000 feet) for the ILS 27 approach. Pilot Monitoring re-selected the ILS 27 connecting the transition from RDFSH (which was not done on initial FMC setup). Our altitude was set at 6000 passed RDFSH. We never set FAF altitude to keep the descent.Houston approach checked if we were cleared for the approach. After that, I realized we were supposed to descend via the transition. No further ATC communication was received however after the crew debrief and looking at the approach plate again, the altitudes were mandatory altitude restrictions and we don't think we made GEYGR and/ or SYYKO. I was the First Officer and pilot monitoring on this flight IAH. We were cleared to descend via the LINKK1 arrival except maintain 300 knots. Then, 320 knots. Then, as fast as practical until LINKK. Then we were cleared for the approach from RDFSH and maintain 210 knots until FESTA. We had 6000 feet in the MCP window as this was the bottom altitude for the STAR. After being cleared the approach, I failed to set a lower altitude. Shortly after RDFSH (and level at 6000') ATC asked if we were descending on the approach. We were immediately aware of our mistake and the captain began descending. GEYGR and SYYKO (the next two fixes on the approach after RDFSH) had mandatory altitudes of 4000' and 3000', respectively. Because of our delayed descent after RDFSH, we were high at both of those fixes. The multiple airspeed changes on the arrival caused a distraction and I failed to notice that I hadn't set a lower altitude to continue the approach after RDFSH. That being the case, it was still my job as pilot monitoring to set the lower altitude and I failed to do it.
1779398: On taxi out of parking, contacted Ground for taxi clearance. Was given instructions to taxi [Taxiway] A, B1, Z, S2 for Runway 10L. On Taxiway Zulu, Ground asked us about the B1 signage. We told him that we saw the [Taxiway] B1 sign and proceeded B1 to [Taxiway] Zulu. After talking with Ground, we looked at the Jepps (Jeppesen) 10-9 taxi page and saw that after [Taxiway] A, the Taxiway B1 turns left to the northwest (approx. a 45 degree angle/ jog) to join [Taxiway] Zulu, where as we turned slightly to the left proceeding north to join [Taxiway] Zulu. The [Taxiway] B1 sign on Taxiway Alpha did not show any kind of directional arrow of the Taxiway B1 like many other airports that have similar offset taxiways. My recommendation is to change the [Taxiway] B1 sign to add the directional arrow to show turn or to rename the 2nd half of the angle/jog of Taxiway B1 to emphasize the direction of taxi that Ground wants us to take.
1779401: On final, Runway XXL, ZZZ, Night, 1000 foot ceiling, Me (Captain) flying, gusty winds, very light load, FO low currency- only 150 hrs in type since hired 1 year ago, and has not been flying much. I was hand flying at 2,000 feet on normal ILS. Called for gear down, flaps 15 at approximately 2,000 feet and flaps 30 landing, check at about 1500 feet. FO ran check list, while I hand flew the approach. The winds were gusty, our target was +15 ref and it was night. I saw flap refs change on airspeed tape, and glanced at gear lights when FO ran checklist, but I did not have full attention to FO duties since it was dark and gusty. We broke out at 1,000 feet, I called clear to land and set missed approach altitude. At 500 feet we simultaneously got the 500 auto call out and Too Low Flaps. I simultaneously, started a Go-Around (finger to toga button) and looked at flap gauge - which was at 25. But I hesitated on the go-around when I saw why we got the GPWS. I commanded flaps set to 30, which the FO immediately did. We were then about 350-400 feet and stable, and I continued to a normal landing. After landing I realized, even though there was adequate time to set the flaps to 30, I should have gone around. We debriefed after parking. The FO said he just missed the flaps in setting and checking on the checklist, most likely due to being low time in aircraft and rusty from time off. I missed his wrong setting, due to the dark and the gusty winds requiring my attention. I said I should have gone around, and that he as well should have told me to. I am confident if I had not immediately recognized why we got the too low flaps and immediately corrected it, I would not have continued.

1779430: While doing preflight walk around, I noticed the fueler was using the pressure refueling when they shouldn't have been because it was MEL'd. 1779446: Captain (CA) was PF and First Officer (FO) was PM. We had a crew alert action of AUTOFLT FCU1 failure not far from our initial descent for the STAR. CA was working the crew alert issue and Center called saying what the CA heard was 'Flight ABC', Direct ZZZZZ descend via ZZZZZ1' (CA was in the QRH, reading about or looking for the crew alert issue). After talking with the FO on the ground in ZZZ, after the event, the FO thought the read back something like 'Flight ABC direct ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1.' Then, PM made sure PF was inserting the bottom altitude of STAR in the FCU (Meaning PM understood the clearance to descend via the ZZZZZ1). PF did insert the bottom altitude. Then, shortly afterwards, we hit some moderate turbulence and PF decided to start descend early because he could not read the QRH, hoping to get into some clear air. Then we were told we descended and there may have been a flight deviation. I did not think so at the time because of the clearance I understood.I believe there were several causal factors on this event. 1) Pilot Inexperience. The FO was on the Type X aircraft and in March was awarded the Type Y aircraft. But from March through December, all the FO did was go to Type Y training, and IOE. This was the FO's first flight since IOE. The FO was going very slow making sure no mistakes were made. The PF was also going very slow to ensure all FO tasks were completed. 2) Task saturation (crew alert event, pilot inexperience, turbulence and clearance understanding). Combined, this put both pilots in a 'caution situation.' The PF, was trying for something like this would not happen from the moment the flight started by making sure he was slow and deliberate on all his thoughts and actions. 3) Turbulence event. We descended early because PF had a hard time reading the QRH. 4) PF flying and completing crew alert actions. In this case, it may have made a difference, but, I do not believe it would have made a difference, because the PM understood the clearance from Center was a clearance to descend Via, and when the turbulence started, the person working the crew alert action would have said descend to get out of the turbulence the QRH could be read. The same outcome would have happened.Suggestions - Verify the clearance, no matter the circumstances...In this particular event, the PF should have verified the clearance knowing the proficiency of the other pilot may not have been 100%. A pilot may be 'Current' with regards to the official written documents approved by the FAA, but they may have not been proficient...(I do not know how this can be fixed...) In preparation for descent, Status Page showed an inoperative system the CA/PF noticed. CA was in the process of investigating the crew alert message that caused it. We had a seasoned CA in the Jump Seat who was assisting in the lookup for the crew alert actions, if any, and the code was send to Maintenance. In that time, we received a call from Center to proceed 'direct to ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1.' I read the clearance back 'direct ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1 arrival'. I then conveyed to the CA/Pilot Flying 'direct to ZZZZZ, we can descend via the ZZZZZ1' and I backed CA up to set direct ZZZZZ in the FMS and dialed in the lowest altitude in the arrival for south landings. We verified the altitude. While inbound to ZZZZZ, we were at FL390 and encountered some occasions of moderate turbulence and continuous light chop. The CA/PF commenced a descent to avoid remaining in the turbulent conditions. I contacted the Center to let them know we were descending out of FL390. They called back to ask what was the reason for the descent. I stated we had encountered moderate to light turbulence and needed to descend to avoid it. They called back asking me to confirm the reason for descent was turbulence. I confirmed. Then, before we were handed off to the next frequency, the controller asked us to contact a number for possible altitude deviation. There was a misunderstanding, on my part, of the vertical clearance in the call with Center with the initial clearance for ZZZZZ1 and I passed that misinterpretation on to the CA/PF.It was my first flight in over a month, preceded only by sim events way back in September and just prior to OE. This was a threat up front. Hadn't flown in this environment in over 18 months. We had multiple distractions due to the crew alert and system loss being addressed, icing conditions and turbulence. The ATC frequency was covering high traffic volume so there was a significant amount of talking on the frequency. We had both been up very early in order to be ready at report time. My expectation bias led me to believe we were cleared to 'descend via' when we were cleared only laterally for the approach.We could have briefed the arrival prior to addressing the crew alert and done a transfer of control of the aircraft and radios. I could have had ATC repeat the clearance, once the PF was back with me, so that they could communicate directly what the intended clearance was. I could have stated the clearance exactly as it was read back to eliminate any 'single point' of interpretation, or misinterpretation.
1779450: FL360 ISA -54C, REC MAX ALT (recommended maximum altitude) 39.8. MCDU weight 132.8. Green dot speed 229 KIAS. Vls 220 [lowest selectable speed for autopilot]. Takeoff Data Performance derived green dot corrected one knot per 1,000 feet above FL200 equals an under FL200 green dot speed of 213. A 213 KIAS green dot from 3.5.4 of the Performance Manual is the speed for a 141 knot jet (8,200 pound difference). FAC1 (flight augmentation computer) and FAC2 averaged to 140 kts. Flaps full landing. Vls 128 KIAS. MCDU Vapp was 123 (5 knots into the hook). Out of an abundance of caution, we added 10 knots to get to Vls+5. Landed uneventfully and under max landing weight even if you added in the 8-9 kts (worst case scenario). Documented all in the aircraft logbook. For the committee, this is the second 319 that has presented a large difference in MCDU weight vs. calculated weight from FAC1/FAC2 (which generates Vapp and Vls on a basic jet). Either the jets EOW (empty operating weight) is wrong, the software is corrupted or the alpha vanes are out of calibration. I think safety and maintenance need to do a deep dive in to the FAC's and alpha vanes and any software changes of late. The only other explanation is an error in the EOW which is hard to envision. I would like a response directly from the committee about this and [another] aircraft which was previously accepted in to report system. I am concerned that given the increase in the number of pilots who are not flying regularly due to schedule reductions, this could result in an incident or mishap.
1779455: This flight is part of the second trip to be on a landing currency waiver. Landings expired [Date]. Waivers issued for the next two pilot trips. I have stated plainly to the training desk I want to regain my currency vs flying not current on waivers. One area of safety concern arose prior to this flight due to being non-current. Scheduling called the CA the morning of the flight asking to crew the leg ZZZ to ZZZ1 with just 2 pilots (CA and myself) because they could not find a replacement FO for the trip. CA agreed after checking with union contracts. Safety Issue: CA was unaware I would be arriving for work on a waiver. The CA should be notified well in advance instead of at sign in that a non-qualified pilot would be on their flight. The only way the CA found out I was on a waiver is when I notified him. To be clear: I was never assigned FO in the system. The situation was resolved without ever assigning me as FO. The safety issue is with the PIC being unaware they will have a non-qualified crew member.Issuance of this waiver is only made known to the non-current pilot. Other crew members are un-aware until sign in.This waiver should be rarely used vs the recent expanded use and it needs to be depicted plainly in schedules being visible to all crew.
1779456: After we were clear for takeoff on the Runway XX, at ZZZ airport. The Captain applied power, he waited for the engine to stabilize, then he pressed TOGA. As the plane started moving, it suddenly started veering to the right. He tried to correct it by pressing the left rudder, but the aircraft did not respond right away. After a few seconds, the plane veer back to the left, but it only went about 45 degrees to the left. After that, the Captain pressed the right rudder and was able to bring it back to control. Furthermore, we stopped at the runway, then, I called the tower to abort the takeoff. Finally, we were able to taxi off the runway and went back to the gate. Cleared for takeoff Runway XX. Engines spooled up 'taxiing' up to takeoff point on Runway XX. With engines at 40% N1 pushed TOGA button and throttles advanced. We observed the white arcs advancing but the plane didn't seem to be accelerating normally. As I glanced inside to ensure the auto throttles were engaged (they were) the aircraft started to drift right. I tried to correct back with the rudder as we always do but it had no effect. As the right drift continued I rejected the take off and had to use almost full nose wheel tiller to correct back to centerline. We smelled burning rubber, so we taxied clear of the runway and had ARFF (Airport Rescue Firefighting) come inspect the gear and wheels. No problems found by ARFF. Tower had the runway inspected. Nothing found. I had ARFF follow us to the gate where we made an AML entry and had a lengthy discussion with Maintenance. During the takeoff roll the throttles never made it to Takeoff Thrust and I was looking outside the whole time, but the speed achieved was well below 80 kts. Probably around 40-45 kts. In addition, on taxi out when brakes were applied to stop in line they often 'chattered.'We suspected a brake problem or asymmetric thrust.I'm not sure why it happened. I've seen asymmetric thrust before and it is easily corrected with rudder to steer back to centerline. This plane was very difficult to get turning back to the left.
1779463: I was the flying pilot, we were kept high the whole time. Then we were given [Runway] XXR GPS Y, as we turned, the turn was inside the approach fix, it was tight. I turned to final and we looked high and I wasn't comfortable, so we asked for a go-around. I initiated TOGA, we were approximately 2,200 feet when we did the go-around, and began the go-around process and around 2,500 feet. ATC asked to maintain 3,000 feet. We got extremely busy and by the time we realized it we were at 3,500 feet. We descended to 3,000 feet and we asked to extend the downwind.I had been out for a year and half, and since I gotten back, I did not fly that much, also was off last month and half of this month due to COVID-19, but also I should have asked for extended downwind in the airport, should not [have] allowed the Controller to rush us and I have learned a lesson.Don't accept any arrival that I am not comfortable with.
1779483: I was acting as pilot flying on the flight to ZZZ. While flying on our assigned course direct to the ZZZ airport, approximately 100 miles from our destination, while conducting the arrival and approach briefings, ATC Center assigned us to turn left 10 degrees, which I complied with by selecting heading mode on the FCP, and selecting the desired heading with the heading bug. Several minutes later, the Controller, again, assigned us to proceed direct to the ZZZ airport. I selected in the FMS direct to the ZZZ airport, confirmed the selection with my captain, and executed the flight plan modification. However, I had neglected to select NAV mode, which resulted in the aircraft continuing on its previously assigned heading for several minutes while I finished the arrival briefing, resulting in the course to show a full-scale deflection to the left (south). Upon finishing the briefing, I realized the missed step, and immediately turned back toward the course and armed NAV mode. Having recently switched over to ZZZ approach, within several minutes the controlled queried us about our position, informing us we were left of course. We notified the controller that we were rejoining the course. The controller then assigned us to proceed direct to the ZZZ airport again, which we selected in the FMS, confirmed, and executed, this time ensuring NAV mode was engaged. The flight continued without issue.This event was caused by lack of recent flight experience, as well as momentary task-saturation.This has not been a reoccurring trend for me during training or during revenue operations. I plan to continue to maintain a high level of situational awareness in the cockpit to trap threats before they become errors. I also plan to ensure I am making appropriate FCP selections when I am making an adjustment to our course.
1779512: During passenger boarding there were many people not wearing their face mask. I was also spending time finding room for bags. It was a busy time and I forgot to brief my exit row passengers.
1779516: Crew stepped off aircraft and was on jetbridge. When I looked at my handheld it said we were boarding. So I replied back we had not been cleaned or sprayed yet so we were not boarding. About 3 to 4 minutes later 2 cleaners came up the airstairs and boarded. One had an electric vacuum in hand the other had [a] trash bag in hand. Shortly after a 3rd cleaner came on board with a bag of supplies and boarded the aircraft and put [the] bag down by the First Class Lavatory. About 5 minutes later another cleaner (gentleman with nothing in his hands) came up the airstairs and boarded the aircraft. Within 10 to 15 seconds the first 2 cleaners came off the aircraft and right after them the other gentleman came off the aircraft saying 'we are good to go.' One of my crewmember's asked him was the aircraft sprayed. He repeated 'we were good to go' and proceeded to exit the jetbridge door and down the airstairs. I and the other crew member both said I don't think the aircraft was sprayed as neither of us saw the cone being put in place nor did we see the sprayer. At this time the last cleaner with the bag with supplies came off. I asked her has this aircraft been sprayed? She said what did he say, I said he said yes, she proceeded to exit the aircraft. I said can you please show me what you have in that bag, because if there is no sprayer in there, then there is no way our aircraft has been sprayed. She then said 'I will tell him to come back.' At this time the Gate Agent came down to see if we were ready to board. I explained the situation to the Agent and she said 'oh no I am so sorry, that's not right.' The Captain was on the jetbridge with us and we were all in agreement that we needed to be sprayed before we could start boarding. The previous gentleman came back up the airstairs with sprayer in hand and sprayed aircraft. When he was done, without further delay, we boarded and departed. The Gate Agent was very apologetic about the incident.
1779519: The hand sanitizer installed on this aircraft is in a dangerous location. Several times I have hit my back center spine and also hit my arm on it. 1779552: Uneventful 3 hour VFR flight from ZZZ1 at 16,500 feet. Just after starting my VFR descent for SRQ was advised by ZJX Center that TPA Approach would not take the hand-off and told to squawk 1200. I switched to TPA Approach for SRQ airport and monitored frequency as I continued VFR descent to 8,500 feet - above the top of Class B. Tower worked me in perfectly on intersecting Runway 4.Although 121 traffic is down considerably, FAA now needs to assess the current flight activity - which for ZZZ Approach certainly exceeded the ability of 1 Controller to control all sectors, and add back controllers before someone gets hurt.
1779571: The landing was excellent, Rollout of the aircraft was straight and smooth. When reaching for the toe brakes, I had a left brake but no right break. The toe brakes are little round pads on the top outsides of each rudder and are not easily identified with your toes even with soft sole shoes which I wear to fly in. I did not realize my foot had slipped off or was not on it properly until it was too late. The aircraft took a left direction as I was wishing to slow down. I let go of the left brake and caught it/straightened it with the right rudder. Right after I had it straight, I removed my right foot to lift it higher up to engage the right brake. The aircraft took a sharp left direction went onto the grass which with then full right rudder and the right brake did not help. The slope away from the runway is very steep and the aircraft was not able to be brought back up onto the runway, so I kept it straight and aimed at the taxiway, With the airplane tailwheel not willing to provide steering since it was on grass and the slope was still steep, the aircraft slid over the other side of the taxiway. The aircraft refused to turn right with all my efforts, so my next choice was to hit trees and or a building, so I choose to ground loop the airplane to avoid the trees and building. NO damage was done to any property including taxi signs or even lights. The aircraft came to a stop 180 degrees to the landing direction. No one was hurt in any manner since the speed was not very fast. The right gear leg collapsed as it stopped and the prop hit the grass and broke one of the tips. The engine was shut down and everything was turned off. The Runway XX is a challenging runway since there is zero room for error.
1779578: I was on a instrument approach to CID talking with Chicago Center and picking up ice. Chicago asked me to cancel IFR clearance as early as possible because a (Company) plane was landing behind me. I changed to the CTAF frequency and made a 10 miles out announcement. I broke out around 2,000 ft msl/1,200 ft. AGL and change back to Chicago Center and cancelled my IFR clearance with ATC. I switched the comm back to CTAF and continued the approach, however, the button push failed to change to CTAF and stayed on Chicago Center and I missed that. During the approach I was stunned to see a vehicle pull out onto the approach end of the runway and stop at the very end just beyond the runway end lighting. I was still approximately 1-1 1/2 miles out. I had to make a decision to land or go back up into the icing. As the runway was 8,000 ft. long I elected to extend and land in the 2nd half of the runway as opposed to risk picking up excessive ice and endangering my aircraft.
1779583: As background, ZZZ was heavily congested with training and weekend aviators. The approach to the downwind leg was reported via UNICOM as 4nm SE to enter a 45 - downwind entry. We coordinated spacing with another crosswind aircraft to follow us for spacing in the pattern.Reported downwind uneventfully and recognized the aircraft we were to follow and minimized their pattern to minimize spacing conflicts. Reported [our] base turn to UNICOM, uneventfully. Our track on base leg was approximately 2 nm from the end of the runway. At no time was our location questioned by the conflicting near miss aircraft.Reported a base to final turn, uneventfully and unquestioned. Upon the completion of the turn to final, I focused on vertical alignment to the runway and did not see the conflicting near miss aircraft. The PNF (Pilot Not Flying), in a radio call questioned the conflicting near miss aircraft to determine the position upon hearing the UNICOM base report. For clarification, the safety pilot - PNF, is a seasoned 121 CA (Captain) and highly experienced in the PA24-250 with close to 2,000 hours in type. After it was determined the conflicting aircraft turned inside of our location, resulting in cutting us off placing our aircraft in a hazardous flight profile, PNF took control of the aircraft in a professionally coordinated manner.At this time, the conflicting near miss aircraft was well within 1/4 NM and somewhat above our altitude, which was approximately 300 ft AGL. Because of the proximity to us, and apparently being unaware of our location, the resolution was complex. Keep in mind in their base to final turn (RH pattern) with a low wing aircraft [they] would have then been unable to locate us.Additionally, as we both rolled out on final we were both nearly lined up on the centerline, the closure rate was approximately 42 FPS and without evasive action, contact would have occurred in about 30 seconds, short of the runway, all due to the difference in V-ref and approach speeds. The PNF recognized this before I had visual contact with the conflicting traffic and they took control of the aircraft and became the PF.The evasive maneuver was complex in that [the other aircraft's] intentions seemed unpredictable and we did not want to initiate a go-around with the associated high deck angle, which would interrupt visual conflict with the conflicting traffic. Communication from their aircraft was weak and seemed confused as they, on short final, radioed 'how many aircraft are in the pattern and where are you located'. We discussed the possibility that they may begin a go around and that would worsen the conflict since we may have lost visual contact and keep in mind... at this time we were behind their location and out of view.In the interest of safety, we chose to sidestep slightly left and to pass them on the level and then after we cleared the aircraft to begin a go around. The point we were trying to achieve was to maintain visual contact with the conflicting aircraft until we passed clear of their position.
1779584: Aircraft X was landing HHR on an IFR flight plan. There were multiple weather cells in the airspace and LAX Aircraft were deviating around the final to the north. I had DYNR/EAFR combined and was quite busy handling the coordination for the deviations with STAR/ZUMR and figuring out the sequence for dependent simultaneous ILS's. I advised Aircraft X of some weather, but did not issue a heavy precipitation on the route to HHR. I asked Aircraft X if they could advise HHR in sight because the HHR weather was reporting BKN045 and LAX Aircraft could not get the visual. We also did not have staffing available in the facility to open up parallel monitors for independent simultaneous approaches. Aircraft X responded HHR in sight and I cleared them for the visual approach. Traffic for LAX was increasing and frequency congestion was becoming a problem. Aircraft x did have delays with their read backs/understanding as well. Aircraft X went down to 1100 ft. in a 2000 ft. MVA and I issued a low altitude alert. Aircraft X responded with, 'correcting'. Then Aircraft X kept heading toward the LAX finals and I asked them once or twice if they still see HHR. Then the HHR weather deteriorated to IFR and I advised Aircraft X that they'd need the localizer approach. I told the CIC (Controller in Charge) to open up monitors, they were trying to find staffing at the time already. I then got Aircraft X above the MVA and vectored them for the approach while continuing to deal with LAX deviations. After clearing Aircraft X for the localizer runway 25, I switched them to HHR tower, monitors had opened at this time. Aircraft X then proceeded to do a left turn southbound on about a 7 mile final without notification to me from HHR tower. Monitor 1 then called HHR and asked what was going on. Aircraft X then checked back on frequency with me heading 160, no coordination. I climbed Aircraft X above the MVA and vectored them for another approach. I also asked the pilot if he could accept the approach and they agreed they could. I was then relieved.[We need] staffing. We have more than enough people on a shift to facilitate monitors being open. So many coworkers are worried about their long breaks and getting done early that we are leaving the operational floor short between shifts.
1779586: Aircraft Y had taxied into parking via Taxiway A and was pulling into his parking spot on the ramp. Aircraft X was doing a touch and go on Runway 14L which is directly west of the ramp.
