1779588: Aircraft X took off RIL climbing to 15,000 feet, at around 10,000 feet, Aircraft X informed me he was having a landing gear issue, could not climb further and needed to return to RIL right away. I sent him direct to RIL. He had good sight of the terrain and once he got the visual he was cleared the visual approach. Aircraft Y was another aircraft going into RIL north of the airport level at 14,000 feet with no approach clearance. Aircraft X appeared to be circling to the runway so I did not clear Aircraft Y into the airport. Aircraft X then popped back on the frequency saying they cannot land at RIL and need to go to [another airport]. Aircraft X at this point was 8,000 feet climbing eastbound still in priority handling status. I re-radar identified Aircraft X and had them climb to 13,000 feet to try to maintain positive Minimum IFR Altitudes. They affirmed they had good sight of the terrain. I called the traffic to both Aircraft Y and Aircraft X hoping to apply visual separation. Neither saw one another so they both remained 13,000 feet (Aircraft X) and 14,000 feet (Aircraft Y).Once able, I vectored Aircraft X south to get him away from high Minimum IFR Altitudes and the RIL approach corridor. I asked Aircraft Y 'if I turn you direct to RIL, do you think you can get a visual with the airport?' Aircraft Y responded he could. I then said 'Aircraft Y, cleared direct RIL' I then went back to Aircraft X and asked fuel remaining, souls on board, what altitude they could climb to, and then explained why 15,000 feet was not feasible. I offered GJT etc. While discussing options with Aircraft X, I noticed Aircraft Y leave 14,000 feet and begin their descent while still 3 to 4 miles from Aircraft X. I gave a traffic alert to Aircraft Y and told them to climb back to 14,000 feet immediately. I then gave the traffic alert to Aircraft X. Aircraft Y climbed back up, I gained the 5 miles and climbed Aircraft X up and gave Aircraft Y the visual approach to RIL. I issued Aircraft Y advisories.In this session I had two separate situations. A pilot deviation, an arrival rush, a handful of ornery pilots on the ground at RIL clogging the frequency looking for releases off the ground. Had RIL sector been separated out through our split frequency procedures, this may not have occurred. There was a lot of frequency congestion between the sector's two frequencies which blocked transmissions to the priority handling aircraft. We used to do this procedure and have been recently barred from doing it again. This procedure could have helped!
1779605: Ten minutes into the flight, we received an ACARS message. It stated that oxygen cylinders were on-board. We did not receive a Dangerous Goods Form on the ground. Once we landed in ZZZ1, we reached out to Dispatch and received a copy of the Dangerous Goods form. I signed it, and it was faxed back to ZZZ. Approximately ten minutes into our climb out from ZZZ, we received a message from Dispatch telling us we had four oxygen bottles in the cargo area. We did not receive a Dangerous Goods Form from the Ramp prior to our departure. We continued on to our destination. In ZZZ1 we were given the proper paperwork. Captain signed it, and paperwork was sent, via fax, to ZZZ.
1779610: We were descending on the DSNEE 1 arrival but had been assigned several speeds, the last was 200 KIAS. I had been using speed intervention (SPD INTV) to manage the speed but switched to Level Change after passing the last intermediary altitude restriction and being asked to expedite our descent through 5000' for traffic. I announced the new mode and verified 4000' in the altitude window (the final altitude on the STAR).After we were clear off traffic, SoCal cleared us for the ILS Runway 30. I closed the discontinuity in the FMS after MIDDS, checked with the Pilot Monitoring (PM) and executed it. My PM then prompted that we could set 1600' in the altitude window for the FAF at GUNEY. I did so but failed to verify that we were in VNAV. At 3800' the PM noticed we were below the 4000' restriction at GOOFY. I reversed the descent and started climbing back to 4000'. We ended up 300' low at GOOFY. At that point, SoCal gave us a heading to join final and a descent to 2000'. We complied with the new clearance, were re-cleared for the ILS, and continued without further event.The continued use of SPD INTV would have done the same job but protected us from descending below a coded altitude on the arrival. Next time I need to descend quickly, I will try to stay in VNAV if I am continuing on an arrival that connects with an approach with step-down altitudes. Also using VVMI to verify my level of automation after an altitude selection will trap this kind of error in the future.
1779621: While on the ZZZZZX Arrival we were at FL350. We were given a descent to FL330 and to cross ZZZZZ at FL240. I set FL24000 in the MCP and the Captain set cruise in the FMC to FL330 and we started down. I looked at the ND display and saw FL240 next to ZZZZZ and a Top of Descent point and thought we were set up correctly. The Controller did not say anything to us and handed us off to the next Controller. You can say there may be some currency issues in that I have only flown about 9 flights since March, and this was 3rd time at the controls in the last 30 days. However I have been on the aircraft for almost X years and I know what it's supposed to do. I just misread the ND display and didn't see the A (At or Above) next to FL240.
1779626: Directed to fly NNCEE arrival. Directed to descend to FL300 and then via NNCEE, subsequently ATC issued a late descent to 10 miles east of LINKK at 17000 feet. Programmed FMS and determined unable to meet restriction without relief from ATC.ATC provided relief, I flew a fast descent, and met altitude restriction. I immediately informed the center controller that we would need relief from this clearance. The controller responded that relief was granted but try to make the 17000 crossing 10 miles east of LINKK and it was okay if we were fast at the intersection.At LINKK we did make the 17000 and were approximately 320KTS and slowing. 1779672: During push back from gate we started engine number 2 and disconnected from the pushback tug normally. We then noticed a faint burning smell in the cockpit that was present for only a moment. During this time we were positioned directly in front of a vehicle access road and there were multiple trucks driving in front of the aircraft. The First Officer and I discussed the smell and determined that due to the smell only being present for a short moment we were confident that it came from the vehicles near the aircraft. We then continued to taxi making a right turn on Taxiway Bravo. While taxiing, we received a call from the Flight Attendant. She told us that the back of the cabin was a little foggy. At this point I had two indications of a possible fire on board the aircraft, so I immediately contacted ZZZ ramp control and Requested Priority Handling and advised them that we had smoke in the cabin of the aircraft and needed to return to the gate. Ramp control cleared us to do a 180 degree turn and taxi to the gate and advised us that the rescue services were on their way. After making a 180 degree turn to get the aircraft heading back towards the gate, I then called the Flight Attendant back. I asked her if she had any updates on the situation with the smoke. She advised me that it was now mostly dissipated and that she had checked the lavatory and the cargo compartment and there was no evidence of smoke in either location. She also noted that she did not notice a smell of any sort during the time the smoke was primarily present. We spoke about the conditions of the passengers and she stated that the cabin was relatively calm and the passengers were doing just fine. I informed her that we would be returning to the gate for an expeditious deplaning. The First Officer and I discussed whether to perform the smoke fire or fumes memory action item but determined that it was not necessary due to the absence of smoke in the cockpit and due to the knowledge that the smoke in the cabin was dissipating. We then continued with the smoke fire or fumes checklist. The checklist had us push out both the re-circulation fan and the Gasper fan switches, and at this point a personnel from fire crash rescue started marshaling us into the gate. In order to return to the gate as quickly as possible to deplane the passengers, I made the decision to discontinue the checklist. To eliminate further potential sources of contaminated air entering the aircraft, I took it upon myself to shut off pack number 2 and the APU bleed at this time. Passenger number 1 was already off. We parked at the gate and performed a shut down checklist. We had the passengers deplane the aircraft using the mobile stairs at the gate. I don't recall the exact number of passengers we had on board but I believe it was less than 10, so deplaning was very quick. To ensure that the aircraft was not powered while emergency services personnel checked for the location of the source of the smoke, we immediately terminated the aircraft. EMS was present to ask each passenger of their condition and I was told that no one had any issue including the crew. Finally, I contacted Dispatch to inform them of the situation, and entered a discrepancy in the maintenance logbook.
1779675: Landed in ZZZ was normal. Visibility was 1/2 mile fog snow RVR 2,400 feet. Runway code was 3/3/3 and the previous landing reported fair braking. We landed flaps 30 auto brake 3. The airplane slowed down normal. Had to roll to the end due to taxiway closures. As we approached the end, I told my First Officer [we] needed to go slow in case it was slick. As we turned off [Runway] XXL the plane started to slide in the turn. Used left engine thrust reverse to help. Hit 3 taxi lights we did not leave the pavement. Taxied to the ramp notified ATC of the situation and was told we hit 3 taxi lights. Called and notified Dispatch and Maintenance Control. Made logbook entry. On walk around no aircraft damaged noted. After an otherwise normal landing in ZZZ, the aircraft started to slide on a patch of ice as the Captain was turning off the runway and onto the taxiway. Although the aircraft never departed the paved surface, we were uncertain if the slide caused any damage to the taxiway lights. We informed ground control of the slide and the possibility of striking a taxiway light. Ground control notified the airport operations to have them take a look. They reported back that there were indeed 3 taxi lights down. Weather conditions at the time were 1/2 mile visibility with snow and fog. The [Runway] XXL runway condition code was reported as 3/3/3. We landed with auto brake 3 and the aircraft slowed normally. ATC requested a turnoff at the end of the runway due to numerous taxiway closures. It was at the end of the runway while turning off that the aircraft entered into the slide. No damage to the aircraft was found by either the flight crew or Maintenance upon inspection of the aircraft at the ramp.Unfortunately despite the rest of the runway having adequate braking, the runway end was incredibly slick. The only suggestion that could've prevented this would have been to make the turn at an even slower speed in order to possibly prevent the slide.
1779677: ZZZ Center queried us about our routing. Apparently they expected us to go further east due to ZZZ1 Center having a limited number of operating frequencies. Our filed routing showed us [on one routing and our clearance was different] based on what we heard and read back. ZZZ Center was under the impression that we had received an amendment to our flight plan. At our departure airport we were unable to get our clearance through ACARS and had to receive clearance on the radio. The flight continued without any further anxiety.ZZZ1 Center connections with their remote receivers and transmitter antennas were not operational, or so we were told. If we had been able to get our clearance on ACARS we could verify the clearance and that nothing was missed on either our part or the Controller's. During cruise, ZZZ Center queried us about our routing. It seems they expected us on a different route further east due to ZZZ1 Center having communication issues. We double checked our FMC and the clearance that we both copied [earlier] since we couldn't get it through the ACARS, and it was clear what our route was. ZZZ ATC thought we had received an amendment but we never did. He explained ZZZ1's situation and what potentially happened, re-cleared us and agreed that nothing wrong on our side had occurred, just ATC misunderstanding. We continued our flight and landed without any further issues.
1779705: [I] missed applying an MEL with a fuel penalty. Corrected the mistake and resent the [release] for the Captain to sign.I got to work 10 minutes early for an [early morning] shift. The license had expired for the Jeppesen chart viewer on my computer. I called the help desk. After trouble shooting for 10 minutes, I was told to find another machine. There were no more licenses available. My workload was 20 fights vs. a normal plan of 18. Seventeen of my flights were scheduled out in a one hour period. (Shift starts at XA:00. First flight due out at XC:00 and the 17th was due out at XD:00). I had a major snow storm out over the plains, frequency outage in the vicinity of ZZZ. I had to build around ZZZ and had a couple of transcontinental flights for good measure. After the computer delay of 30 minutes I went to work at XA:30 looking at weather and MELs and contacting ramps with restrictions. I have long advocated for a maximum of 18 flights on [this] desk. They were originally designed for this number (some dispute this claim). I have had discussions with numerous members of management, [supervisory dispatchers] and coworkers about why this should be the maximum. We have experienced and documented problems when the number of flights exceeds 18. When coupled with the compression (numerous departures in a short time period) it only makes these types of mistakes more likely. Today, it caused me to rush and miss a MEL item. I feel like I was setup to fail when I walked through the door. An inoperative computer system, excessive number of flights and a tight compression of departures. I realize that responsibility rests on me for my work, but these issues continue to be ignored time and time again. first release was generated at approx. XB:05. This particular flight had two MELs. The first was a broken lock and the other was a fuel penalty. I looked at the lock MEL first, called the ramp with the restrictions and then failed to go back and account for the fuel penalty.
1779712: We were cleared for the ILS for Runway XXR in ZZZ. ZZZ at the time was CAT II minimums showing 3/4 mile visibly and 300 feet ceilings. We started getting a LOC flag prior to final approach fix. We broke off the approach and executed a missed approach. Knowing that there are many variables as to why we would not be getting reliable LOC information we elected to try a CAT II again but to a different runway. We go set up again for the ILS for Runway XXR. While intercepting we received a LOC flag again about 18 DME from the LOC. Again knowing that there are many variables that go into receiving a good signal we decided to give it a few more miles. We caught the LOC and GS and executed a CAT II to a landing. The only thing I can think that was improper about this circumstance was the continuation of a CAT II after receiving a LOC flag. It's being 18 miles out I believe we were in some gray area. At any rate we wrote up the LOC on the aircraft so that it could be ruled out as the cause. Perhaps the LOC on Runway XXR was not strong enough or there was interference from the proceeding aircraft causing the localizer. Or it was the aircraft itself. I think we did most everything right. It just felt weird to write up the LOC after a successful CAT II approach. I didn't see any reason we shouldn't try the CAT II we had plenty of fuel and had an alternate already specified.
1779722: [We were] inbound to Ontario, CA. Prior to the descent the flight was brief following the [approach briefing]. Ontario was landing 8L and 8R, with good VFR weather and a light wind from the west. The crew descended on the Ziggy 7 arrival and was given a clearance to track outbound on 270 radial after Paradise VOR. There was a distraction trying to set up the tracking of a radial in the FMS by the pilot monitoring. As the pilot flying I decided to use the VOR and VOR mode to accomplish this. We complied with clearance and were cleared to 3,000 feet.After leveling at 3,000 feet a traffic report was issued for a helicopter at 1 o'clock and 4,000 feet. We were given a base leg heading of 320. After starting this turn an amber target showed up on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) at our altitude. I was looking out the window for traffic, in a matter of 2 seconds the Captain pushed forward on the controls, we got a TA/RA descend descend warning, I saw a small aircraft at 2 o'clock and 100 yards, I turned off the Autopilot and Autothrottle stopped the turn towards the small aircraft and descended to 2,500 feet. [We were] cleared to remain at 2,600 feet and received radar vectors to join the Localizer and landed 8L. The Captain was the pilot monitoring and the First Officer was the pilot flying. The ATC controller did make some kind of apology regarding the event. There was a minor distraction regarding the tuning of our radios. I had the VOR tuned and needed to make a switch to the ILS frequency. This took a matter of seconds to correct and we had the airport in sight the entire time.The Captain and I debriefed the event and felt we made all the correct decisions. The next day we confirmed how to track a radial using the FMS and LNAV mode. A note regarding small aircraft in vicinity might be a good idea. Knowing how to set up the FMS to track a radial would be helpful. Above all fly the airplane, keep your eyes outside, and expect the unexpected. Descending on the ZIGGY ARRIVAL ATC gave clearance to fly the PDZ 270 radial after PDZ. PM (Pilot Monitoring) was unable to input the radial to fly in LNAV and the PF (Pilot Flying) flew the radial using raw data. ATC gave clearance to descend from 4,000 to 3,000 with a right turn to a heading of 340 for vectors to 08L. ATC advised traffic (helicopter) in the turn at 3,500 and gave clearance to continue turn to 020. Helicopter traffic was never observed. On TCAS PM saw a target which appeared to be at 3,000 feet on the 020 heading and advised PF to stop turn. TCAS aural warning TA 'traffic traffic' annunciated and PM saw traffic as TCAS aural alert advised an RA 'traffic descend now'. PF and PM both pushed controls forward as conflicting traffic continued to descend and turn into the jets path. PM advised ATC of the new heading altitude deviation due to the RA. Conflict was resolved at 2,300 feet, PF leveled off and started climb back up to 3,000. ATC advised stop climb at 2,600 and continue turn to 020 to intercept 08L LOC with an apology for conflict. PF intercepted GS inside NAROD (FAF 08L) due to ALT (Altitude) assignment by ATC of 2,600 feet. PF and PM had field in site and terrain in site during all phases. ATC reported 'helicopter' traffic at 3,500. Both PM and PF did not observe the traffic on TCAS at 3500 nor saw any helicopter traffic in the initial turn. Controller change during the descent from 4,000-3,000 feet. Weather was VMC daytime.The clearance received to fly the 270R outbound caused PM and PF to be distracted. PM could not get the radial to input in the FMC and therefore the PF flew raw data. This created additional threats which created additional distractions at the low ALT 2,600 with terrain all around. Having had to use RAW DATA the radio panel had mismatched frequencies and MCP had mismatched courses in the selectors which caused FD to give incorrect LOC info. PM was able to configure the MCP/radio panel and EFIS in time to capture LOC before crossing LOC. It caused the PM to be heads down instead of assisting PF in confirming the airport in sight for a visual backup. During debrief both pilots agreed that asking for a climb back to 3,000 may have helped with visual guidance to help with positional awareness. The following leg PM/PF practiced input of radials off VOR stations to create a less threatening environment for the 'next time.'
1779728: Upon gear retraction, after departure from [Runway] XXL at ZZZ, we heard a loud bang in the nose wheel well with an associated yaw of the aircraft. A burnt rubber smell was also detected and dissipated after 5 minutes. My thoughts ranged from, 'something hit us' to 'we blew a nose tire.' All engine and hydraulic indications were normal and the plane was flying fine with no control problems. I decided we had no immediate safety of flight issues and we continued the climbout. At 25,000 feet I had the First Officer take the radios and I messaged dispatch that I wanted to talk to Flight Operations. The Dispatcher and I talked briefly on the SATCOM and he put me on hold to get Flight Operations online. While waiting I ran through the QRH to see if there was a procedure for this issue and found 'Tire Failure.' That seemed to most agree with the possible problem and I was pleased to see that it called for us to proceed normally to the destination since that's what we were doing. Discussing what we knew with Flight Operations we all agreed that the problem was probably the tire and proceeding normally was the action we would take. Flight Operations also said they would call the Tower and Approach control to let them know we might have an issue.After level off the 'A' Flight Attendant came to the cockpit and asked if we heard a bang on takeoff. She said some of the 1st class passengers asked her if we were alright and she said that she was able to reassure them that we were. I told her what we suspected and that I would brief the FA's (Flight Attendants) near top of descent.We had plenty of time and I didn't want to get caught unawares so the FO and I briefed various scenarios and reviewed checklists including 'manual gear extension' and ' partial or all gear up landing'. By the time we were ready to brief the arrival I felt prepared to handle any scenario.Unrelated to the wheel issue, about halfway to ZZZ2 the FO fwd window overheat-light illuminated. We ran the checklist and never got it back so, knowing we had clouds and probably ice to descend through I opted to do the landing. I had considered it anyway, but that clinched it. Sure enough the FO's window was opaque until about the outer marker.ATC was ready for us thanks to the Flight Operations phone call. They set us up for [Runway] YYL and slowed us to 170 around ZZZZZ [Intersection]. I put the gear down at that time to give us some breathing room if it didn't come down. The nose gear was the first to show down and locked and I relaxed a bit. We told tower we anticipated a normal landing but they still asked for souls and fuel, which we gave them. They had an operations vehicle shadow us to check for debris. Touchdown was normal and the nose wheel felt fine when it made contact so we told Tower we could taxi in unaided.We were met by the ops manger and several mechanics. Disappointingly, the nose wheel and the well area looked perfectly normal. After all that build up, I admit I wanted to see some torn metal or bits of tire. It will be interesting to see what maintenance discovers.What I can say I learned from this, is that we have a solid system of communication at (Company). The call to ATC by Flight Operations and Dispatch saved us a lot of on air negotiation for 16L. My FO contributed many helpful thoughts that aided our preparation for just about any gear scenario. The FA's took the news of a possible irregular landing calmly and knew what roles they would play should things get sticky. Although it all turned out to be much ado about nothing, it was a good test of the system and the system works.
1779731: Departing ZZZ1 for ZZZ2 I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) and the CA (Captain) was the PF (Pilot Flying). We planned a low altitude flight due to the shortness of the leg. Some altitudes in the legs page were edited to allow the lower cruise altitude to be selected. The flaps 10 takeoff went as normal (LNAV/VNAV). The PF called for flaps 1 as near as I can recall. I believe this is the case as most if not all of our previous legs had been flaps 5 takeoffs. I was distracted with a radio call or frequency change and I moved the flaps to 1 and did not catch the error. Shortly after that, the FMC changed to the descent phase and the speed bug moved to the flaps 5 maneuver speed, and the A/T (Auto Throttle) mode went from N1 to FMC speed, which resulted in the flaps 5 maneuver speed being the A/T target. As, or just prior to this happening the PF called for flaps up. I moved the flap lever to the up position, and since we were no longer accelerating got a momentary stick shaker. The PF instinctively lowered the nose reducing the AOA (Angle Of Attack). I increased the speed in the MCP window to get the A/T to command acceleration. The remainder of the flight was normal.Suggest crews be alert for unusual mode reversions when using low altitudes for cruise. I would probably use non VNAV takeoff procedures in the future. The big lesson is not new, vigilance absolutely has to be maintained during the 'red' parts of the flight path. The PM job is challenging and can be intolerant of errors.
1779774: While performing task card Passenger Compartment Seat Installation in conjunction with the STA (Station) 540 slot sealant inspection seat row 12ABC was inadvertently reinstalled in the wrong seat row position. Although we do not remove seat row 13ABC for this inspection, somehow row 13ABC and 12ABC were in swapped positions as reported by an inflight crew member due to tray table operation being impaired due to the armrest tray table seat row being installed in the wrong seat row position. Although I know I verified part numbers and serial numbers of all rows of seats after they were removed to facilitate the STA 540 slot sealant inspection, I cannot be certain that I verified part number and serial number of seat row 12ABC after final installation as required per the task card step. Seat row 12ABC being swapped with 13ABC is an anomaly that I can not explain as we do not remove seat row 13ABC during this process. I understand that I could have possibly transposed part numbers during my inspection and let the incorrect part number get reinstalled in the wrong position if that seat row arrived in the wrong position which is the only way I can account for this seat row being in the incorrect position per the drawing as we never removed row 13ABC.
1779802: During cruise at FL410 there was an uncommanded disconnect of the Automatic Flight Control System (AFCS). Loss of Autopilot (AP), Yaw Dampener (YD), and Auto Throttles (AT). Dutch Roll developed becoming divergent. Attempts were made to reengage the YD. Switching AFCS channels initially unsuccessful. As the Dutch Roll was increasing in amplitude, continued manual flight was proving difficult. Crew elected to initiate immediate descent to FL370 and inform ATC. AFCS restored as aircraft descended out of FL410. Descent continued to FL370. Operations normal, QRH consulted - continued flight on one remaining AFCS channel.
1779805: We were approximately 20 miles SE of the airport in the mountains on a sight-seeing flight. I was PIC (Pilot In Command) and the only pilot on board with 2 passengers. At 4,500 MSL the AWOS was intermittent because of the mountains. The MEF (Maximum Elevation Figure) on the sectional chart was 4,400 MSL and I was working my around some shorter hills. While experiencing some lighter bumps over a ridge, the 'GEAR IN TRANSIT' annunciator light lit up. I immediately checked to make sure I hadn't selected the gear handle down because we were too far away from the airport to have the gear down. The selector handle was still in the 'GEAR UP' position so my next instinct was to grab the emergency gear override and hold it in the 'UP' position to keep the gear from extending so far out. I checked the circuit breaker and everything seemed normal. I cycled the gear down and got 3 green lights and when cycled back up the green lights went away but the transit light never turned off. The AWOS suddenly kicked in and led me to decide on Runway 8 which meant I would cross the airport midfield and enter a tear drop for a left downwind to Runway 8. On the sectional I saw the altitude as 1,907 and decided to over fly the field at 2,500. In my mind 1,907 was pattern altitude and not the airport altitude. My mind was still on making sure my gear didn't fall down and create more drag for me that far away from the airport. About 1.5 miles to the south of the airport I once again communicated on the CTAF of my intentions to over fly the field at 2,500. One aircraft said they were back taxiing and going to depart Runway 8. As we approached the airport I felt like I was too low even though I was at 2,500 and then realized my mistake by how well I could see details on the ground. I quickly announced my intentions to climb up to traffic pattern altitude of 2,900 feet just before reaching the south side of the airport pattern which meant I was then climbing into the pattern instead of already being at the correct altitude. Directly over the runway we were back to 2,900 feet and I continued out to do a right hand turn and enter a tear drop to the left downwind. The gear came down fine and we landed safely. The combination of trying to troubleshoot an annunciator light while listening to incoming traffic and the intermittent AWOS left me to be distracted and mixing up proper altitudes for the pattern.Better self-briefing prior to arrival to an airport would have greatly reduced the chance of this occurring. Along with remembering that I had plenty of fuel and could have circled at a safe altitude to troubleshoot and then with a clearer mind come up with a plan to land at the airport normally.
1779816: The mission was practicing landings at ZZZ on Runway XXR. Weather was VFR. All 4 fuel tanks were full at the start of the flight. No issues were noted with the aircraft during preflight, taxiing, or run-up. The plane behaved normally for the first two takeoffs and landings. The engine had been running for approximately 40 minutes at that point, all drawing from the left main tank, with ~60% of the tank remaining. During the climb-out from the 3rd takeoff, at about 700 ft AGL, the engine had a momentary loss of power (lasting about a second). In an effort to troubleshoot, I switched tanks from left main to right main. A few seconds later, another momentary loss of power occurred (again lasting about a second). Note that this was with everything in takeoff configuration, full throttle, max RPM, mixture full rich, electric fuel pump on, and carburetor heat was already on (keeping the carburetor temperature gauge above 40 deg F). At this point I felt there was a significant risk of the engine having an impending permanent loss of power and decided the most expedient option to get the plane safely back on the ground was to do a left 180 deg turn to land in the opposite direction on the parallel runway. I stated the situation and my intention to the Tower over the radio. The turn, descent, and landing on XXR were completed uneventfully. There was no traffic actively using that runway at the time, so that wasn't a factor. At this point, it's unclear what the root cause was for the engine's momentary power losses. I've contacted my local shop and have no intention of flying the plane again until after they investigate. Of note, the engine stayed running seemingly normally at idle during the descent, landing, and subsequent taxiing. However, during taxiing, the engine would run rough at any throttle setting above idle. Also, during preflight, the tip tanks both had some water that was sumped out, but the main tanks (the only tanks used during the flight) didn't show any noticeable water when sumped.
1779821: I had taken position after coming down from the tower working Ground Control. A priority handling had been coordinated with Aircraft X with an engine out. This had been coordinated at least 45 minutes prior to the aircraft's arrival. It was briefed from the relieved controller that this aircraft had requested 'wide vectors for an ILS.' At the same time Aircraft Z was inbound on the RNAV arrival along with Aircraft Y call sign unknown. In my judgement as well as the relieved Controller both of these aircraft would have arrived easily before Aircraft X came in on the ILS. I cleared Aircraft Y for the Visual Approach to the right parallel runway and decided to change the Aircraft Y to the left after they requested the ILS. Aircraft X changed his mind for the Visual Approach which I approved. I asked Aircraft X if they could visually follow the Aircraft Y and they said they would not because of wake turbulence. Since I did not issue a 30 degree intercept we coordinated with the tower to issue a go-around to Aircraft Y. We decided not to send the Aircraft Y around because he was established on the ILS even though I had not issued a 30 degree intercept for Aircraft X. In my opinion wake turbulence to a priority handling aircraft was more of a factor than a parallel runway approach.Due to the busy nature of this session I think splitting the radar position may have been warranted. The relieved Controller had been on position for over 1 hour and 45 minutes. Aircraft X changing his mind mid sequence also caused a lot of problems. I was wary of issuing delay vectors to an aircraft that was a priority handling.
1779822: ZZZ1 Center had a positive COVID test from an individual in their building. The decision was made to go ATC-0 in the middle of the afternoon to perform a Level 3 cleaning. I would completely understand the need to do the cleaning immediately, even if it was a high traffic time, if the individual had started not feeling well during that shift, or during the any shift in the previous 24 hours. This was not the situation here. The positive test came from an individual that had not been in the building in X days! Every Controller that had worked in the previous X days already had worked in a potentially contaminated area. There was zero benefit to go down at that time. The decision makers did nothing that was reasonable and responsible in this situation. Reasonable and responsible would have been to wait for a slower traffic period to get the clean accomplished. I had Aircraft X that had been in the air for 15+20 hours. I was forced to route him over an hour [out] of his way which put him in a minimum fuel situation. We had MedEvac flights, on critical missions that were not allowed to pick up their patients. I would hate to know how many passengers missed their connecting flights. We put our controllers, pilots, and flying public in an unnecessary unsafe situation.When an individual has not been in the building in the past 24 hours DO NOT CLEAN during a high traffic period.
1779835: We were cleared for the visual approach to Runway 35R at 9,000 feet. The DRUMM approach segment was to 9,000 feet, and we started down to 7,000 feet for FRONZ approach segment. ATC alerted us of a MVA altitude alert. We corrected up to the altitude of 7,500 feet as ATC said that altitude was needed for that segment. We were cleared for the visual and were following the step down altitudes.I contacted one of our managers here at the Company, and they followed up on it for me and there was no documentation noted by ATC of any issues or violations. Company Manager said that we might have touched the Class B airspace limit and that would trigger the same alert per DEN ATC. The rest of the flight was uneventful. We were at 9,000 feet MSL approximately three miles east of DRUMM on the visual to Runway 35R. We had Runway 35R in sight and were cleared the visual. Abeam DRUMM we started a descent to 7,000 feet MSL. We leveled at 7,000 feet in between DRUMM and the FAF FRONZ. ATC informed us of a low altitude alert and advised the MVA was 7,500 feet. We were approximately 1,200 feet above the terrain and out of caution climbed up to 7,500 feet and intercept glidepath shortly later. No GPWS alerts occurred.
1779850: We took the aircraft that was returned to service after a large bird was ingested into the #1 engine on the previous flight. The #1 engine was started first prior to taxi out to ensure no issues with the engine. All engine indications after start were normal. The takeoff was normal with no abnormal engine indications. On departure just after retracting the landing gear, a strong smell from the previously ingested bird permeated throughout the aircraft. Shortly after, the forward lav smoke detector sounded. The aircraft was leveled off, and then we began to execute the Smoke, Fire or Fumes Checklist. Once stabilized on a left downwind with Departure Control notified, First Officer (FO) now flying, I contacted the Flight Attendants to confirm the status of the forward lav. They indicated that there was NO fire, just a very strong and pungent smell throughout the entire cabin. Fully aware that the cause of the alarm was the heavy fumes from the bird, we continued with the checklist and decided to discontinue the flight and return to the airport. We removed our masks, coordinated with Dispatch, and continued on downwind to set up for a visual approach and landing. Engine indications were normal the entire flight and the smell slowly dissipated. The forward lav alarm continued to sound, no fire though. No priority handling was requested. We landed uneventfully and taxied to the gate.The aircraft was returned to service after a bird was ingested on the previous flight. The engine contained a large amount of bird parts around the fan blades and some appeared to be ingested into the compressor section. Contract Maintenance cleaned and inspected the engine in coordination with Maintenance Control and signed off on the logbook. I did inquire of Maintenance about an engine run. They indicated it was not needed. I should have pushed them on it, as we were concerned about the large amount of bird guts all around the fan section. I did not inspect the engine after Maintenance completed their work and felt confident it was accomplished correctly, my mistake, should have crosschecked. The FO did a walkaround prior to departure and noted some bird parts still remaining. A borescope was not accomplished as Maintenance Control indicated it could be done within a couple of flight hours, most likely after the next flight since we were heading to a Maintenance base. Not sure Maintenance Control realized the significant amount of bird ingested into the engine. Could have communicated better with them.
1779868: We were cleared for a visual approach following a Boeing 777 to Runway 25L at LAX. On short final we encountered what was most likely wake turbulence from the proceeding aircraft on short final ~300 feet AGL. This presented as a roll and shear to a headwind. This apparent shear to a headwind along with an addition of some thrust put me high on the profile and ~15 knots above target speed. The severity of the event was below what I would describe as an 'upset'. When the turbulence subsided we appeared to be in a good position to land, so I continued the approach and landed. Being high on profile and bleeding off the excess speed in the flare resulted in a touchdown that was most likely beyond the touchdown zone. Despite this we were in position, with normal braking, to exit at taxiway H8. Tower instructed us to exit at H9. Upon landing on Runway 25L at LAX we landed outside of the normal 3000 feet of the touchdown zone after being preceded by a 777 to landing during light tail wind conditions. The briefing and approach were completely routine. We had originally planned to land on 24R but we were prepared for a possible change to Runway 25L. We were told on downwind that we would be following a heavy 777 and could expect 25L. Conditions were clear and we had the aircraft in sight. As I reconfigured the aircraft for landing on the south runway, the Captain made the comment that he would be prepared to fly a dot high. The Captain flew as he briefed and we experienced mostly calm winds all the way down the glideslope. By 200 feet AGL, we were back on glide slope. The aircraft sank somewhat and by 100 feet we were almost a half dot low when we started to feel some of the wake of the 777. The winds were still light, about 300/7. The plane was very controllable and the Captain pitched up and added power slightly to stay on top of the wake. In doing so, the speed increased almost 15 knots and I considered calling for a go around. It still appeared that we were going to be touching down in the first 3000 feet so I allowed the approach to continue. The Captain flared the aircraft so that it looked like we would touch down right at about 3000 feet. Without trying to hold the aircraft off, the plane continued down the runway at what seemed like 1 foot. The aircraft finally settled a couple hundred feet later and we turned off the runway and proceeded to the gate without any further issues.This was a case where one limit almost being crossed led to another limit being crossed. It looked like it was all going to work out. We have all encountered 'disturbed' air from a wake before on landing especially at busy airports like LAX. The question is how much of an adjustment do you have to make and at what point do you go around. This looked very doable. We had plenty of runway and performance. This looked familiar with a landing in the touchdown zone. I only thought later and realized that the Captain had elected to do a flaps 40 landing in a 737-900ER. I know I have not done many flaps 40 landings in a 900ER in the last couple years, so I think my sight picture was off a bit for the flare and the touchdown. We may have also gotten a bit more of ground effect than what I would have imagined. The speed did not bleed off as fast as I had anticipated.
1779895: I was the pilot flying into ROA at night. We were at 6,000 abeam the airport on a left downwind for Runway 6. We were cleared for the visual approach and I asked for 3,000 feet to be set into the FCP (Flight Control Panel). I was aware there was a ridge we would need to cross on our left base turn, charted at 2,000 feet on the RNAV (GPS) Y approach plate. I planned to descend to 3,000 while turning base and turn onto final at HIVLU, charted at 2,700 on the vertical profile of the approach plate. I began a descent at 2,000 FPM just prior to turning base. On the base leg, I believe due to the rate of descent, a GPWS terrain warning occurred. I immediately increased the power, increased pitch, and arrested the descent. The warning stopped. The ridge was visible throughout the event and the aircraft did not descend below 3,000 until past the ridge and beginning a turn to intercept the final approach course. We continued and made a normal landing.Being unfamiliar with this approach I should have communicated my plan to the Captain and asked if he agreed. After landing we discussed the approach and he explained that we could have descended on downwind to 5,200, continued past the ridge, turned base at or just inside DIXXY, and then followed the descent profile on the approach plate. I agree with his assessment, that would have been a better course of action. In the future I will verbalize my intentions, particularly on approaches I am unfamiliar with, and have a discussion to collaboratively determine the best course of action.
1779908: After landing on Runway 12R, Tower instructed us to exit the runway at Taxiway C3, hold short of Taxiway C (parallel taxiway) and contact ground on 121.7. As we approached Taxiway C3, I saw an Aircraft Y taxiing northwest on Taxiway C with moderate speed. The Aircraft Y was approaching Taxiway C3 and it appeared that we had been instructed to hold short of Taxiway C so the Aircraft Y could pass in front of us right to left. As the CA (Captain) made the ninety-degree left turn to exit the runway onto Taxiway C3, I switched to ground control frequency 121.7 as instructed. The CA then stopped with the nose of our aircraft near the runway holding position marking on Taxiway C3. This left the aft end of our aircraft on the runway. The Aircraft Y then stopped short of Taxiway C3. As I was about to ask for clarifying instructions after switching frequencies, Ground Control instructed the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing and then asked if we were on his frequency. I responded that we were and then Ground Control instructed us to turn right on Taxiway C (behind the Aircraft Y that had by this point passed through the intersection) and then left on Taxiway B4 to our gate. As we taxied southeast on Taxiway C Ground Control advised us that we had created a dangerous situation by not fully exiting the runway. He informed us that a light general aviation aircraft had taken off while part of our aircraft was still on the runway. At the time it happened, I agreed with the CA's decision to stop the aircraft since we were unaware of the Aircraft Y's taxi instructions (we had just switched to Ground), and the appearance that the Aircraft Y may taxi through the intersection due to its rate of speed and remaining distance to C3. I also wondered why tower control had cleared an aircraft to take off while we still occupied the runway. On the taxi out for our return leg, we observed that there was a taxiway hold short line further ahead on C3 that would have allowed us to pull further forward, but our tail would still likely have been over the runway hold short line.Limited distance between the runway and Taxiway C. Lack of communication at a critical juncture: we were unaware of the Aircraft Y's taxi instructions as we had just switched to ground, and Tower didn't advise us of them when issuing us our initial taxi instructions (ie '... Aircraft Y will hold short.') The Tower Controller cleared an aircraft to take off while part of our aircraft was still within the boundary of the runway. The Ground Controller did not instruct the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing with a sense of urgency. Better communication from ATC. Better awareness of the location of taxiway hold short lines (of possible runway turn-offs) as a part of our approach brief. After landing on Runway 12R, tower instructed us to exit the runway at Taxiway C3, hold short of Taxiway C (parallel taxiway) and contact Ground on 121.7. As we approached Taxiway C3, I observed an Aircraft Y taxiing northwest on Taxiway C with moderate speed. The Aircraft Y was approaching Taxiway C3 and it appeared that we had been instructed to hold short of Taxiway C so the Aircraft Y could pass in front of us right to left. As I made the ninety-degree left turn to exit the runway onto Taxiway C3 at less than 12 knots of ground speed, the FO switched to ground control frequency 121.7 as instructed. I stopped with the nose of our aircraft near the runway holding position marking on Taxiway C3 because of the short distance to Taxiway C in front of us. This left the aft end of our aircraft on the runway. The Aircraft Y then stopped short of Taxiway C3. Ground Control instructed the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing. After the Aircraft Y passed Taxiway C3, Ground Control asked if we were on his frequency. When the FO responded in the affirmative, ground control instructed us to turn right on Taxiway C then left on Taxiway B4 to our gate. As we taxied southeast on Taxiway C Ground Control advised us that we had created a dangerous situation by not fully exiting the runway. He told us that a light general aviation aircraft had taken off while part of our aircraft was still on the runway. At the time, I felt that I could not have fully exited the runway considering the limited distance available to me on Taxiway C3. I also wondered why Tower Control had cleared an aircraft to take off while we still occupied the runway. On the next flight, we taxied out on Taxiway C. As we passed Taxiway C3 I noticed a taxiway holding position marking on Taxiway C3 that I had not observed on the inbound flight. Although the taxiway holding position marking appeared too close to Taxiway C, I could have taxied farther onto Taxiway C3 after exiting the runway on the inbound flight. If I had taxied to what I considered a safe distance from Taxiway C, our tail probably would not have been within the lateral boundaries of the runway, but it would have been on the runway side of the runway holding position marking on Taxiway C3. Limited distance between the runway and Taxiway C prevented us from fully vacating the runway while complying with the instruction to hold short of Taxiway C. The Tower Controller cleared an aircraft to take off while part of our aircraft was still within the boundary of the runway. The Ground Controller did not instruct the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing with a sense of urgency. When instructed to hold short of a taxiway after vacating a runway, stop the aircraft as close as safely possible to the restricting taxiway. Even if your aircraft is not completely clear of the runway, risk will be diminished by reducing the amount of your aircraft remaining within the runway boundary.
1779910: Cleared for visual approach to Runway XXL on modified downwind, at 3,000 feet. Maneuvered aircraft to arrive at ZZZZZ at 3,000 to intercept LOC/ Glideslope simultaneously. Thought I was going to be above glideslope at ZZZZZ, asked FO to set 2,000 feet acquired Localizer inside of ZZZZZ, still at flaps 3. Drove into glideslope, selected flaps full. Radio altimeter briefly showed 800 feet due to terrain variation. Broke SOP of being fully configured by 1,000 feet.I accepted a night visual approach after a 12 hour, three leg duty day. Fatigue was a contributor. Hurried visual, should have intercepted final at IAF vs. FAF. My currency was spotty due to reduced flying on reserve.Never accept short visual approaches at end of long duty day. I was acting as PM. Approaching ZZZ at night from the SW with a high overcast layer above. ATC had us on a downwind leg for [Runway] XXL at 4,000. The autopilot and auto thrust were engaged. Approximately abeam the end of the runway, ATC asked us if we had the field in sight. The CA/PF says he does, so I reported the field in sight. ATC then cleared us for the visual XXL. The PF then set 3,000 in the FCU and I confirmed and referenced the plate showing the FAF ZZZZZ at 3000. I believe the PF went open descent to 3,000 from 4,000. The PF then began his base leg turn. The intercept angle initially looked like it was going to join the final just outside of the FAF. As we approached 3,000 the PF continued the turn in. He asked me to set 2,000 into the FCU and set 1,000 v/s down. I complied as it appeared to me that the PF was trying to intercept the course and I assumed he was going to join inside of ZZZZZ/FAF. He readjusted his intercept to join the final at ZZZZZ or just outside it. By that time I began to realize we were getting low on the profile. I still had visual contact with the runway. At approximately that time, the airplane leveled at 2000 just inside of ZZZZZ and ZZZ tower advised us of a low altitude alert and to check our altitude with the current altimeter setting. I replied with our call sign. We continued at 2,000 until intercepting the glideslope and landed safely. We were approaching the end of a long duty day and it was a non eventful and quiet flight, so fatigue was a possible factor. I am also familiar with operating into ZZZ, so I was a bit complacent, as well as being in VFR conditions and being able to see the runway. Having both pilots confirm and verify any further altitude changes in the FCU after the setting of the lowest charted altitudes for the approach used.
1779934: We were established on final a few miles outside of the FAF. All was as it should be. We were stable on the localizer at 170 knots with flaps 15 autopilot on. Winds were 210 at 50 knots, steady. In a split second we went from straight and level to a left hand bank I'm guessing 20 degrees maybe more and the hook came up and we got a momentary stick shaker. As it happened I added power as we rolled wings level. We were about 20 degrees off heading, but the autopilot recovered to intercept the localizer, and we never lost any altitude. Like I said, it happened so quickly and recovered that I saw no need to disconnect the autopilot. We re-intercepted the localizer followed by the glide slope and shot the approach with no other concerns. I'm not sure if the winds were the reason or we hit someone's wake turbulence. I'm guessing it was wake turbulence. [Cause:] not sure - perhaps wake turbulence. The winds were strong but steady. 210 at 50 knots at 3000 ft. Perhaps ATC had us too close, but as I recall my traffic was a 757, 7 miles ahead, maybe it was wake from a plane on the parallel runway.
1779935: MD-11 loaded with aft CG. Careful taxi at departure airport. Uneventful except minor nose tire scrubbing during turns. Departure weather conditions dry and good at ZZZ. At landing airport, ZZZ1 the weather was low ceilings, reduced visibility and snow and ice covered runways, taxiway and parking ramp. Used very slow speeds for taxi. Nose tire slid during turn from runway to taxiway exit. I controlled slide with some small amount differential thrust, slowest taxi speeds and differential braking techniques as necessary. Aft TOCG (Take Off Center of Gravity) combined with wet or snow or icy taxi presents unnecessary risk to operations. I recommend target TOCG be limited to less than 28.0 when any weather forecast or actual conditions are wet or worse. I recommend Dispatch be more involved in CG planning and coordination when conditions are less than good.
1779944: On the taxiway contacted Tower. After check in we thought we heard 'clear for takeoff;' but neither of us were sure so I asked the First Officer to confirm if we were cleared for takeoff. The First Officer asked this question and the very clear reply was 'affirmative.' We entered the runway and were subsequently told while finishing our line up on centerline to stop and hold position. After a delay we were told of 'pilot deviation' and then cleared for takeoff.I allowed an 'affirmative' reply by Tower to suffice for a query on were we cleared for takeoff. That is the root cause. 'Affirmative' is not the correct response and in retrospect I believe Tower perhaps misunderstood our query. Choice of words and insistence on clarification. I should have asked the First Officer to say 'Tower say again.' Tower would then have repeated all instructions. Looking back the word 'Affirmative' is not enough. I allowed my leeway on foreign controllers English and accents to accept 'affirmative' for a cleared for takeoff query rather than insisting on hearing the entire standard 'cleared for takeoff' verbiage. The Tower could have easily misunderstood us and replied 'Affirmative' to what Tower believed was the question.
1779947: The incident occurred during an otherwise uneventful reposition flight from ZZZ - ZZZ1. The PIC was acting as Pilot Monitoring, and the FO as Pilot Flying. The filed altitude was FL200, but the flight had requested and received FL220 approximately 45 minutes to an hour prior to the incident to escape some moderate turbulence. At the time of the incident, the conditions were IMC with intermittent patches of VMC, light turbulence, and trace to light icing at about -23 deg C. The aircraft was on the western edge of the occluded segment of a frontal low. The first indication was the De-Ice Boots CAS. The FO remained Pilot Flying, and PIC attempted to troubleshoot the problem with the QRH. In addition, the QRH checklist was cross checked by the FO. Unfortunately, the problem did not reset, so the crew determined that it was not safe to remain in icing conditions without wing De-ice capability. The crew then examined alternates, eventually deciding on ZZZ2 due to the availability of a runway greater than 10,000 feet in length, its position behind (west) the front, and the prevailing conditions of unrestricted visibility and a 900 foot ceiling. The PM then informed ARTCC of the need to divert and received a vector for the ILS XX. During the descent, the PM calculated the required landing distance for the Flaps 0 deg Boot Fail scenario, the approach was set up and briefed, and the appropriate checklists were run. Due to the failure of the De-ice Boots, some mixed icing on the leading edge, clear runback ice on inside third of the upper surface, and rime on the underside of the airfoil accumulated during descent and approach. The crew monitored the accumulation visually and by referencing the trim indicators to ensure that abnormal force was not required to control the aircraft. The approach and landing was conducted at Flaps 0 deg and in accordance with procedure for landing with inoperative boots.
1779962: While on the visual approach into LEX Runway 4, inside the final approach fix and following the precision approach path indicator (PAPI) lights with two white and two red lights indicating on glide path, we started to feel we were low according to our actual sight picture. After referencing the electronic glide slope from the ILS we saw we were slightly more than half scale deflection low and corrected back onto the glide slope. We received a 'GLIDESLOPE' GPWS indication while correcting. When back on the glide slope we looked out at the PAPI again and saw it still showed two white and two red lights despite the change in glide path. The ILS chart for runway 4 does not mention that the glide slope and visual glide path are not coincident. I believe when we noticed we were low on the glide slope, the PAPI should have been indicating three reds and a white or maybe even four reds.There is something wrong with the alignment of the PAPI equipment for the runway. It should not have shown us to be two white and two red lights that low on the glide slope. The conditions were visual and easily fixed once we referenced the electronic glide slope fully.The Airport Operations Staff and the FAA need to conduct an alignment of the PAPI equipment. There could be a situation in low visibility or very dark conditions where an aircraft arrives at the minimum decision altitude, has the runway environment or approach lights in sight and relies on the PAPI to help keep the pilot's eyes outside to land, which could lead to an issue where they either see themselves as too high according to the PAPI (if it's aligned too low) or, if it only indicates two white two red at any altitude, may follow the PAPI to an unsafe landing either outside of the touchdown zone or short of the runway.
1779965: About 10 minutes prior to scheduled passenger flight pushback at ZZZ, received a HAZMAT NOTOC (hazardous material notice to Captain). There were 6 lines of HAZMAT of which 5 were normal but one stood out with lithium metal batteries, ERG (emergency response guidebook) code 12FG. I queried the messenger about them, he said he could take a picture of the box to show me. While he went to do that I discussed the situation with the FO (First Officer). The battery weight was.15 kg or just a bit over 5 ounces and contained in equipment. That size battery is similar in weight to our iPad batteries. 12FG code is risk of fire/heat/smoke with the additional risk Z 'aircraft cargo fire suppression system may not extinguish or contain the fire. Consider landing immediately'. When carried in our cargo hold, with passengers on board, that sort of risk gets my attention. When the messenger returned with the picture I queried him about carrying that cargo in the cockpit or passenger compartment where we at least have our BCB battery containment bag, in case something went wrong. He said they didn't know which box batteries were in so that wasn't possible. It was almost push time so I called and discussed the situation with Dispatch. They agreed with my concern and said they weren't experts on HAZMAT but could research who was or we could just remove the batteries in the interest of expediency. We then opted for removing the lithium batteries for simplicity and timeliness. After this was accomplished, we got a revised load closeout and were on our way about 20-30 minutes late. The rest of our flight was uneventful. Having reviewed FOM guidance on this issue previously, I consider it somewhat vague. While the likelihood for these batteries to start burning is slim, the impact would be catastrophic and the ERG code even warns us of this. This could easily be mitigated by having an item like this in the passenger cabin or cockpit where FAs (flight attendants) or pilots could at least deal with the threat with the BCBs which are provided for an unlikely event such as this. FOM deal[s] with this and state or imply that these types of things should not be in the cargo compartment. FOM addresses HAZMAT codes but really gives no guidance other than inspecting NOTOC paperwork for date, tail number etc.I've been involved in carrying lots of hazardous materials in aircraft over my career and believe I'm well versed on the risk vs reward of it. While technically the NOTOC I received was legal per our FOM, the risk of these batteries also noted on the NOTOC, didn't appear to make sense from a risk management or an SMS (safety management systems) standpoint. Thus my questions about better potential options. If we are intentionally doing something like this, I, Dispatch, other pilots etc would probably be better served with more of a heads up on the decision process and other options sooner in the departure process. Were we just doing the minimum legal or is there a more appropriate way in hindsight? It certainly seemed like pushback time induced pressure discouraged discussion/questions about this sort of thing.
1779972: While on a visual approach to [Runway] XXR, I was the PF. I hadn't flown in a month and a half or so, and the weather was conducive to trying to practice skills, so I turned off the AP/AT/FD. While over the ZZZ1 area, we received an RA directing me to level off. After complying with the RA, I began to descend to catch up to the approach, but at the altitude I was at, and the descent rate required to get back on the approach, I would not have been able to do so within stabilized approach criteria, so I conducted a go-around.The go-around was not smooth, and left room for improvement, but all call outs were made, and the checklists were accomplished. After passing through about 1,300 feet or so, we were assigned an altitude of 2,000 feet. The FO selected 2,000 feet and made the comment that we were about 700 feet away. We were climbing at a high rate as we were in TOGA (Still no AP/AT), and I was trying to get the plane slowed down, and arresting the climb rate, the FD began to turn to follow the missed approach for the ILS, as we had loaded it as the backup. We had yet received instruction as to what direction to turn, since we were assigned the visual approach. Between the FD turning and leveling off, it was at this point that I was focused on wanting the aircraft to continue straight on runway heading, and I flew through the 2,000 feet restriction, to my recollection by about 300 feet. The PM attempted to get some sort of instruction from ATC as to what they would like us to do, but struggled to get a word in on the radio. Finally they called and assigned us a vector. They also said since we went past 2,000, to level off at 2,500 feet. At this point, we had a moment, and was able to match up the information on the PFD with what I was wanting, and was able to add back in the AP/AT.This event felt like a culmination of a few problems. The root cause is that I, as the Captain, wasn't as prepared as I should have been. Having flown so little the last few months after upgrade sign off in month, I have been limited to just XX hours of total flying since month, my skill upkeep has been mainly book studying. While this is important, it does not replace being behind the controls of an aircraft.
1779979: Operating at FL190. After cruise checklist was completed, cabin altitude was indicating approximate 10,000 feet. After 5 to 10 minutes' elapsed, I felt a change in pressure inside the aircraft. When I crosschecked the cabin altitude climb was indicating 4,000 feet climbing, a minute later, the cabin altitude warning illuminated. This was followed by aircraft memory item and checklist. I pulled O2 knob located left upper just left of the external power switch and as I pulled the mask I placed the O2 mask on emergency mode and no oxygen was flowing. I placed it back on normal operation and nothing happened. I switched the mic to the O2 mask and advised ATC for urgent descent 10,000 feet. I discovered that ATC was unable to hear me at all. I looked over and the switch for the microphone was placed on oxygen mask and nothing seemed to fix the problem. The cabin altitude was indicating roughly about 20,000 to 21,000 feet from what I recall. I switched again to my headset and requested '...priority, need to descend now to 10,000 feet pressurization problems.' As soon as I talked to ATC, I started immediate descent memory item and checklist, while descending, I took the First Officer mask to see for O2 flow and no O2 was flowing, I double checked the O2 handle. I pulled both located on the Captain left hand side upper and lower, and nothing resulted for O2 function. Since I was indicating 60 miles from my departure airport, I decided to return since for my judgment it was unsafe to continue the flight without O2 flow, no O2 mask microphone and pressurization problems. Upon reaching 10,000 feet the cabin stabilized and the cabin altitude indicator was no longer illuminated with a cabin altitude about 9,000 feet.ATC gave me instructions to descend to 5,000 feet and while at it, the cabin altitude started to jump 5,500 feet up followed by a descent to 4,000 feet and this continued all the way to 3,000 feet. At that moment, I was feeling uncomfortable since my ears where hurting and I knew I was not feeling 100%. At 3,000 feet, I turned off my bleed air and flew the aircraft unpressurized. Why ? I had 'ears popping' several times at this time and I wanted to make the little time left comfortable in order to make a safe landing, since this constant climb and descend from the cabin was making me feel really weak. Landed the aircraft successfully without any major issues. After landing Maintenance and Station manager met me at the airplane. I took time at the crew van to see if I felt better and I did. This resulted in a maintenance write up for 3 items. Unable to control cabin altitude, O2 Mask Mic not operating, O2 not flowing properly.
1779981: Onboard the aircraft was a piece of Hazmat which I was unaware of. The company manifest did not disclose it and I was not notified by any company personnel. I am unsure of when the piece was loaded, if it was during the preload process or while I was present. Upon finding the Hazmat during aircraft unloading, I reported it to Dispatch.
1780003: A Flight Attendant in my recurrent class notified the company on [date] that they tested positive for COVID-19. Company notified me [10 days later].
