1780021: I'm making a landing at ZZZ, I executed a missed approach on the first attempt. On the second landing I failed to initiate a missed approach in time and had to continue to the landing due to obstacles that would possibly be in the flight path of a go-around. Upon landing I was unable to stop the aircraft before exiting the end of the runway and hitting mowing equipment.
1780029: VFR flight from ZZZ1 towards ZZZ2 and return with no specific route. Tablet GPS lost connection with autopilot and I lost situational awareness trying to get the GPS reconnected (using AVARE app). When I finally abandoned the effort and looked at the GPS I realized I was in ZZZ Class B airspace at approximately 3,200 MSL instead of below the 3,000 MSL floor as I usually am. Corrected altitude immediately and left the Class B, went home and landed.I should have had the GPS completely set up before departure and should also have stayed at my usual altitude of 2,500 MSL for local flights. I really don't have an excuse for losing situational awareness. Problem was exacerbated by opening a 2nd app (Naviator) at which point I didn't know which app might have been trying to control the autopilot. I will certainly not make that mistake again! Had not flown at all from 5 months so I am admittedly not as proficient as I would like to be. Will be correcting that situation shortly also!
1780032: After having sent 2 test balloons (party balloons with helium) to check winds and finding they both showed no more than 7 knots of wind and practically went straight up as far as I could see them. Only clouds in the visible area were small white cumulus approximately 10,000 feet high. I chose to launch my hot air balloon near in a dirt lot with no obstruction down wind and more than enough room to move around in case of wind gusts. Knowing I might experience some gusts of wind due to only one local airport having seen gusts up to 14 knots. During my entire set up and inflation, I hadn't experienced any gusts more than 10 knot. After inflating the balloon to an upright position and the balloon maintaining its usual shape and taking pressure as normal I asked the passengers to load into the balloon basket. I was still tied to the van with a 5/8' polyester yacht braided rope and started heating the balloon with a fuel tank only used for the purpose of inflation to buoyancy.Before I could heat the balloon to buoyancy the wind hit the balloon from the opposite direction pushing me toward the passenger van westbound. Then hit me again heading east at an estimated 30 knots while dragging the balloon to the end of the tie down rope. The rope then broke and the balloon began to drag across the large lot. I gave full power to the burners trying to heat the balloon into flight knowing I wouldn't be able to stop the balloon on the ground in that speed of wind before hitting something. We started to lift off the ground approximately 10 to 15 feet off the ground and the balloon started descending again toward a chain link fence. Once hitting the fence was inevitable I started opening the deflation port. It took an additional acre of land for the balloon to come to a complete stop on another chain link fence.After this was all over the wind had completely stopped, and had relatively calm winds the rest of the evening. All of the small cumulus clouds were completely gone after this incident with clear skies. Making me assume those clouds had dissipated causing outflow gusts of at least 30 knots. In total hitting 3 chain-link fences. All passengers and myself were unharmed with no injuries and no damage to the balloon to cause it to be unairworthy.
1780043: I had heard that the FAA had suspended/extended GA compliance regulation deadlines due to COVID-19. I have operated an aircraft outside of my normal deadline date for medical and BFR requirements. In the last two days I have found that this might not be the case. I purchased an additional aircraft and I don't know if the deadline for registering the plane has also been extended or not.I shouldn't be making assumptions or go by information that I am hearing from the airport/other pilots or online. No additional flights will be made until I verify that I am in compliance with the proper FAA office.
1780048: I was at FL240 enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1 when the aircraft started picking up ice. There had been PIREP reports of ice between 14,000 to 18,000 and 22,000 to 24,000. I requested to descend and was given 22,000 by ATC. I was still picking up significant ice at 22,000 and requested lower altitude. The ice was continuous and becoming moderate at 20,000 and the aircraft was accumulating a significant amount of ice. I had to keep descending and while trying to control the aircraft, I got into a left turn bank thereby deviating from the assigned heading. The ice piled on extremely quickly and it wasn't until I got around 15,000 that I finally got out of the ice and got back on course heading westbound. Although I was in significant ice, I believe my attention became too focused on the ice accumulation thereby distracting me from maintaining the heading and also assigned altitude.
1780049: This was a second flight of the night shift, and was unusually busy, because the hospital we are associated with is understaffed because of COVID. We got the call to go to ZZZ, and the weather was marginal, but good enough to get in. We accepted the trip, and flew the RNAV approach to Runway XX. Later, I looked at the approach chart, and it said that the approach was not authorized at night. I think that being busy after a long period of hardly flying contributed to the error, and also that it was XA:00 in the morning. Also, due to COVID-induced rules, we had to wear masks flying, and it fogs up my glasses, making it harder to see. I need to make sure that I check all the notes on an approach before accepting a trip.
1780052: The weather enroute to ZZZ1 wasn't too bad. I would characterize the clouds as scattered around 9,000 to 1;0000 feet with periodic cells of precipitation. Low temperatures meant icing conditions so we avoided all precipitation. Preflight planning weather briefing was in agreement with what we were observing, and we listened to each Automated Weather of the airports we passed.The area was nearly clear skies. Few clouds if any and no observed precipitation within 20 miles. Winds and clouds were moving east, following a cold front which passed the day prior. We encountered one broken cell at 10,000 feet off our left and few clouds off our right. We climbed to 11500 feet and passed above and well clear of that cell within a short period of time.We stayed VFR, away from known icing conditions and moisture. The ride was uneventful. On the ride back, I expected the same weather. Conditions at my destination were VFR with scattered clouds up high, and a nearby airport was reporting the same. I did not check one of the airports enroute. Radar returns on the map showed the same few cells scattered without only light precipitation. In the same region we encountered what I believed to the be the same cell we crossed over in the previous flight. We took note of precipitation left, right and ahead to the left. With a large enough gap of scattered clouds ahead to the right. We continued, and I made the decision to climb up to 10,500 feet to determine the height of the clouds. The clouds which were still only 500 feet in height, were now based around 10,500 feet.I made the decision then to climb to 12,500 feet to cross over them. I knew we were less than 30 minutes from an area which previously was nearly clear skies. Upon reaching 12,500 feet, I started the timer and we continued to cross well above the layer. I would describe this layer to be 6/8 to 7/8 as there were often breaks where we could see ground and see that the layer was not very thick in height. Roughly 10 to 15 miles, 5 to 8 minutes we noticed the clouds were becoming higher altitude, and we were losing spacing from them. We maneuvered around them as best we could, but would need to climb to stay above them and away from icing conditions. I absolutely knew that we would not be putting the airplane into known icing conditions. At this point, turning back didn't seem to be any more promising than continuing on course. We had confidence that the weather in the area was better beyond this cell, and we just witnessed the weather make a change of heart behind us.At this point, I knew that things could turn worse. As contingency, we began direct course for an airport with good weather. In the event that we reached 30 minutes above 12,500 feet or encountered any ice, we would immediately descend through the nearest break and land the airplane.As we continued, the clouds continued to rise. Still broken and overcast beneath us, we were faced with few options. Climb higher, enter known icing, or drop through a break and hope there is not precipitation around which would become ice.Entering icing conditions was not an option, or if anything a very last resort. Hypoxia was our biggest threat at altitude, and we were well aware and cautious of any symptoms. Luckily, I have had the experience of an altitude chamber and know my symptoms and signs. But we had to climb higher to avoid the icing conditions. We climbed up to 14,500 feet briefly and descended back down when able. Then the weather cleared up, the clouds became scattered, and we were able to descend back down to 8,500 feet. A total time of 24 minutes was observed above 12,500 feet. I would estimate that only 2-3 minutes were spent above 14,000 feet. No signs or symptoms of hypoxia were observed. The remainder of the flight was VFR and uneventful.The challenge was the lack of weather reporting equipment to determine the weather enroute, but this is not an excuse. I will exercise more resources such as a phone briefing or additional charts next time. I will also remember to never expect the weather to remain the same. Next time I will remember my favorite motto, Plan for the worst, and hope for the best.
1780055: Passengers X and Y interfering with crew members duties FAR 121.580, refusing to wear a mask and consuming alcohol they brought with them on board the aircraft FAR 121.575.Causing disruption in the cabin.
1780058: Aircraft X was an arrival into PVU airport. He came to my sector from the northwest. I had to vector the aircraft to get him in trail of SLC arrivals. I turned the aircraft in trail of a SLC B752. As I turned the aircraft further north so final turn wasn't so tight, the pilot called the airport in sight. PVU was advertising Visual Approach Runway 13. I cleared the aircraft for the Visual Approach. They turned towards the airport, I shipped them to the Tower approximately 10 miles out when I saw them turning towards the airport. Almost immediately the aircraft started turning further south towards a 8,900 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude descending out of 8000 feet. I called PVU and they said they were talking to him. I asked what they were doing and was advised the pilot stated they were making S turns or something. The aircraft descended to 5,100 feet 7 miles from the airport, elevation 4,497 feet. At that point PVU called stating the pilot had lost the airport and was climbing to 9,000 feet. The pilot checked in with me heading 180 and climbing to 9,000 feet. I said roger. They then asked for vectors to an ILS and I stated I would when they were at Minimum Vectoring Altitudes. I vectored for the ILS with no further complications. I don't really have recommendations on my end. PVU after this incident continued to advertise Visual Approaches. My Supervisor did not want to fill out any paperwork on the incident, so they said nobody did anything wrong and to leave it at that. I felt like this should be reported somehow. The pilot was extremely low a long distance from the airport trying to scud run the Visual Approach. I knew visuals were iffy because when I descended the aircraft to 9,000 feet they were IMC, I turned them and descended them to 8,000 feet (also telling them to expect the ILS) and they called the airport. It's not surprising they were able to call the airport in sight at that point, the mountain sits below and often they can descend slightly and get the airport in sight. What's surprising is the pilot accepted the approach if clouds were that bad, that we didn't 'declare an emergency' for the aircraft when they lost the airport at 5,100 feet in an 8,900 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude MVA, and that the supervisor wouldn't at least want to follow up with the pilot. I truly don't know why we wouldn't want to look at this further.

1780112: After V1 the First Officer and I noticed an odor that smelled wet, damp, musky, wet sock type of smell. This odor did not clear and remained strong throughout the duration of the flight. 1780127: It was an uncontrolled airfield, visual approach, left traffic to Runway 17. Daylight calm winds and ceiling and visibility unlimited. Terrain factors were discussed on our briefing. 1780133: We were at cruise when we noted the right engine oil pressure at 6 (normally around 12). We see that the number was going down, showing that we are losing oil. I started to go through the iPad QRH for an appropriate checklist. While looking, the Captain said 'your aircraft' so I took over pilot duties (it was his leg). He was looking at the Low Oil checklist when the oil qty went to zero, and the Captain decided to just shutdown the engine before it got worse. We [advised ATC] and a turn back towards ZZZ. We ran the engine shutdown checklist. I was flying, he was doing the checklists, radio, and the procedures, as recommended by our training department. We were still over max landing weight, and needed time to run all the supplemental checklists and procedures, so we decided to land at ZZZ and burn fuel to get under max landing weight at the same time. The single engine ILS into ZZZ was textbook. We taxied off the runway, was inspected by CFR, and then taxied to the gate.The Low Oil Quantity checklist is not easily found, as it is not in the index as 'low oil quantity' or 'oil low quantity' and it only reference oil pressure in the index.There was no audio or visual alert, when the oil quantity was half what it was supposed to be. We just happened to catch the small indication on the lower screen, and watched it drop to zero. I don't think we could have caught it any faster than we did. Oil quantity on the Number 2 engine went to 0.
1780134: We had no operational issues whatsoever. This debrief is simply an observation. The SNA Tower closed for COVID exposure and SNA has become an uncontrolled field. The flight experience of the GA traffic that saturates that airspace is typically very beginner level and a Control Tower is essential. Uncontrolled field operations were nothing short of chaotic at that airport, and I really do see a potential for an accident to occur. Simply put, the pilots that are operating at that airport don't have the experience they need to merge with airline operations. The radio was saturated, there was confusion of who's going to take the runway next, a twin engine airplane decided to do a 360 to provide spacing while a commercial aircraft was 4 miles behind them on final. A small aircraft almost took the runway with an aircraft on short final. I saw another small aircraft make left traffic for [Runway] 20R when the traffic pattern is only right. In my professional opinion, I suggest that SNA be only an IFR only operation only during non-towered operations. The amount of threats at that field are countless. Every pilot has to start somewhere and I'm sensitive to that, but a new small aircraft pilot practicing landings, turning an early base while an air carrier is on final (hypothetical example, that didn't happen), has no business in such a busy environment without a Tower Controller there to mitigate risk.Again, there was no event. This is an observation. Lack of traffic management is the factor in a potential disaster.If there is to be no tower at SNA, it needs to be commercial or IFR only operations.
1780135: Passing FL230 in VNAV Climb FMC airspeed was set at 310 KIAS. As airspeed approached Vmo, power was reduced but the airspeed briefly passed Vmo by about 5 knots and for 3-5 seconds. I failed to enter .81 after 310/. As the aircraft climbed speed approached MMO at FL 230. Adjusted speed in FMS but the aircraft was empty and continued to accelerate. I manually reduced the throttles, but not enough we exceeded about 5 knots before we slowed down.New to the aircraft. I had not flown since OE ended. Fly more. But we all know the environment.
1780155: After landing at ZZZ, during taxi from Runway XXL, the intersection at [Taxiway] 1 and 1X was braking action extremely poor. The Captain was unable to slow to turn and drifted through the intersection. With snow plows in the area to clear a route back to Taxiway 1 via 1Y, it was safer to not turn on the snow and ice and request the plows to clear a path to the Ramp.Cause - Poor taxiway conditions. Suggest quicker plowing at the Airport taxiways. Landed ZZZ Runway XXL. Weather was near mins. ATIS was reporting RCC 5/5/5, with taxiways and aprons covered with snow covered icy patches. Prior aircraft reported braking action med-poor. The FO and I ran the numbers, after considering elevation, gross weight, and reported braking, the APS showed plenty of room to brake with a 1X;000 feet runway. After landing, we also reported 'medium to poor' braking action to Tower with the midfield having the poorest braking action. We taxied clear and had to advise Tower of our exit and position as visibility continued to drop. Clearance was given to taxi to ramp via [Taxiway] 2, left onto [Taxiway] 3, cross [Runway] XXR, right onto [Taxiway] 1 to 1Z, report clear of XXR. Taxi was slow as the taxiways had icy patches. We were also advised that the prior aircraft had taken 30 mins to taxi to their gate. On making left turn from [Taxiway] 2 to 3, it was readily apparent that the taxiways were indeed slippery as even a turn at 5 knots still allowed some traction issues. Upon nearing XXR westbound, we noticed XXR and [Taxiway 1] appeared snowed over (not cleared). After advising tower that we were clear XXR, and upon applying brakes for the turn northbound onto [Taxiway 1], it became obvious the braking action was worse on the west side of the airport. Once the aircraft came to a complete stop, we were past the centerline of [Taxiway] 1, or at least the best we could tell as the taxiways were covered with fresh snow (blue taxiway lights were visible). On a dry day with fillets, it would still be doable to make the turn. But with the taxiways in worse condition than I've ever experienced, we relayed to Tower the taxiway conditions and whether we could instead proceed straight via [Taxiway] X1 to X3 as the snow plow trucks were clearly visible on [Taxiway] X2. Tower advised the ground crew to clear [Taxiway] X2 to X3 and cleared us to the ramp.Cause - Bad weather, mainly icing under snow covered runways and taxiways.Allow PIREPs to more directly affect the RCC reported on ATIS. Even after we reported medium to poor braking action after the previous landing aircraft had reported the same, the ATIS was still indicating RCC of 5/5/5. This in my opinion is misleading and contrary to the whole purpose of reporting RCC's.
1780179: ATC said there was rain on the field. There was a B737 flight ahead of us on the approach by 5 to 10 minutes. We were listening to both Approach and Tower to monitor their approach and landing. We discussed holding, prior to the preceding aircraft landing. The preceding B737 reported safe on deck, medium braking, and no issues. They said they broke out 300 feet above minimums, 500 feet above ground. This gave us confidence to conduct the approach and landing. We complied with the wet runway requirements on the 10-7 page (max braking).We were fully configured with flaps 30 by the final approach fix with the landing checklist complete. We were stable at both the 1000 feet and 500 feet calls. Approach was mostly smooth in the clouds with no turbulence. Auto throttles moved very little. The rain was moderate, maybe moderate to high. Once we broke out, we could see the runway the entire time. Wiper were keeping up, but on high. We broke out about 300 feet. Saw some ground before that, so knew we were close to breaking out. Saw the Runway End Identifier Lights at 300 feet and the runway edge lights and center line lights shortly after. Captain called 'approaching minimums' just prior to breaking out and I said I had the field in sight. The auto pilot and auto throttles were disengaged around 200 feet.Landed a little left of center line, but the right main gear was to the right of the center line. Nose was pointed down the runway. Landing was firm to hard. Flare was normal. Raised nose to arrest descent at 30 feet and power was at idle at touchdown. We were both surprised by the firmness of the landing. Nose wheel was set down normally. I thought we might have skipped a little bit, but the Captain did not think so. Maybe we hydro-planed then the tires grabbed. We immediately started sliding left. I don't remember us turning to the left. It seemed we were pointed down the runway but going left. I stepped on the right rudder, but it didn't seem to have an effect. The left main mount went off the pavement on the left side of the runway. It seemed to take a while to get it back on the pavement with full right rudder and full manual braking. With both pilots stepping on full manual brakes, the aircraft did not seem to slowdown. Never felt the brakes grabbing, and with max brakes, we should have felt the brakes grab. I do not know if that Captain was using the nose wheel steering to assist getting it back to the right.Once back on the pavement, we started to veer to the right, but never left the pavement on the right side. Once on the runway, we added full reverse. We put in full left rudder to keep it on the runway. We got the aircraft direction under control, but it was still pulling to the right with full braking and full left rudder. I think the Captain was countering the pull with nose wheel steering. The aircraft was still difficult to slow down.We exited the runway on the high-speed taxiway on the right at a slow speed and came to a stop just off the runway. Tower asked about our position and if we needed assistance. The aircraft instruments, indications and controls were all normal. The only noticed adverse indication was an 'anti-skid inop ' light. The Captain released the brakes and rolled forward a little to check for a blown tire and brake function. All seemed fine so we said we can proceed to the gate. The taxi in was uneventful.On the taxi in we informed Tower that we may have departed the paved surface and there may be Foreign Object and Debris (FOD)on the runway. After shutdown, the Captain got up and checked on the Flight Attendants and passengers. All seemed fine. One Flight Attendant said she was scared while it was occurring, but otherwise no adverse comments. They were obviously a little shaken at the time, but not excessively so. We contacted Company maintenance and wrote up the maintenance items that we knew about. Several of the Flight Attendants were working our deadhead flight back the next morning. Theystill did not seem to have any after effects from the event and were friendly toward us.Maybe the initial left drift was due to the right gear hydro planning while the left gear had full auto-brakes using anti-skid. Once the left gear returned to the pavement, it's ant-skid may have been damaged, causing the veering to the right under full brakes. Leg 3 of a transitioning First Officer on a 4 day 15 hour IOE (Initial Operating Experience). The First Officer had just flown the previous leg and done well. He shot the ILS Approach and flew a nice approach to a very nice landing. During the 3 hour sit prior to our flight we discussed the upcoming flight including the special airport requirements and 10-7 pages. Reviewed the flight plan NOTAMs and maintenance status of the aircraft. Noted the sequenced flashing lights to our planned arrival runway were out of service.First Officer made a nice takeoff and climb out to cruise and we continued to update the weather forecasts on the flight. Reviewed 10-7 pages decided to use max braking for training and for possibility of a wet runway. Worst weather report we saw was 4000 feet broken, light rain, and winds 240 at 8. Briefed the arrival and RNAV Approaches due to winds. We also briefed the ILS. Approaching top of descent asked Center which runway was in use. The ILS was the approach in use. Pulled up the landing data. Approaching with radar on noticed a cell and heard [an] aircraft ask for deviations. We asked for and received direct ZZZZZ on the arrival. Descending to 12,000 feet were cleared for the arrival and preceding aircraft ask for direct to a fix. There appeared to be cells just south of the approach. Approach informed us there was rain on the field, we discussed possible holding when we heard [another aircraft] cleared for the approach.I tuned VHF 2 to Tower frequency to get a heads up on the preceding aircraft. They were cleared to land and reported to Tower breaking out a few hundred feet above minimums landed and reported braking action medium. Approach cleared us direct to a fix and to report on the localizer cleared for the approach. Slowed toward 180 kts., flaps 5 auto pilot on LNAV/VNAV, armed the app mode, made 2,500 feet call, reported established and was told to switch to Tower. Called Tower and reported 9 mile final was cleared to land. I believe Tower also said preceding aircraft broke out at 500 feet and braking action medium. Localizer and glideslope engaged set Touchdown Zone Elevation. Approaching the final approach fix gear down flaps 15 rolled speed back then selected flaps 30 and landing checklist.IMC and moderate rain but little to no turbulence or wind shifts. Passing approximately 1,000 to 800 feet saw ground and lights looking down called 1,000 feet then set Missed Approach altitude. Approach was stable and verified at 500 feet. Called approaching minimums slightly early approximately 400 feet to prepare for possibility of a go around. Approximately 300 feet broke out with Runway End Lights, High Intensity Runway Lights and runway center line in sight. First Officer disengaged the auto pilot and auto throttle approximately 150 to 200 feet. Still raining with wind shield wipers on high but could clearly see the runway environment. Short final dipped 1/4 dot low to try and land in the first 1,000 feet. Heard 50 feet just prior to crossing the threshold then 40, 30. At 30 the First Officer began the flare slowing the rate of descent then began reducing power. Everything appeared normal till the last 5 to 10 feet when it felt like the bottom dropped out to a firm to hard landing. Written up as a hard landing.There was no bounce. Power levers at idle and speed brakes deployed. I have used max auto brakes often due to the demo requirement for Operational Experience. Ordinarily they grab and push you forward in the seat. There was no such sensation other than a feeling the anti-skid was cycling and the aircraft did not appear to be slowing. I believe the nose was pointed straight down the runway and the touchdown had the nose just left of the center line. On touchdown the aircraft began to immediately slide to the left. I believe the aircraft hydroplaned after landing. The First Officer depressed full right rudder with no effect. First Officer was slow to go into reverse so I came on the controlsset max reverse and followed full right rudder yet the aircraft continued to slide left and the left main mount left the prepared surface. I used nose wheel steering to bring the aircraft back toward center line. All this happened immediately after touchdown or so I believe. As we continued down the runway with both of us standing on the brakes the aircraft began to slide toward the right side of the runway. With full reverse full manual brakes and what I believed to be full left rudder it required nose wheel input to keep the aircraft from leaving the right side of the runway. At no point in time did I feel the aircraft nose was pointed at or mostly toward either side of the runway from initial touchdown to stop.As we continued down the right side of the runway the aircraft still did not appear to be slowing normally. Approaching the high speed taxiway on the right side of the runway I elected to allow the aircraft to veer onto the taxi way. We had finally slowed where we were able to bring the aircraft to a stop. We were not 100 percent sure the left main mount had left the prepared surface so we discussed the possibility and the possibility of blown tires. Tower asked if we needed assistance. We did not note any usual indications or issues all instruments appeared normal. With the exception of the anti-skid fault light. I allowed the aircraft to roll forward checking the brakes which appeared to operate normally at slow speed and we had no indication of a deflated tire. I decided the aircraft could be taxied to the gate to deplane the passengers safely at slow speed and was cleared by Tower to do so. We also informed Tower there may be FOD (Foreign Object and Debris) on the runway. Uneventful taxi to parking with good clear area all the way into the gate. Performed the parking checklist then left the flight deck to check on the passengers and flight attendants. No injuries were reported. One flight attendant said she was a little shaken. Conferred with base ops then did a walk around with the contract mechanic. Called Company maintenance and made maintenance write ups.
1780188: I am writing this because I'm concerned about the safety of the ZZZ - ZZZZ - Chengdu Airport - ZZZZ - ZZZ pairing. Starting on date, it was changed from a 4 person crew to a 3 person crew. This is NOT SAFE. I understand why [it] changed is because the duty time went from XX:25 to XX:20 and so only 3 pilots are required. I've flown this trip X times and it's challenging with 4 pilots let alone 3 pilots. The primary purpose of this report is to identify this [pairing] as a safety event. My goal is to provide a corrective measure that will mitigate a safety issue, before it becomes a Incident/AccidentTHREAT: Personal Fatigue. This trip is on the back side of the body clock with a late night pick up out of ZZZZ. This trip becomes close to a XX hour duty day because of the 1:10 ride from downtown [city] to the airport and back. The flight from ZZZZ is often 2 hours longer than the flight coming back from Chengdu due to the Jet stream. Often, because of this jet stream, there is moderate turbulence along the route, making sleeping in the bunk difficult. The Captain must be in his seat for the take-off and landings for both legs. With a three pilot crew, it is difficult coming up with a plan for breaks, especially on the shorter Chengdu - ZZZZ segment. The relief Pilot will hardly get a break, besides being upset for not getting a break, they will be very tired. The relief pilot is one of the most important people in the crew, and you want them alert. They often see threats before the flying pilots do, and can bring the threat to their attention.THREAT: Environmental. Often there is low visibility in Chengdu and ZZZZ this time of year, increasing the work load. There is a X:10 break in Chengdu which is a very busy time for the pilots. We have to flight plan, pre-flight (with full suit) deal with the Chengdu police and customs. With the boarding of cargo (very noisy and moves the plane around a lot with loading of cargo containers) it is impossible to get any rest while on the ground.THREAT: Technical. Chinese airlines are almost back to normal, leaving Chengdu is a very busy time for ATC. I have flown with new pilots that haven't flown China and between operating in meters and the difficulty with the Chinese ATC language it is impossible, and irresponsible leaving the flight deck out of FL180 to go on break. Because of this, it isn't until reaching cruise altitude until the Captain can start his break. Meters can be challenging and causes a lot of missed ATC calls, or repeats. The 4th pilot is a huge benefit for listening to ATC and providing back up!I've flown this trip X times now, having 2 Captains and 2 FO's was by far the safest. It gave everyone a break and each Captain had a leg which helped mitigate stress, and fatigue. With one Captain and 3 FO's it is not nearly as safe as 2 Captains, but it is bearable because you get more of a break. With one Captain and 2 FO's it is impossible to get a break, of good rest.Another thing the company needs to think about, this is China during COVID times. The company realizes the difficulty of a layover in China for the crews. The duty time with 3 crews is reduced to XX hours. There can only be a X:10 delay in Chengdu before an extension takes place. After doing this trip X times I know for a fact that the likelihood of me extending is nil, due to fatigue.The mitigation is simple. Make it a 4 person crew.
1780218: Hand flying on climbout on the SID I exceeded the 12,000 feet restriction at ZZZZZ by a few hundred feet. There was no communication from ATC regarding the exceedance.Cause - Concentration on hand flying the aircraft.With as little flying as we are doing recently it would be better to engage the autopilot sooner and monitor.
1780240: Shortly after takeoff from ZZZ-ZZZ1 both flight deck and cabin crew members detected a mild smell of burning oil or engine exhaust. Smell lasted for approximately 3-4 minutes during climb, with the strongest smell in the aft galley area. There was no fire, smoke or mist present, only a strange smell of what I would classify as oil burning. The fumes did not increase and began to stabilize and finally decrease after a few minutes. The crew began the Smoke, Fire or Fumes checklist but the fumes decreased before the checklist could be completed. The cabin crew investigated all lavs, galleys, and PEDs for any source of fumes. Dispatch and Technical Support Maintenance Control were contacted via Commercial Radio and an ELB write up was made. Since the fumes ended and did not appear to emanate from within the cabin or flight deck, I opted to continue the flight to ZZZ1. The flight concluded uneventfully and a written Smoke/Fume Report was filed with ZZZ1 Maintenance. Subsequently, the Chief Pilot was verbally debriefed. The aircraft was removed from service upon arrival at ZZZ1.
1780246: There is a trend with 737 windshields in that they no longer repel water when operating in rain. In addition, multiple aircraft I've flown have window crazing exacerbating the visual distortion in rain. In the past, I have contacted Maintenance and completed write ups which all resulted in being told there is no mitigation for this. Upon doing some research I learned Boeing used to have, and may still have, a procedure for applying Rain X to the windows. In the interest of safety, I'd like to suggest crazing be polished out of windows in accordance with Boeing's procedures, and some sort of hydrophobic coating be applied. It can be argued that windshields should be written up prior to accepting an aircraft, but there are two reasons this argument doesn't stand. First, a crew may fly an aircraft from an area with no rain to an area with rain and not realize the windows don't allow for adequate visibility until in the landing phase, and second, because I've attempted to rectify this numerous times either with Maintenance or through the reporting process with no changes being made. As far as writing an aircraft up after an event, I know there won't be anything done about it from past experience.
1780247: Climbing to enroute altitude of 33,000 ft. MSL, received an advisory of malfunctioning outflow valve. Eventually, after being unable to establish control of cabin pressure altitude, failure of both automatic pressure controllers and no control over manual control, we requested priority handling and ATC cleared us to a lower altitude where we were able to maintain a safe cabin altitude. Diverted into ZZZ2. ZZZ2 Maintenance discovered on inspection that the aircraft fwd outflow valve had become obstructed from loose insulation material and prevented its operation. We had reached cruise at FL330 enroute from ZZZ-ZZZ1. The ECAM gave us an advisory that the cabin altitude was above normal. I was the PF (Pilot Flying). The Captain worked the problem. We noticed that the cabin altitude was approaching 8,700 ft. and had a trend to climb higher at 50-200 fpm. Looking at the pressurization schematic, we could see that the forward outflow valve was full open and should have been full closed. The aft outflow valve was normal at full closed. We referenced the QRH for all actions. The Captain switched the pressure controller to manual mode and attempted to close the forward outflow valve but it would not close. We discussed diverting to ZZZ2 and requesting priority handling. At a certain point, the ECAM indicated that both auto pressure controllers failed. As we could not control the cabin altitude in any mode, we requested priority handling and asked for a lower altitude. Initially, ATC cleared us to FL 240 and then later 16,000 ft. while we were descending. We were able to maintain terrain clearance and stay above the weather. We were cleared direct to the ZZZ2 airport and set up for an ILS to Runway XXR. We encountered moderate turbulence while we were at 320 kts. This caused the airplane to momentarily overspeed to about 335-340 kts. I slowed the airplane and we continued our descent. We flew an uneventful approach to Runway XXR and landed safely and taxied to parking. Upon inspection, we were told Maintenance discovered a piece of insulation stuck in the forward outflow valve the prevented it from closing. We later continued on with a separate flight to ZZZ1.
1780260: While descending via the ZZZZZ2 STAR into ZZZ, we were given a direct, followed by a heading and a descent to 6,000 feet and a request to fly our best forward speed for spacing. In complying with the instructions, I descended below 10,000 feet at 300 knots. At approximately 9,000 feet, I recognized the error, leveled off and slowed to 250 knots. We continued the flight to an uneventful landing.Although I had gotten a full night's sleep the night before, I was feeling somewhat fatigued by the time we began the flight to ZZZ. I had been flying long days from the previous 4 day trip that started with a very early commute on the morning. Compounding this is the fact that my recency of experience is lacking. I had flown very little during the previous 3 months due to a problem with my international qualifications.I believe that if I had not gotten distracted with the revised clearances from ATC this would not have happened. I had been flying in VNAV, but opened the speed window when a higher airspeed was requested by ATC. My improper monitoring of the automation led me to descend below 10,000 feet at a speed above 250 knots. Unfortunately, my First Officer did not catch the error either.
1780264: We were on the ZZZZZ1 arrival into ZZZ and we had a clearance cross the ZZZ1 VOR at Flight Level 260 and then to descent via the ZZZZZ1. We were in a managed descent with 4000 feet set for the bottom of the ZZZZZ1 arrival. Nearing ZZZ1 I thought that we were high on the profile. I selected open descent intending to level off at FL260 and then continue on profile but I did not select FL260 in the FCU window. The airplane was very light at 113,000 pounds and descended very quickly right through the assigned FL260. I intervened by leveling off and we continued in a managed descent on profile for the remainder of the arrival.My estimation that we were high on the profile was inaccurate due to the fact that the airplane was light and capable of descending very quickly, I had not taken that into consideration. The pilot monitoring was heads down and I did not tell him I was changing the mode of descent from managed to open and explain why I was doing so. Had I done so, he would have caught it. This was my first day back to work after two months of leave. I had prepared to return by studying flows, call, procedures, etc. and had briefed the other pilot hoping to prevent errors from happening.Suggestions - Keep the other guy in the loop. Tell him when making a change especially if he is heads down. Always check the altitude selected when changing modes. Always focus on the next restriction. We were south of ZZZ1 arrival validation completed, arrival briefing completed clearance to cross ZZZ1 at FL260. We were then cleared to descend via ZZZZZ1 Runway XXL. The Captain set 4,000 feet in the FCU. We both verified the altitude selected and the aircraft was in managed decent. I verified the aircraft was on profile and would cross ZZZ1 at FL260. I then updated the MCDU with the new ATIS, did an in range and verified arrival gate and set ramp frequency in the number 2 standby radio. The Captain then said, 'I messed that up', or something like that. I didn't realize the Captain had changed modes to open descent and had descended through the FL260 restriction at ZZZ1. He said he felt the aircraft was not descending quickly enough. We crossed ZZZ1 approximately 1,000 feet low. There was no call from ATC. The Captain then went back to managed descent and we continued to ZZZ without and further incident.Cause - Lack of communication from the Captain letting me know he went to open descent. Captain had been on extended time off the last 7 months.Suggestions - Communication of mode changes in decent to Pilot monitoring. Resetting FCU to next altitude constraint when operating in open decent.
1780276: I wanted to take a few minutes to relate to you my personal experiences during the events that transpired. We were at the tail end of a lengthy four day trip, with the usual holiday related challenges, weather, maintenance, crew-placarding, lengthy sit times, de-icing etc. On the third day of the trip, we were waiting in line for departure on [Runway] XXL at ZZZ, when the tower informed us that the operation was shut down for a 'deep-cleaning' at ZZZ1 Center. Having personally experienced the same the same scenario last year when both the ZZZ2 Tower and ground were shut down for a COVID spread throughout their Tower, it didn't take long for us to figure out the reason for the closure.Like everyone one else in our situation, we opened up the FOM and began compliance with the notification processes for the passengers, the Flight Attendants, and ZZZ Ops. My First Officer (FO) and I immediately began working the 14 hour duty day issue, (FO A was my second FO during the course of the trip, and he had a less restrictive duty day constraint than I did). After nearly two hours at the hold short line, we began the process of finding a gate, with the intent to avoid the prospective government fines levied for lengthy delays. It was the usual chaos, with ZZZ Ops being overwhelmed by this unforeseen event. As we approach the two hour FOM deadline for locating a gate, we were assigned DXX via ACARS. While taxiing to the gate, we made multiple attempts to get guidance from Ops, Ramp, Dispatch, etc., to see what the intent was for the passengers, my crew, and the aircraft. We were unable to get any specific guidance. Following our arrival at the gate, an Agent opened the main door, and told us that the flight would be cancelled. As directed by the agent, the passengers disembarked with their bags. Since we had seen no changes to our crew schedule, nor had we received any kind of communication from crew tracking, we assumed that the agent was correct regarding the cancellation, and as such, we began reviewing our required duty time obligations. Absent any further guidance, we subsequently put the aircraft 'to bed;' and once again we attempted to contact crew tracking, (no luck there). Rather than exit into the terminal, we elected to continue to wait on the aircraft.After 20 minutes or so, a new Agent came down the bridge, and asked me if we were ready to board the aircraft. Needless to say, I was a bit astonished. I asked her what the plan was, and she said that we were going to resume the flight to ZZZ3, ASAP. I reminded her that the airspace was still closed, and that we had not received any contact from either dispatch or tracking, regarding an updated release, and that we would need additional fuel, lavatory/water service, and a resupply of the delay rations that the Flight Attendants had used for the passengers during our time spent waiting on the taxiway. I also told her that both of us, along with two of the Flight Attendants had duty-time issues that we have to calculate and resolve before departure. She promptly replied and asked me, 'Captain are you refusing to board the aircraft?'I immediately realized that this was the standard pass-the buck/assign the delay language, that some Agents use in an attempt to intimidate Pilots. I took several deep breaths, before I stated to her in no uncertain terms, that we would need to at least begin to address the aforementioned issues, before we would be comfortable boarding the aircraft again. Her reply was, 'Captain, are you refusing to board the aircraft?' I answered that until we get some of these issues resolved, yes. What was clear to myself, my FO and the number one Flight Attendant, is that this was clearly an attempt at pilot-pushing. [In my opinion], this Agent had one concern, and that was to make sure that these passengers would become someone else's problem, (namely ours).Long story short, and after significant efforts by all involved, we reconstituted the flight and determined that without further lengthy ground delays that we would likely arrive in ZZZ3 within our respective 14 hour duty day window. We then performed our usual checklists, flows, refueling, new clearance etc.After push-back, start and taxi instructions were received, I made my first mistake of the flight, and turned in the direct opposite direction of ground's instructions on the taxi clearance. It was at this point that I realized I was a lot more tired than I thought. My FO and I discussed this, and we agreed that though we were both somewhat tired, it was safe to proceed, and that we should just take extra time and precautions going forward.Mistake number two on my part was that when ATC changed our departure STAR, we briefed it at the gate, had it up on our iPads, but I had failed to enter it in the MCDU. After wheels up, ATC gave us direct-to clearance to a fix that wasn't on the legs page. My FO quickly realized that I hadn't entered the new departure STAR, and he rapidly remedied it on the MCDU. I was mad at myself for making this series of unprecedented and inexplicable mistakes. Those mistakes continued as we descended on the type of complex STAR with a series of 'at or above' altitude constraints, that confounds the logic on some of the older 'Basic' airplanes.Needless to say, we landed safely in ZZZ3 later that evening. After block-in, I determined that I was within my duty legality, by 20 minutes or so. It had been a very long day. We had departed ZZZ4 that morning before the sun had risen, and we had left the gate at ZZZ for the second time, well after the sun had set. In summary, I had made many embarrassing operational mistakes during the course of the last leg, beginning with my pre-flight, push back, all the way through the descent into ZZZ3. The only explanation for my numerous mistakes was fatigue. In short, I will never, ever, again allow the 'system' to push to me beyond my own personal safety limits. I will take my First Officers counsel more seriously when it comes to considering just how tired we are.Additional factors include that when you consider the cumulative effects of four and five day trips on us, along with a 14 hour duty period, it can be well beyond the average pilot's limitations to safely operate. And while I don't blame the agent personally, (like everyone else, she was just doing the job in the manner that she was trained), and like everyone else she's just under time pressure. As time has gone by at our company, it has become clear to me, that the safety culture at the top of this airline, is in many respects, mostly honored and kept in place, by those who of us, who are at the pointy end of the spear.In retrospect, the main causal factor was fatigue due to a lengthy delay.Two suggestions. The first is that [in my opinion], we need to take into account the cumulative effect of a lengthy four and five day trip on pilot fatigue. The other issue is Gate Agent conduct and verbiage regarding flight Ops as it regards to boarding the passengers.
1780282: After an unplanned diversion to ZZZ, we did not deplane since it was a short wait for our departure to ZZZ1. ZZZ Center closed from XA:00Z-XB:30Z for COVID cleaning. Because we did not deplane no passengers or bags left the aircraft. When completing the manifest we were unsure of how to get the clearance and passenger count without the station uploading via ACARS. I called Dispatch to help with some of the numbers like cargo weight and passenger zones. With Dispatch I could get weight for cargo but not zones, for passengers we were able to get the zones. I told the ground crew that if they could figure out the cargo bag count then we would be good. They tried to look into it but they were unable. So with Dispatch's help we got our manifest and had good numbers. But after we got it from Dispatch the station's last minute help with an ACARS upload caused a mix up with the passenger count and weight discrepancy.I should have printed the manifest before starting the new flight on the FMS. We need a way to maintain the passenger zones and cargo report since we don't have paper reports anymore. The close out report only has the total adults and children but not their zones, and the cargo only has total weight and not which bags go where. After an unplanned divert to ZZZ we did not offload because it was a short wait for our departure to ZZZ1. While completing the manifest we contacted the Dispatcher to get the numbers from our previous flight as they had dropped from our FMS. 1780300: Shortly after takeoff As the PF I experienced intermittent failure of both roll and pitch modes (with no flags, just the disappearance and reappearance in erratic random failures of pitch and roll indications separately) of my flight director during climb through approximately 6,000 ft. Obviously the auto pilot A disconnected and I was unable to reacquire it due to the erratic nature of the problem. Communicating to my FO (First Officer) of the issue, we recognized that his flight director appeared to be operating normally. This allowed us to use autopilot B to reassess our condition. With the auto throttle on with autopilot B the Number 2 throttle advanced rapidly approximately 5 knobs forward of the Number 1 throttle and I returned it to a symmetric condition (the auto throttle disengaged itself as well, Autopilot B still was working). While bringing the throttles to an asymmetric condition to stabilize the thrust setting the Stab Trim Light illuminated, the left fuel pump light of the center tank illuminated (approximately 22,000 lbs of gas in the center tank). We requested to level off at 16,000 ft. and 250 knots and indicated to ATC that we needed a few minutes to access a condition, that we would maintain our flight plan. We executed a transfer of controls to the FO making him the PF as he also communicated with ATC. After consulting the Quick Reference Checklist, it was clear the we had multiple failures not covered by the Quick Reference Checklist. In addition, the MA lights for both Flight Directors were alternating flashing in sequence. I Acquired the appropriate enroute Airinc VHF radio frequency from the chart and phone patched both dispatch and Maintenance Control. With no solution, both Maintenance Control and Dispatch agreed with my decision to divert back to ZZZ as opposed to continuing to ZZZ1 5 hours away in mountainous terrain with automation issues at night and a potential 12 hour+ duty day. FAs (Flight Attendants) were advised, ATC was advised (Requested priority handling and equipment requested to check brakes and tires), company was advised, and an announcement was made to the pax. We used the Landing Distance Normal Configuration chart for our aircraft to obtain landing distance as Saber wouldn't calculate for us the landing performance in our overweight condition at landing (approximately 161,000 lbs). It was my judgement to forego flying for however long it would take to burn 15,000 lbs of fuel to reach landing weight, so I opted to land overweight in light of the distance required from the chart. Once ATC cleared us on a vector heading for approach to land X in ZZZ, I assumed the PF role. Landing was inconsequential and smooth exiting X, X, holding short of X on X while ZZZ Fire assessed our brakes and tires. All normal, proceeded to Gate X. On departure out of ZZZ, the Captain experienced intermittent failure of his flight director. Both his roll and pitch command bars would randomly disappear and reappear without any warning annunciations. Autopilot A disconnected and was unable to reengage as we continued the climb. As the Captain and I began to analyze the situation, we recognized that my flight director appeared to be working normally and the Captain was able to engage Autopilot B. A short period after engaging the autopilot, the autothrottles disengaged as a result of the Number 2 throttle advancing several knob widths forward of the Number 1 throttle. The Captain returned the throttles to a symmetric condition and the autothrottles were reengaged. We had been given a climb to 16,000 ft. and decided to maintain that altitude and our current airspeed of 250 kts. as we continued our flight plan route. The Captain transferred the aircraft control to me, and I kept the radios while he further analyzed the situation and referenced the QRG. I told ATC we were working an issue but required no assistance at this time. The autothrottles once again disconnected as a result of asymmetry and we elected to keep them off for the remainder of the flight. During this time we also notice the MA light for the flight director switches was cycling back and forth from the Captain's side to the FO side. Additionally, the left center tank fuel pump LOW PRESSURE light illuminated with over 20,000 lbs. of fuel in the center tank. Lastly, the STAB OUT OF TRIM light flickered despite any changes in pitch or airspeed. It was clear that we had multiple issues not covered by the QRG, and the Captain quickly tuned the appropriate ARINC VHF radio frequency and established a phone patch with dispatch and Maintenance Control. Since there was no clear solution for our situation, dispatch and Maintenance Control agreed with the Captain's decision to divert to ZZZ as opposed to continuing. This decision was made after the Captain and I discussed the threats involved: automation issues, night landing in mountainous terrain, long duty day. The Captain advised the FAs (Flight Attendants) and made an announcement to the passengers. He then took the primary radio back from me and requested priority handling with ATC in addition to coordinating for aircraft rescue and firefighting to meet the aircraft to check our brakes and tires since we would be landing overweight. The Captain briefed the approach and calculated the landing distance using the Landing Distance Normal Configuration chart for our aircraft since Saber would not calculate at our current weight which was approximately 161,000 lbs. I agreed with the Captain's decision to land overweight, given we had the landing distance, as opposed to holding for almost 2.5 hours to burn fuel. The descent checklist was accomplished, and the Captain took over as the PF once ATC cleared us on a vector for the ILS X. A 30-flap landing was conducted and a normal landing was made. We exited on X, X, and while holding short of X, aircraft rescue and firefighting checked our brakes and tires. With an all normal, we proceeded to taxi to gate X.
1780305: Loss Blue Hyd system. Applied QRH procedures and advised ATC. Approximately 200 nm south of ZZZ we received our first indication of any issue with the blue hydraulic system. In level cruise flight we received an ECAM for HYD B SYS LO PR. While running the ECAM we noticed that the hydraulic quantity was low. The procedure calls for the Blue Electric Pump to be shut off, and as we did so, we monitored the quantity indicator. As it dropped, we received an ECAM for Hyd B RSVR LO LVL. After running the ECAM, finishing the QRH and conferring with dispatch we advised ATC for the loss of redundant systems. We chose to divert to ZZZ for a multitude of reasons including the nice weather, long runways, availability of ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) and the fact that it's a maintenance hub. We immediately received vectors and a descent from ATC for an arrival into ZZZ. The Captain finalized his briefings to both the flight attendants and passengers. We then updated the FMC, applied the landing distance procedure and landing calculations and briefed the descent and approach. We completed the RNAV to [Runway XX], landed and had ARFF inspect the aircraft for any potential hazards or safety concerns. Once complete, we taxied to the gate and completed the diversion safely.

1780335: The left yaw damper was deferred on the initial paperwork. Upon logbook review at the aircraft, the mechanic informed us the deferral was cleared which left us with no MELs. Pre-flight and taxi were uneventful. Shortly after takeoff with the Captain as PF, the L HYD QTY EICAS illuminated, followed by the L HYD ENG PUMP EICAS. As we were handed off to Departure on the ZZZZZ 5 SID, I saw the L HYD SYS PRESS, RUDDER RATIO, and YAW DAMPER EICAS messages momentarily appear, but they quickly extinguished without an associated Master Caution (that I can recall). The Captain elected to leave the Flaps at 5 and bugged the speed back accordingly. Departure cleared us to 10,000 ft., but allowed us to stay at 5,000 ft. to run the QRH checklists. ATC provided vectors in the vicinity of ZZZ while we worked the problem. At the time the QRH was referenced, we had two EICAS messages displayed. The L HYD QTY checklist did not have any action items. The L HYD ENG PUMP checklist directed us to turn the engine pump OFF. Since I had momentarily seen the L HYD SYS PRESS message and the Status page indicated a loss of fluid in the left system (magenta RF), we referenced the L HYD SYS PRESS checklist, but did not perform any of the actions at that time since the EICAS was not illuminated. As we discussed a return to ZZZ, the L HYD SYS PRESS message reappeared, along with the YAW DAMPER and RUDDER RATIO messages, an associated Master Caution, and the SYS PRESS light on the overhead panel. We accomplished the QRH checklist up to the deferred items and advised ATC. The controller passed word of the priority handling to The Company at the Captain's request while we completed the DIVERT ACARS, got performance data with the L HYD SYS non-normal, and set up for an ILS to Runway XX. While on extended vectors, we tried extending the gear normally which resulted in a GEAR DISAGREE EICAS and POWER XFER UNIT Status message. In accordance with the deferred items on the L HYD SYS PRESS checklist, we accomplished the alternate gear extension procedures. Once turned back towards the airport, we attempted normal flap extension from 5 to 15. The TE FLAP DISAGREE message appeared, so we again followed the deferred items for alternate flap extension. I sent for performance data reflecting the new non-normal (L HYD SYS WITH TE FLAP DISAGREE) accounting for the Flaps 20 Vref 20 landing configuration. With the QRH complete, the Captain called for the applicable normal checklists and we briefed the approach with attention given to non-normals (manual speedbrake extension before right thrust reverser deployment, manual braking, etc) and how a go-around would be handled (gear would remain down, flap speeds, etc). Once handed off to Tower, we relayed that we would not have nose wheel steering. Our plan was to clear the runway onto a high speed taxiway to be towed, but if we couldn't stop by XX, we would probably have to shutdown on the runway for tow. Tower told us the runway was ours with CFR standing by and said they had notified Company of the need for tow. We had a jumpseater onboard that is another 757 First Officer. He had plugged a headset into the observer panel for assistance as needed and checklist backup. The Captain queried the crew as to if we thought everything was in order as we approached the FAF. We were in agreement that all checklists were complete and we felt comfortable with the approach and landing. The Captain landed, manually pulled the speed brake lever, deployed the right reverser, and conducted manual braking. He cleared [the runway] where we were met by CFR vehicles. After performing the After Landing flows (except leaving the flaps at 20), the engines were shutdown for CFR to inspect the aircraft/brakes. Once cleared by CFR, the priority handling was terminated and we were towed into Ramp by Company. There was not any visible hydraulic fluid on the aircraft exterior when maintenance first looked. We performed a Shutdown/Secure checklist, conducted aquick debrief with the mechanics to include the wording of the Captain's logbook write up, and left the aircraft with maintenance as we were directed to tail swap and continue to ZZZ1 under a new flight number. As the crew van arrived, hydraulic fluid was leaking onto the ramp from the left side of the aircraft while the mechanic continued to evaluate the problem. I still do not know what the root cause of the problem was and/or if there was anything that could have prevented the loss of fluid in the left hydraulic system. I feel our crew worked well together to safely recover the aircraft despite the backside of the clock showtime and it being our first leg flying together. ATC and CFR were very helpful throughout the event. I think our training prepared us for situations like this (heavy system hydraulic loss) and CRM principles were used to efficiently handle the issue to the best of our abilities at that time. Shortly after takeoff (ZZZ) and passing approximately 1,000 ft. AGL, we heard a caution aural and saw L HYD QTY EICAS Msg. There was also an audible thump sound and slight feedback through the flight controls (yoke). This was followed quickly by L HYD ENG PUMP Msg. We were flying the SID (I was PF) and the aircraft was in LNAV and VNAV. I called for A/P CTR CMD, confirmed the A/P FMA and that the A/P was in fact functioning properly. Initially, we remained on the SID while analyzing our problem. A quick check of the status page confirmed that the left hydraulic reservoir had lost a significant amount of fluid (high of .98 to low of .21, .30 after shutdown). We also had a momentary L HYD SYS Press message that extinguished and came back on later (on downwind). Considering an air turn back likely, I decided to keep the flaps at 5. We requested a level off at our initial altitude of 5,000 ft. We let ATC know we had a hydraulic issue and that we desired vectors for a likely return to Runway XX at ZZZ. With the initial 'aviating, navigating and communicating' complete we agreed that L HYD QTY was, at that point, our first priority. After running this checklist the L HYD SYS PRESS light came on continuously leading to the running of that checklist. Having reached the deferred items section of the checklist we briefly discussed contacting dispatch. I decided that a return to ZZZ was clearly the safest and best option and that direct notification by us would be more of a distraction than help. I decided to advise ATC and request ATC notify 'company' of our hydraulic system issue. This and quick divert message sent via ACARS, satisfied the notification requirement. We had good weather, a long runway (at a very familiar field) and were well below max landing weight. Before beginning the configuration process we completed our normal procedures, including after takeoff and approach checklists, and set up & briefed the ILS for Runway XX. We began configuring and quickly discovered that the PTU was not operating properly, requiring the alternate extension procedures for flaps and landing gear. After requesting and receiving landing data for our non-normal configuration (per checklist), we requested a vector to intercept final. With the assistance of our jumpseater we reviewed all the pertinent notes and made sure we had considered all the pertinent variables, no autobrakes, manual speedbrake extension on landing, R thrust reverser, only after speed brakes extended and no nose wheel steering (differential braking only) on roll-out. We notified approach and Tower of need to have aircraft towed to parking either from runway or after clearing runway (high speed taxiway). I planned to use differential braking to exit the runway, but wasn't sure how effective this would be. As it turned out, aircraft control was more than adequate for exiting via the high speed exit taxiway. After taxiing clear of the runway we stopped the aircraft and coordinated a quick inspection of the aircraft by crash/rescue and a tug to tow us to parking.
1780356: During passenger loading, ramp crew received a motorized wheelchair/scooter for an elderly passenger. The passenger declared that the scooter had a dry cell battery and the key was removed. Ramp agents filled out air carrier battery powered wheelchair form mobility device tag and gave the flight deck crew a copy. Upon receiving this form and observing the type of chair through the cockpit window I became suspicious that this particular type of scooter probably contained a lithium ion battery and the tag was improperly labeled based on the passengers assumption. The flight attendant also made a similar remark and I wanted to exercise caution before the scooter was loaded into the baggage compartment. We decided to have ramp personnel take the scooter out of the baggage compartment and with the assistance of the passenger open motorized mobility device to ascertain the actual type of battery. Upon opening the device we discovered it did have a lithium ion battery with 25.2 V and 11.5 a/h. Based on the formula the battery had less than 300 watts maximum for transport. We elected to remove the battery and transport it in the passenger cabin to ensure we had access do it during flight. A new mobility form was signed indicating there was a lithium ion battery for the mobility device and I made a correction to the CLR [form] indicating the actual battery type.Members of the flight crew were able to spot a potential hidden dangerous good and miss labeled document based on passenger assumption. The flight crew worked with ground personnel to ensure the mobility device was not loaded onto the aircraft until we were able to ascertain the actual type of battery was confirmed and under the appropriate limits prescribed in our dangerous goods manual.

We were at the missed approach altitude and Captain called for the auto pilot on. During this time there was a bit of confusion and the right turn and swapping the navigation displays and setting the new course for the back course was slow to be executed. We turned to the heading too slow and never intercepted the back course. Once we figured out that we didn't intercept the back course we had the Course Deviation Indicator full-scale deflection. ATC gave us a new altitude and a new heading to start the restart the approach. We got vectored around to the Initial Approach Fix to restart the approach and completed the second approach stabilized without any issues. Failure to comply with the approach profile and the missed approach profile. I neglected to call for the First Officer to start our descent. The First Officer noticed my mistake, but by this time we were very high. My initial reaction was to deploy the boards and steepen the descent in an attempt to get back on profile, however I quickly realized it wasn't going to work and we were unstabilized. I called for a missed approach when we were at roughly 11,000 ft. Because we went missed early, I called for the autopilot on once we reached the published missed approach altitude of 14,200 ft. This caused confusion as to who should complete the tasks of spinning the heading knob to the 300 heading, swapping the RTU's, and setting the course to 303. I decided to have the First Officer complete these to stay as on-profile as possible. The first two tasks, the 300 heading and swapping the RTU's, were completed however the task of setting the 303 course was not. This led to ATC querying us about our progress on the missed approach and soon after issuing an altitude alert with an instruction to climb to 15,000 ft. By the time we figured out our mistake we were showing full-scale deflection on the Course Deviation Indicator. In addition to not setting the course, I made the mistake of accelerating to 200 kts. and calling climb sequence once level at 14,200 ft. instead of waiting until outbound per the profile. I should also add that the First Officer MFD failed enroute and this most likely caused a reduction in situational awareness throughout the rest of the flight. Failure to comply with the LOC/DME 15 approach profile, especially the missed approach segment.
1780384: While operating a part 135 trip from ZZZZ to ZZZ1 we experienced a runway incursion while departing on runway 14. The possible incursion happened at intersection Lima and runway 14 which is approximately 9000 ft. from the start of the runway. I am also confident that the other aircraft was a Medium Transport. At the time, the ground and tower controllers were operating on separate frequencies by two different people. Once holding short, we advised tower that we were ready for departure to which he responded for us to line up and wait as he had landing traffic a few miles out on runway 10. A few moments later, he cleared us for an immediate departure to which we thought he was trying to get us out before the traffic inbound for 10 landed. From our position on the runway, we could not see that landing traffic and could only go off what he told us earlier. As pilot monitoring, I completed the before takeoff checks and the pilot flying released the brakes and started to advance the throttles. As we rolled down the runway, I made the call of 'airspeed alive both sides;' and at that moment I could see in my peripherals that an aircraft far down the runway was approaching a hold short at intersection Lima. I called out to the PF (Pilot Flying) that there was an aircraft nearing the runway at a rather quick speed on the right side and keep an eye on him if possible. As we passed 80 kts and were quickly approaching V1 the aircraft began crossing the runway I called for an abort. It is hard to recall how long I waited for a response from the PF, but it had to have been about a half a second to a second and at that point I looked down again and we were passed V1. I called 'V1, rotate' and we took off and started the climbout. When we passed the aircraft that crossed, we were a hundred feet or so in the air and they were turning on to taxiway hotel. We climbed out as usual and once above 10,000 ft. the PF engaged the autopilot, and we began talking about the situation. My first question was if he heard me call the abort, to which he replied that he did. He then told me as he was processing everything, he made the decision that a high-speed abort would have been more dangerous as we were just about to rotate, and the incursion aircraft was still almost a mile down the runway from us. We had switched to Center at that point already and I took the second radio to call back Approach and let them know what happened. I informed the controller that we had a possible runway incursion, and that the Medium Transport was just finishing crossing the runway as we had taken off. They said the supervisor was following up with the situation, had no further questions and appreciated the report. When thinking back to the situation we were guessing that the tower controller wanted to get us out before the landing traffic on runway 10 while at the same time the ground controller wanted to get the Medium Transport across the runway before we took off. Due to runway crossing clearances being given on the ground frequency, we have no idea that was happening while we were given our takeoff clearance while on tower. Finally, we talked about the importance of when a decision is made, to verbalize it so that we remain an effective crew. When one pilot makes a decision without informing the other of that decision, especially at high speeds during takeoff, it is imperative that everyone is on the same page. We continued our way to ZZZ1 with no additional issues.The whole situation is complex and looking back it is hard to think of things we could have done differently. Due to operating procedures at the airport, we had no way of expecting that aircraft to cross in front of us down the runway as we executed out expedited departure. It is most important to maintain proper crew coordination and CRM through communication to remain a safe and efficient flight crew.
1780389: Minimum Crew Requirements were not followed during a crew change while through the Passengers were onboard. We had two through Passengers onboard that were continuing on to ZZZ1. I had a great conversation with them while I was tidying the aircraft. Our D Flight Attendant was the first Inbound Crew Member to leave the plane. There was a female Outbound Crew Member that came on to help clean, as well as a COVID-19 Cleaner from the Ramp. A second Outbound Crew Member came onboard as well, he stood in the forward entry area. I heard the Inbound A Flight Attendant ask him if all of the Outbound Crew Members were at the gate, I guess he said yes because she collected her things walked off the plane. The COVID-19 Cleaner and the Outbound Crew Member that helped us clean walked off the plane as well. I also noticed that there was an Above the Wing Supervisor standing in the jet-bridge. I think he was there because we arrived late and it was an aircraft booked FULL out of ZZZ to ZZZ1. The two through passengers had moved from the back of the aircraft to the front of the aircraft and sat in row two. They were seated below the overhead bin where my crew luggage was stowed, and they were asking me if they could use the lavatory. I brought my things down and thanked the male Outbound Crew Member for stepping onto the plane. I think that all of my other Crew Members had already walked off the plane, and that I was the last Inbound Crew Member to step off the plane. This is the part were the COVID-19 Brain Fog comes in. I'm not sure if the B Flight Attendant or myself was the last Inbound Crew Member to leave the plane. I do know that there was only one Outbound Crew Member onboard an aircraft with through passengers onboard. There was a lot going on during the crew change and I didn't think about having two Outbound Crew Members onboard before leaving the aircraft. Three months ago I had an on the job COVID-19 infection, and I was off work for three months recovering. I still have a couple of the COVID-19 'Long-haul' symptoms such as Brain Fog and some occasional fatigue. I should have made sure that two Outbound Crew Members were onboard before I stepped off the plane.
1780393: Kit was sealed [correctly] but did not have all contents inside. Gloves were only in the pouch with the protective gown and the pocket mask. Only one pocket mask was inside when there should be 2. No gloves inside the kit with the red biohazard bag either. Several other items were missing. The time it took to retrieve the bag from the front of the aircraft to the back of [the aircraft] and to open the kit and rummage through it to find gloves was too long. Also, the [other kit] had an oximeter with dead batteries.Universal precautions are important. Gloves need to be easily found in a medical emergency as they are to be used in virtually all contact we have with a patient. Not every situation requires a pocket mask or biohazard bag. A suggestion would be to place a supplemental bag at each FA jumpseat containing gloves and a face mask. This suggestion has been made before but sadly ignored. The batteries in the oximeter in the [the other kit] need to be changed regularly. Hope someone reads this report and considers my input to avoid problems with future medical events.

1780427: [There is] minimal to no fencing around the airport property of at least 10 feet tall to keep deer off airport property to mitigate someone impacting deer while in the phases of landing and takeoff into Lonesome Pine Regional Airport (LNP).
